#7656. Tiny Grains of Sand Could Reveal What the Weather Was Like on Mars Billions of Years Ago

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (713 w)

Tiny Grains of Sand Could Reveal What the Weather Was Like on Mars Billions of Years Ago

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (713 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scitechdaily

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Scientists have discovered a surprising connection between sand grain size and the winds that shape dunes on Earth and Mars.
  • It has been revealed that the size of a sand grain could reveal how fast the wind was blowing when a desert dune formed, even billions of years ago.
  • Windblown dunes and ripples have been identified on Venus, Mars, Saturn’s moon Titan, and even a comet orbiting the sun.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Scientists have discovered a surprising connection between sand grain size and the winds that shape dunes on Earth and Mars.

It has been revealed that the size of a sand grain could reveal how fast the wind was blowing when a desert dune formed, even billions of years ago. Stanford University researchers have discovered that dunes on Earth and Mars are primarily shaped by winds traveling just above the minimum speed needed to move sand. Their findings offer a way to reconstruct ancient winds using sediment preserved in planetary landscapes.

Windblown dunes and ripples have been identified on Venus, Mars, Saturn’s moon Titan, and even a comet orbiting the sun. Their shapes and patterns provide evidence of prevailing wind directions and how consistently winds have blown, but determining wind speeds has been much more difficult.

In a study published November 16 in Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, researchers demonstrated that the wind speeds responsible for most dune formation are closely linked to the median size of the sand grains. Stronger winds can transport larger particles, while finer grains generally require less force to move.

In a recent development, the relationship depends on a critical threshold: the wind must be strong enough to set sand grains in motion along the ground. Although faster winds can transport more sediment, the researchers found that winds only modestly exceeding this threshold account for much of the sand movement that builds dunes.

Industry observers note that the research builds on a hypothesis proposed by University of Pennsylvania scientists in 2010, suggesting that dunes develop mainly under winds slightly stronger than those needed to initiate sand transport. “Since then, nobody’s really looked at this idea, even though it’s really powerful because it tells you something about the environmental conditions that formed the dune fields that we see on not just Earth and Mars, but on a variety of other planetary bodies,” noted lead author Colin Marvin, who conducted the research as a PhD student at Stanford.

In a recent development, to test the idea, the team examined 30 years of wind observations alongside sand grain measurements from 24 dune fields worldwide. The sites encompassed different dune shapes, sizes, and environments, including Coral Pink Sand Dunes State Park in Utah and the ancient desert landscapes of Namibia.

It has been revealed that for each location, the researchers calculated which wind speed transported the greatest amount of sand over time. Across all 24 fields, that speed was closely associated with grain size and remained only slightly above the threshold required to move the sediment.

The team next examined measurements from a Martian dune field, where the relationship between sand size and the winds responsible for dune formation was similar to that observed on Earth. This held despite major differences in atmospheric pressure, gravity, and sediment density between the two planets.

In a recent development, the results suggest that the same basic process may govern dune formation on other worlds, provided loose sediment is abundant and stronger winds become progressively less frequent. Marvin described dunes as a “great recorder of what happens on a planet’s surface, and particularly the interactions between what’s happening in the atmosphere of a planet and what’s happening on the surface.”.

According to recent reports, because sand grains can survive long after the winds that transported them have disappeared, the relationship could help scientists estimate ancient wind speeds from sedimentary rocks. It may also provide a way to test models of atmospheric circulation during periods when Earth’s atmosphere differed substantially from its present state.

The discovery could help researchers “better reconstruct winds and climates through time, on Earth and beyond,” remarked senior author Mathieu Lapôtre, associate professor of Earth and planetary sciences at the Stanford Doerr School of Sustainability. “It works for modern dunes and for sandstones dating back three billion years.”.

Industry observers note that such reconstructions could be used to investigate the atmospheric histories of both Earth and Mars. According to Lapôtre, the research is already moving in that direction. “Colin is actively working on that, actually. He’s already pushing on to the next steps.”.

The study was supported by a National Science Foundation CAREER grant.

#7655. Republicans tap Moreno and Jack to lead Senate and House campaign arms

Republicans tap Moreno and Jack to lead Senate and House campaign arms

📅 10 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (677 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Bernie Moreno will chair the National Republican Senatorial Committee during the 2028 cycle.
  • Sources indicate that house and Senate Republicans picked their latest campaign chiefs Tuesday, tasking Ohio Sen.
  • In their new positions, both will spearhead Republicans’ push to win back majorities on Capitol Hill after Democrats seized control of both chambers of Congress by flipping more than 40 House seats and at least seven Senate seats in last week’s midterm elections.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Ohio Sen. Bernie Moreno will chair the National Republican Senatorial Committee during the 2028 cycle. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call file photo).

Sources indicate that house and Senate Republicans picked their latest campaign chiefs Tuesday, tasking Ohio Sen. Bernie Moreno and Georgia Rep. Brian Jack with leading the GOP campaign arms for the 2028 election cycle.

In their new positions, both will spearhead Republicans’ push to win back majorities on Capitol Hill after Democrats seized control of both chambers of Congress by flipping more than 40 House seats and at least seven Senate seats in last week’s midterm elections.

Republicans returned to Capitol Hill this week still reeling from their losses but resisted calls to delay Tuesday’s leadership elections. In the Senate, South Dakota’s John Thune was reelected Republican leader without any opposition, while Ohio Rep. Jim Jordan defeated Louisiana Rep. Steve Scalise in a closed-door, secret-ballot election to lead House Republicans next year.

In a recent development, moreno will succeed South Carolina Sen. Tim Scott as chair of the National Republican Senatorial Committee.

“Republicans must enter this next election clear-eyed: the road ahead back to a Republican Senate majority will by no means be easy but the fight has never been so important,” the Ohio senator said in a statement.

Speaking to reporters on Capitol Hill, Moreno described his fresh role as “a hell of a job.” He said Republicans would be “absolute savages” on ending government corruption and continuing “to work for the American people.”.

“I suspect the best tailwind we’ll have is that the Democrats will learn all the wrong lessons,” he told reporters.

Moreno, a close ally of President Donald Trump, is at the moment serving his first term. He first ran for Senate during the 2022 cycle but dropped out of a crowded GOP primary eventually won by JD Vance. Two years later, buoyed by an endorsement from Trump, he won a contested primary for the state’s other Senate seat and went on to oust Democratic Sen. Sherrod Brown that fall.

Brown is poised to return to the Senate after defeating appointed Republican Sen. Jon Husted last week in a special election for the remaining Senate term of Vice President Vance. While Ohio has swung heavily toward Republicans over the past decade, Democrats scored significant wins in the Buckeye State last week, winning several statewide offices and flipping three seats in the U.S. House.

But assuming he runs again for a full term, Brown will be on the ballot in 2028, setting up what’s likely to be a tense home-state fight.

Recent findings suggest that in an apparent reference to the returning Brown, Moreno offered some Washington advice Tuesday: “Make sure you rent. Do not buy.”.

It has been revealed that the 2028 Senate map gives Republican pickup opportunities in a handful of swing states, including Arizona, Georgia, Nevada, Upcoming Hampshire and Pennsylvania. The party will also be defending battleground seats in Alaska, Iowa, North Carolina and Wisconsin. Also on the Senate ballot are races for Republican-held seats in Kansas and South Carolina, where Democrats scored surprise wins last week.

On the House side, Jack defeated Indiana Rep. Rudy Yakym III to become the next chairman of the National Republican Congressional Committee. He takes office after one of the worst elections for the GOP in recent decades and will succeed outgoing NRCC Chair Richard Hudson, who lost his own North Carolina seat last week.

House Republicans face the tough task of cutting into Democrats’ 40-plus-seat majority next cycle. But the party will have a slew of pickup opportunities, given the sheer number of seats Democrats won in historically red territory this year.

Recent findings suggest that like Moreno, Jack was first elected to Congress 2024, leveraging a close relationship with Trump to win an open seat outside Atlanta. He previously was White House director of political affairs during Trump’s first term and was a senior adviser to the president’s 2024 campaign. Over the past two years, he served as the NRCC’s recruitment chair.

Savannah Behrmann contributed to this report.

#7653. How to Make Whipped Cream Perfectly, Every Time

📅 27 Jul 2017 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1415 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Bonappetit ↗ Open Full Page

How to Make Whipped Cream Perfectly, Every Time

📅 27 Jul 2017 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1415 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Bonappetit

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that if you love a low-effort, high-reward kitchen assignment, learning how to make whipped cream is a walk in the clouds.
  • In whipped cream, and in life, the key challenge is knowing when to stop.
  • Industry observers note that to make whipped cream at home, all you need is cold heavy cream, a large bowl, and a whisk.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that if you love a low-effort, high-reward kitchen assignment, learning how to make whipped cream is a walk in the clouds. The only ingredients are time and heavy cream. You can use an electric mixer, a whisk, or a mason jar and strong-armed devotion.

In whipped cream, and in life, the key challenge is knowing when to stop. Desserts like Strawberry Eton Mess or Triple Chocolate Mousse Cake fare best with silky, unsweetened, soft-peaked whip. Others, like this show-stopping Berries and Cream Mille-Feuille, gain structure from sturdier peaks.

Industry observers note that to make whipped cream at home, all you need is cold heavy cream, a large bowl, and a whisk. You can also use a handheld mixer or a mason jar and some elbow grease (more on that later).

If you’re opting for a bowl-and-whisk combo, choose your tools wisely. Cream roughly doubles in volume as you whip it, so use a bowl with three to four times the capacity of your liquid. A large balloon whisk, rather than a narrow sauce whisk, helps incorporate plenty of air into the cream.

Be strategic in the dairy aisle too. Heavy cream and heavy whipping cream contain at least 36% milk fat and can be used interchangeably. Skip anything labeled simply “whipping cream”—or, heaven forbid, “light cream”—which contains less fat and won’t hold its loft as well.

Industry observers note that for a basic batch, start with 1 cup cold heavy cream, which makes about 2 cups whipped cream. For lightly sweetened whipped cream, add 1 Tbsp. powdered sugar; for vanilla whipped cream, add ½ tsp. vanilla extract or paste.

With your equipment and ingredients in hand, there are only five steps and infinite possibilities.

Because whipped cream is usually eaten with or as dessert, you might not need to sweeten it at all. To keep flavors balanced, we tend to serve whipped cream au naturel with Bourbon Caramel Apple Pie or Diner-Style Rice Pudding.

But there are no hard-and-fast rules. Maybe you love sweetened whipped cream, or you’re serving it with something less sugary—like, say, a bowl of tart blackberries and torn mint leaves.

For lightly sweetened whipped cream, start with about 1 Tbsp. sugar per cup of cream. Powdered sugar dissolves easily and contains a little stabilizer (usually cornstarch), which can lend the whipped cream some extra holding power. Some cooks prefer the cleaner flavor of granulated sugar, which takes a little longer to dissolve. Either way, add the sugar before you start whipping.

If you’re gazing at a bowl of fluffy, ethereal whip and thinking, “Could I make this even more enchanting?” the answer is yes. There are two primary ways to make flavored whipped cream: infuse or stir.

Recent findings suggest that kitchen professionals and advance planners tend to cold-infuse. Combine your cream with flavorings like rice (for a creamy Horchata) or bourbon (to take a classic pumpkin pie over the top), then store it in the fridge anywhere from three hours to overnight. Strain out any solids before whipping.

Recent findings suggest that you can also add simple flavorings, like vanilla extract, a small splash of liqueur, cocoa, ground spices, citrus zest, or coffee syrup, before you start whipping. For heavier or chunky additions, such as toasted nuts or chopped chocolate, use a rubber spatula to gently fold them in once the cream is whipped.

Peaks are the shape your whipped cream takes when you pull the whisk out of the bowl and hold it upright like the Statue of Liberty’s torch.

Soft peaks are cloudlike and slump over when you lift the whisk. Stiff peaks stand upright and hold their shape. Somewhere in between are medium peaks, which have enough structure to hold a shape while remaining soft and supple.

According to recent reports, most Bon Appétit recipes, such as these Mix-and-Match Fools, involve whipping cream to soft peaks. That velvety texture is our go-to when we’re dolloping whipped cream atop pecan pie.

But we aren’t always such softies. Medium peaks help this Ginger-Raspberry Icebox Cake keep its shape. And old-fashioned chocolate mousse involves whipping batches of cream into stiff and soft peaks: The former is folded into the chocolate mixture for structure, while the softer stuff tops the dessert.

There’s more than one way to whip.

It has been revealed that by hand: Our preferred method, whipping cream by hand requires the most time and effort, but it also gives you optimal control over its final texture. Even if you use a mixer to get your whipped cream started, switching to a whisk for the final few moments makes it easier to stop exactly where you want.

In a recent development, in a Mason jar: No whisk? No mixer? No problem. To make whipped cream with your bare hands, put a container with a tight-fitting lid, large mason jar, or leak-proof cocktail shaker into the freezer for five minutes. Get the heavy cream very cold and make sure you have ample headspace in your vessel of choice. About one cup of liquid in a four-cup container is a good amount.

Sources indicate that secure the lid and shake it like you mean it. For the creamiest results, a consistently assertive pace is better than intermittent spurts of brute force. When the liquid stops sloshing and starts feeling and sounding heavier, open the lid and take a peek. If it looks underwhipped, close it back up and keep shaking.

According to recent reports, good news for meal preppers: You can make whipped cream hours in advance. Err on the side of underwhipping it during your prep. Store the lightly whipped cream, covered, in the fridge for up to four hours before serving, then give it a few energetic whisks to bring back its bounce right before you dollop it onto dessert.

You can also freeze whipped cream (no, seriously). It takes a bit of effort, though. Line a baking sheet with parchment, then pipe or scoop spoonfuls of whipped cream onto it. Freeze until the whipped cream nuggets are solid, then peel them off the parchment and store them in an airtight bag in the freezer for one to two months. When you’re ready to serve, let them thaw at room temperature for about 15 minutes.

Instant vanilla pudding is the key to luscious, long-lasting whipped cream.

Recent findings suggest that need it to hold up longer? Instant vanilla pudding mix is one of BA’s favorite shortcuts for stabilized whipped cream. For every cup of heavy cream, add 1 Tbsp. instant vanilla pudding mix (call it pastry cream powder if anyone gives you sass) and 2 tsp. powdered sugar, then whip as usual. The modified starch in the pudding mix absorbs excess moisture and helps prevent the cream from separating, keeping it fluffy for up to 24 hours.

For something tangier, sour cream adds both flavor and body. Our Pecan Cream Pie whisks ¼ cup sour cream into 1 cup heavy cream; the sour cream cuts the richness while helping the topping hold its shape.

In any case, your dinner party guests don’t have to sit quietly as you furiously whisk their dessert topping to order. Prep work never tasted so sweet.

Recent findings suggest that if your whip isn’t coming together quite right, don’t fret. Simple solutions abound.

Recent findings suggest that this is probably a temperature matter. Cold cream whips more readily and holds onto the air you’re incorporating more effectively, so it comes together faster—and stays fluffy longer. Pop the bowl, whisk, and cream back into the freezer for five minutes, or into the fridge for up to 30. Once everything is cold, resume whisking.

In a recent development, another possible culprit is the fat content of your cream. Opt for heavy whipping cream or heavy cream over half-and-half or other heavy cream substitutes.

Sources indicate that if the cream is just a little too stiff or starting to look grainy, add a splash of chilled heavy cream and slowly whisk it in. Add more, a little at a time, until the texture smooths out.

Keep a close eye on it: If you whisk for too long, you’ll end up with a bowl of butter.

According to recent reports, editor’s note: This story was originally published in 2017 by Julia Black. It has been substantially updated with latest reporting and additional advice from the Bon Appétit archives, including contributions by Amiel Stanek, Christina Chaey, Rochelle Bilow, and Elyssa Goldberg.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Prepare for fellow guests to go back for seconds when you bring these editor-approved dishes to the function.

In a recent development, there’s an inherent camaraderie in potluck dinners that makes it one of the best ways to feast. And, whether it’s Friendsgiving or an anytime dinner party, potlucks make hosting more of a group effort and a participatory activity. The final dish lineup is often greater than the sum of its parts, thanks to the personal efforts of each of the guests.

Sources indicate that granted, hosts should keep track of what categories (sweet, savory) they have designated or delegated to their guests in order to avoid a smorgasbord of, say, 12 onion dips (although that sounds like heaven to me). Otherwise, enjoy the far more unbuttoned, go-with-the-flow glow of a holiday potluck dinner, which thrives when it rounds up travel-friendly feuilletés, pillowy focaccia loaves, and vegetarian-friendly options.

Below, the Eater staff chimed on a handful of our annual favorites.

Stack more, spend less. Amazon Grocery lets you spend less on all the people who eat your food. Shop Amazon for everyday low prices on groceries and get free same-day delivery with Prime.

Making this appetizer is kind of like making a giant sandwich (positive). The feuilleté is filled with layered, thin slices of ham, Swiss cheese, and Dijon mustard, and given a nice heavy cream-and-egg wash sheen. If I have time, I’ll head to my local cheese shop and see what Swiss varieties the mongers are excited about, but I also love the ease of using a pre-sliced cheese [assumes Sandra Lee voice] from the grocery store. My favorite is Sargento’s baby Swiss for its mild, nutty flavor and creamy texture. I should also mention that this appetizer is easy to transport; you can cut it into a million tiny squares if you’re attending a major party, or several larger squares if it’s a more intimate event. — Francky Knapp, staff writer.

Industry observers note that this is a bit of a project dish, perfect for a competitive friendsgiving or a cold weather potluck with a collection of amazing home cooks. Don’t skip the fried garlic breadcrumb topping, I think it completes this luscious macaroni and cheese. But I’ve also had plenty of friends adjust this recipe for picky family members, just using the incredible bechamel cheese sauce without all the herbs and garlic topping. — Emily Venezky, social media manager.

Dirty martinis have never been dirtier or more ubiquitous (at least not in my elder millennial lifetime) and, like the Caesar, the briny, olive-y flavor has become a format that can be replicated in other edible forms. (Dirty martini deviled eggs, hello.) This dirty martini dip is a perennial fave for the savory snackers; it’s a classic cream-cheese-based party dip but with big flavor. I like it with ridged chips, like Ruffles. I always serve it at my annual holiday party to rave reviews. Would be incredible alongside a caviar service! — Hilary Pollack, deputy editor.

Deb Perelman, Smitten Kitchen; Shilpa Uskokovic, Bon Appétit.

I love to cook, but I’m generally not much of a baker — I don’t generally have the patience for fiddly presentation or precise measurements, and given I lack a sweet tooth, there isn’t a ton of motivation for that to change. The one exception is bread, where I’ve steadily improved my game over the years, and I’ve found focaccia to be a welcome addition to any potluck. I have a standard recipe from a bread-making class that I tend to default to, but sometimes the occasion requires something more festive. In those instances, I turn to variations like this bagel-esque concoction from Smitten Kitchen (a great addition to any brunch spread), or this cacio e pepe twist from Bon Appétit, which adds a bit more zip and character to a standard focaccia recipe. And if you have less of an aversion to fiddly-ness than I do, just Google “decorative focaccia” to see how people much more artistic than I am fashion flowers from tomatoes, rosemary, and onion slices to top their breads — if you really want to show off. — Missy Frederick, editorial director, dining.

Sources indicate that back when I was deep in my potluck moment, a friend at a gathering once remarked, “You love a phyllo pie.” It was then that I sheepishly realized that I did, having brought one to several gatherings this friend had attended. There are many reasons for that. They travel well: You can pack the pie up still in the springform to provide support during the journey. They’re easy to prep: You can make the fillings ahead of time and assemble the day of. And they’re not very fussy when you arrive at your destination: Simply ask your host if you can pop it in the oven briefly, and at this time of year, you can almost always glom the warmth off something else that’s in there.

The recipe that set me off on this course came from Ottolenghi’s Shelf Love. It features cauliflower in a thick cheese sauce, making it perfect for the colder months when people want hearty food. I’ve found that the concept is welcoming to many different vegetables and all kinds of cheese; I’ve swapped in mushrooms and beans, or added caramelized onions or leeks, or taken liberties with Gruyère and greens. At gatherings with attendees who are vegan or lactose-intolerant, I’ve made them dairy-free (store-bought phyllo is generally vegan). In warmer months, or when I’d rather bring a skillet instead of a loaded springform, I opt for an approach to phyllo pie more like this spanakopita-esque recipe from Hetty McKinnon. But the format pairs well with many vegetables, and I always want to make sure to keep the vegetarians at the potluck well-fed. — Bettina Makalintal, senior reporter.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A familiar song can pull you back decades in an instant, and the chemistry behind that rush of memory may hold clues to what separates human minds from AI.

Industry observers note that how does the brain turn a collection of memories into thoughts, emotions, and the experience of being conscious? Scientists have spent decades studying how neurons communicate through electrical and chemical signals, yet the physical processes that allow us to recall experiences, attach feelings to them, and give them meaning remain incompletely understood.

A new scientific review suggests that part of the answer may lie in the complex chemistry surrounding brain cells. Rather than viewing memory primarily as a product of neuronal activity, the researchers propose that interactions among neurons, supporting brain cells, and molecules in their surrounding environment could play a fundamental role in shaping thought and conscious experience.

Dr. Gerard Marx of MX Biotech Ltd. and Prof. Chaim Gilon of the Hebrew University of Jerusalem’s Department of Chemistry present their theory in Consciousness, Memory, and Intelligence: A Mechanistic Perspective. Building on earlier research into how experiences might be physically stored in the brain, they examine whether the chemistry of memory could help explain the origins of thought and consciousness.

Their proposal also raises a question about artificial intelligence: If human memory and emotion depend on the chemistry of living cells, can computers ever develop consciousness simply by becoming more powerful?

Recent findings suggest that scientists have long studied how neurons communicate to form and retrieve memories. But Marx and Gilon suggest that notable parts of this process may also occur in the molecular environment surrounding brain cells.

Their model, called the Tripartite Mechanism of Memory, involves three interacting components: brain cells, particularly neurons and astrocytes; the molecular material surrounding those cells; and chemicals such as metal ions, neurotransmitters, and gliotransmitters.

Sources indicate that according to the theory, these components could allow the brain to chemically encode and retrieve information. Rather than serving only as a support structure, the environment surrounding brain cells may actively participate in memory storage.

It has been revealed that astrocytes, star-shaped cells that interact closely with neurons, play a central role in the proposed mechanism. The researchers suggest that coordinated activity among these cells, neurons, and surrounding molecules could contribute to how memories are formed and processed.

Recent findings suggest that A familiar song can bring back memories from decades ago, complete with feelings that seemed long forgotten. Such experiences show that remembering involves more than retrieving information.

Marx and Gilon propose that the emotional content of memories may be linked to their chemical encoding. In their model, signaling molecules, including neurotransmitters and gliotransmitters, help connect stored information with the feelings associated with an experience.

The researchers also suggest that retrieving and interpreting these chemically stored memories may contribute to the emergence of thought. In this view, memory is not simply a record of past events but an active process through which the brain assigns meaning to experience.

Industry observers note that computers and brains both store and process information, but the underlying mechanisms differ. While computers rely on electronic hardware, biological memory involves living cells and complex chemical interactions.

Marx and Gilon argue that this distinction could matter for consciousness. AI systems can perform increasingly sophisticated intellectual tasks, but their ability to process information does not establish that they experience thoughts or emotions.

For example, an AI system can identify a familiar song and describe the memories or feelings it might evoke in a person. Whether such a system could actually experience nostalgia is a different question.

The researchers suggest that if consciousness depends partly on the biochemical processes involved in human memory, greater computational power alone may not be sufficient to reproduce it.

The proposed model offers a possible connection between memory, emotion, and thought, but it does not establish how physical processes in the brain produce conscious experience.

The authors acknowledge that consciousness remains poorly understood and do not claim to have demonstrated that AI cannot become conscious.

Recent findings suggest that instead, their work suggests that investigating the chemical mechanisms of memory could help explain how stored experiences acquire emotional meaning and contribute to thought. Whether those processes are essential for consciousness remains an open question.

Recent findings suggest that reference: “Consciousness, Memory and Intelligence: A Mechanistic Perspective” by Gerard Marx and Chaim Gilon, 4 August 2026, International Journal of Psychiatry Research. DOI: 10.33425/2641-4317.1251.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Scientists have identified three distinct patterns of brain activity in children with ADHD, anxiety, or both, revealing biological differences that traditional diagnoses often overlook.
  • Brain scans have uncovered three distinct patterns of disrupted brain activity in children with ADHD, anxiety, or both conditions.
  • The findings come from a Stanford Medicine-led study published October 16 in Nature Mental Health.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Scientists have identified three distinct patterns of brain activity in children with ADHD, anxiety, or both, revealing biological differences that traditional diagnoses often overlook.

Brain scans have uncovered three distinct patterns of disrupted brain activity in children with ADHD, anxiety, or both conditions. These patterns do not align neatly with conventional diagnoses, suggesting that children with similar symptoms may have different underlying neurological differences. Some patterns were even detectable years before children received a diagnosis.

The findings come from a Stanford Medicine-led study published October 16 in Nature Mental Health. By combining artificial intelligence with thousands of functional MRI (fMRI) scans, researchers identified three brain biotypes associated with different combinations of behavioral, emotional, and attention difficulties.

According to recent reports, ADHD and anxiety are among the most common childhood mental health disorders, and their symptoms frequently overlap. Clinicians typically diagnose these conditions using behavioral assessments and symptom checklists, but those categories may not fully capture the neurological differences between children.

“The high overlap between ADHD and anxiety actually hinders our understanding of the neurobiology underlying traditional, symptom-based diagnoses,” remarked Yu Zhang, PhD, assistant professor of psychiatry and behavioral sciences at Stanford Medicine and co-senior author of the study.

“We wanted to know whether the biological differences among children with ADHD and anxiety follow the diagnostic labels used in the clinic,” Zhang stated.

Recent findings suggest that the researchers found that children diagnosed with ADHD, anxiety, or both could belong to any of the three biotypes. Although particular brain patterns were more common with certain diagnoses, no biotype corresponded exclusively to a single disorder.

The researchers identified three neurological profiles, each associated with a distinctive combination of symptoms:.

Each child belonged to just one biotype (each child was in only one biotype), but the three patterns appeared across all conventional diagnostic categories.

The model also identified two underlying dimensions of brain dysfunction: cognitive-behavioral dysfunction and emotion-attention dysfunction. Each involved different networks of brain regions, with the three biotypes reflecting distinct combinations of these disruptions. The findings suggest that differences in how brain circuits communicate may help explain variations in children’s symptoms.

The researchers drew on the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development study, a long-term investigation of more than 11,000 U.S. children who entered the project at ages 9 or 10.

Sources indicate that their analysis included 3,508 children initially diagnosed with ADHD, anxiety, or both; 693 children who received one or both diagnoses later; and 1,947 children who never received either diagnosis. The researchers also examined brain scans from 224 children with ADHD or anxiety in the separate Healthy Brain Network study to validate their findings.

Recent findings suggest that an AI model examined functional connectivity, which describes how activity in different brain regions is coordinated. By combining these measurements with diagnostic records and cognitive and behavioral assessments, the researchers identified brain connectivity patterns associated with ADHD and anxiety that differed from those seen in children without either diagnosis.

The researchers also detected the biotypes in initial brain scans from children who had not yet been diagnosed with ADHD or anxiety but developed one or both conditions later. This suggests that certain patterns of brain connectivity may emerge before symptoms lead to a clinical diagnosis.

Industry observers note that “We think this means we may be able to use the biotypes as an early indicator of these conditions,” Zhang remarked. He identified the early appearance of these patterns as one of the study’s most surprising results.

“It could help us provide more timely intervention for these conditions and slow down or, we hope, even reverse their progression.”.

The findings do not establish that brain scans can reliably predict which individual children will develop ADHD or anxiety. Further research is needed to determine whether the biotypes can serve as clinically useful biomarkers for early identification.

Beyond early detection, the researchers hope the findings could eventually help clinicians select treatments based on a child’s underlying brain activity rather than relying entirely on symptoms.

Current treatment decisions often involve considerable trial and error, particularly when medications do not produce the expected improvement.

“When doctors prescribe a fresh medication, it can take quite a long time, a couple of weeks or months, to see a response,” Zhang said. “If the first medication doesn’t work, they switch to a different one,” a process that can be costly, slow, and frustrating for families.

Recent findings suggest that zhang does not expect brain biotypes to replace existing diagnostic methods. Instead, he envisions using them alongside conventional assessments to provide a more detailed picture of each child’s condition.

Future clinical trials could investigate whether particular treatments improve the brain connectivity abnormalities associated with each biotype. Researchers could then examine whether these neurological patterns help predict treatment responses.

“We want to find biomarkers that can really inform the right treatment at the right time,” Zhang noted.

Reference: “Deep learning of brain–behavior dimensions identifies transdiagnostic biotypes in youth with ADHD and anxiety disorders” by Yong Jiao, Xiaoyu Tong, Gregory A. Fonzo, Ian H. Don’t let cocktails fall by the wayside in the flurry of holiday dinner prep — these drinks make the party.

In the endless iterating that goes into devising a menu for a holiday dinner, there’s one finishing touch that really makes or breaks the vibe: the drinks. The wine and beer will, of course, flow — at these festive events, a bottle of Champagne or sparkling rose is likely to make an appearance — and it’s easy enough to throw together a gin and tonic or screwdriver. But nothing makes a holiday gathering feel chic, totally put together, gloriously intentional, like a batch cocktail, made-to-order martini, or gussied-up punch.

In a recent development, now, we all have our preferences when it comes to strength, spirit, and format. The host’s bandwidth is also a consideration; do you want to make a lot of one thing, or tailor your options to your guests’ preferences? Those questions are for you to answer, but our staff is here to help by providing this rundown of six tried, vetted, and loved drinks to make at your own celebration.

Below, find Eater editor-approved recipes for cocktails that will add the most festive of feelings to every holiday gathering.

Industry observers note that stack more, spend less. Amazon Grocery lets you spend less on all the people who eat your food. Shop Amazon for everyday low prices on groceries and get free same-day delivery with Prime.

It has been revealed that I host a holiday potluck with a core group of friends in December, and one of my favorite potential additions is whatever punch that drinks columnist M. Carrie Allan is cooking up over at the Washington Post. A favorite from 2022 was a meringue-topped citrus punch, featuring blood orange, Aperol, and a dramatic meringue topping. Mentioned topping adds undeniable flair and drama to the presentation, but if you’re daunted by the idea, the punch itself is still a festive, not-too-sweet drink to serve, celebrating winter citrus. —Missy Frederick, editorial director, dining.

Meaghan Dorman’s modern classic is a favorite year-round, but there’s something about the holidays that calls for Scotch. No shade to the nog freaks, but the subtly spiced sour is a pleasant counterpoint to the onslaught of holiday food and beverage maximalism. No need to break out the single malt either, your dusty bottle of Dewars or Monkey Shoulder will do just fine. —Allison Hamlin, director of network development.

The French 75 — the effervescent classic cocktail made with gin, Champagne, and lemon — is already one of my easy-drinking favorites, and I like it even better in punch form, accented with an aesthetically pleasing ice block of cheery lemon slices. What makes it 77 instead of 75? The substitution of St-Germain (or any elderflower liqueur) for simple syrup, adding just a tiny touch of herbal complexity. It’s perfect for Fresh Year’s Eve, but just as refreshing at Thanksgiving or any other holiday table where you want something light and zesty. —Hilary Pollack, deputy editor.

As the de facto cook for Thanksgiving, I like to keep the drinks options simple so I can focus on food prep. This cocktail recipe requires only two ingredients, doesn’t require pre-batching, and is easy enough for people to pour on their own. I also like how it uses Basque cider, which is drier than the typical ciders, so it’s not too sweet while still tapping into that cozy fall feeling —Rayna Rossitto, editor, branded content.

I grew up guzzling Broguiere’s eggnog, but I love the more tropical combination of rich, creamy coconut milk, rum, and cinnamon in coquito; the Puerto Rican holiday cocktail was first described to me as “eggnog, if it went on vacation,” and I haven’t looked back since. This version is by bartender Shannon Ponche, and gets extra dressed up in spice for the holidays with the addition of a homemade cinnamon simple syrup, a woody, nutty oloroso sherry, and a splash of spiced Braulio. —Francky Knapp, staff writer.

Industry observers note that there are two schools of thought on a post-dinner drink: You could go for a bracing digestif to “aid digestion,” or you could indulge in a liquid dessert that swaddles you in sugar, fat, and everything nice. I’m notoriously bad at decision making, so I tend to split the difference with an eggy flip tinged with something bitter. Together, a whole egg and syrup (in this case honey syrup) build a comforting base, while an entire 1.5 ounces of cocktail bitters (as opposed to the usual dash or two) ensure you don’t entirely fall asleep in your glass. Angostura is a great option, delivering some classic holiday spice, but any style of cocktail bitters would probably work, as would an amaro. Dry shaking (shaking the liquid ingredients without ice) is key to achieving a frothy texture, and don’t forget the half-ounce of whiskey, which punches up the rest of the flavors. —Nick Mancall-Bitel, editor.

In a recent development, several members of my husband’s family are Manhattan drinkers, so I expect that my decision to serve the Grandfather cocktail during Thanksgiving appetizers will be a hit. It’s a riff on the classic drink with a hint of fall, courtesy of the addition of Applejack, an apple brandy. It’s smooth and well-balanced. It’s also quite boozy, so I’ll probably look for a slightly lower-proof option to tide us over after that initial round. I’ve had success with a bourbon and ginger ale bar (with various sodas and mixers) in the past, as well as Smitten Kitchen’s fall sangria; maybe this year we’ll go with her (okay, still pretty boozy) apple cider Old Fashioneds. —Missy Frederick, cities director.

Scientists Find That Mice, Not Deer, Hold a Major Clue to Lyme Disease Risk

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1488 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scitechdaily

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that A 35-year study reveals that mice, acorns, and unexpected environmental forces hold surprising clues to predicting Lyme disease risk.
  • Recent findings suggest that diseases transmitted by ticks are becoming increasingly common across the United States.
  • Industry observers note that for more than 35 years, scientists at the Cary Institute of Ecosystem Studies in Millbrook, New York, have investigated the complicated relationships among oak trees, acorns, rodents, predators, ticks, and climate.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that A 35-year study reveals that mice, acorns, and unexpected environmental forces hold surprising clues to predicting Lyme disease risk. A remarkable 35-year study is challenging long-held assumptions about Lyme disease, revealing that mice, acorns, and even extreme weather influence tick populations in unexpected ways. One of the biggest surprises is that deer, often associated with the spread of Lyme disease, may be less important in predicting the numbers of dangerous ticks than researchers once believed.

Recent findings suggest that diseases transmitted by ticks are becoming increasingly common across the United States. Lyme disease is the most frequently reported, with nearly 500,000 people diagnosed annually. The infection is caused by the bacterium Borrelia burgdorferi, which typically reaches humans through bites from infected blacklegged ticks. Antibiotics can successfully treat Lyme disease, but without treatment, the infection may spread to the joints, heart, and nervous system. Some patients also experience symptoms that persist over time.

Industry observers note that for more than 35 years, scientists at the Cary Institute of Ecosystem Studies in Millbrook, New York, have investigated the complicated relationships among oak trees, acorns, rodents, predators, ticks, and climate. Their goal has been to understand how these interconnected factors influence the risk of Lyme disease in humans.

A fresh study published in Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences highlights nine particularly unexpected discoveries from this decades-long research effort. Several findings challenge conventional thinking about how tick populations grow and what determines the likelihood of disease transmission.

“On balance, these surprises have enriched our knowledge of this system, helping us to inform management of tick-borne disease risk,” mentioned lead author Richard Ostfeld, a disease ecologist at the Cary Institute who leads the research program alongside Shannon LaDeau.

According to Ostfeld, the unusually extensive dataset has been essential for separating meaningful ecological patterns from random fluctuations and misleading correlations. Relationships that seem convincing over a few years can look very different when examined across several decades.

Sources indicate that “Studies of this depth and length are incredibly rare,” said LaDeau. “This research has followed an ecological community — including oak trees, mammals, and microorganisms — examining how interactions like predation, parasitism, and competition shape the system over time. The evolution of understanding summarized in this paper is something you simply cannot get without such a long-term and system-focused study.”.

When scientists first identified Lyme disease in the United States during the 1980s, white-tailed deer were considered a likely factor in the disease’s spread. Hunters frequently encountered deer carrying large numbers of adult ticks, suggesting that deer populations might strongly influence how many ticks would emerge in subsequent seasons.

In a recent development, deer do not directly transmit the Lyme disease bacterium to ticks. However, they provide blood meals for adult female ticks, allowing those ticks to reproduce. Researchers therefore suspected that larger deer populations would support more egg-laying females and ultimately produce more young ticks.

Decades of field observations have complicated that theory. At the Cary Institute’s 2,000-acre forested research site in Dutchess County, Latest York, researchers found no statistically significant relationship between deer abundance and the number of nymphal ticks. Nymphs are immature ticks and represent the life stage most likely to transmit Lyme disease to humans.

“We had detected a weak positive relationship between deer and subsequent nymph abundance over short subsets of the data,” remarked Ostfeld, “but the whole data set in its entirety demonstrates no such thing.”.

Although deer numbers did not reliably predict nymph populations, mouse numbers told a different story.

The researchers discovered that years with abundant mice were followed by an approximately 40% increase in nymphal ticks the next year. This relationship makes white-footed mice particularly notable to understanding changes in tick populations.

These small rodents provide an excellent food source for blacklegged tick larvae. They are also highly effective at transmitting Borrelia burgdorferi to the young ticks feeding on them.

Sources indicate that once infected as larvae, ticks can carry the bacteria into their next developmental stage. When they feed again as nymphs, they can transmit the infection to humans.

One of the study’s most striking discoveries involves something seemingly unrelated to human disease: acorns.

Oak trees occasionally produce unusually large quantities of acorns in a synchronized event known as acorn masting. The sudden abundance of food benefits mice, allowing their populations to increase during the following year.

That population boom then provides more feeding opportunities for young ticks. As a result, the researchers found that a particularly large acorn harvest can reliably predict increased numbers of nymphal ticks two years later.

This creates a remarkable ecological chain reaction in which events beginning in the forest canopy can influence tick populations years afterward.

The relationship between mice and Lyme disease produced another unexpected finding.

Because mice are so effective at transmitting B. burgdorferi, the scientists initially assumed that years with more mice would also have a higher percentage of infected nymphal ticks. Early observations appeared to support that prediction.

However, the connection gradually disappeared as the research team accumulated more years of data.

“It kept me up at night,” said Ostfeld, “because it meant that my understanding of how the system works was incomplete or wrong.”.

Further investigation pointed toward a more complicated explanation involving other animals that provide blood meals for ticks.

When mouse populations increase, populations of other potential hosts, including squirrels, skunks, and opossums, may also rise. Most of these animals are much less effective at transmitting the Lyme disease bacterium to ticks.

Consequently, a greater share of ticks feeding on these alternative hosts can reduce the overall percentage of infected nymphs, even when mice are plentiful.

Recent findings suggest that “So the infection prevalence in the nymphs really depends on how all the larval tick meals are distributed across all the hosts,” explained Ostfeld. “It would have been convenient if one host predicted that for us, but that has not been the case.”.

The findings demonstrate why predicting the total number of ticks is different from predicting how many of those ticks carry Lyme disease.

Another surprise emerged when the researchers compared laboratory experiments with conditions in the wild.

In a recent development, previous laboratory studies had suggested that extreme heat and severe cold could kill blacklegged ticks. Yet observations in natural habitats revealed that the insects were far more resilient than expected.

The researchers suspect that ticks escape dangerous temperatures by moving deeper into the soil or hiding beneath fallen leaves, where conditions are less extreme.

However, temperature still appears to influence tick populations in key ways. The team found that years with generally warmer conditions tended to be followed by fewer nymphal ticks than usual.

This creates an intriguing contradiction. Warmer years typically benefit mice, which should help support larger tick populations, yet the researchers have not observed a corresponding overall increase in nymphs.

Understanding how these opposing effects interact remains an vital focus of the ongoing research.

Together, the discoveries suggest that Lyme disease risk is shaped by a complicated network of ecological relationships, but one that contains patterns scientists can use to make predictions.

Recent findings suggest that the strong connection between mouse abundance and future tick numbers could help public health officials anticipate periods of elevated risk. Likewise, recognizing that deer abundance is not a reliable predictor of nymph populations at the study site, and that severe winter weather may not substantially reduce tick numbers, could improve disease prevention strategies.

Important questions remain, particularly about how climate change will influence the relationships among ticks, rodents, oak trees, and other wildlife.

Industry observers note that “You would expect that a warming climate, which makes life better for the mice, would eventually make life better for the ticks, but we have not seen that so far,” mentioned Ostfeld. “We need to know what to expect from the different manifestations of climate change, which are sometimes warmer and drier, and sometimes warmer and wetter. The time of year when it’s very warm also matters to ticks, oaks, and acorn production.”.

Since the monitoring program began in 1991, its research site in Dutchess County has undergone numerous environmental changes, including shifting climate conditions, changes to the surrounding landscape, and the arrival of invasive species.

Recent findings suggest that the scientists intend to continue tracking how ticks and the animals they depend on respond to these changes. By extending an already exceptional research record, they hope to uncover more of the hidden ecological patterns that could help predict Lyme disease risk and protect human health in the years ahead.

Industry observers note that reference: “The ecology of Lyme disease: Long-term data, surprises, and a synthesis” by Richard S. Ostfeld, Shannon L. LaDeau, Kelly Oggenfuss, Charles D. Canham, Michael Fargione, Raymond J. Winchcombe and Felicia Keesing, 17 August 2026, Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences. DOI: 10.1073/pnas.2610907123.

  • “We hired you to fix the Biden economy and you failed.” Pretty simple.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that A group of latest senators-elect gather for a photo in Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer’s office in Washington on Monday. The large class of incoming Democratic senators was propelled by votes from independents, Winston writes. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call).

According to recent reports, once more, independents were the decisive factor in what amounts to the Republicans’ midterm disaster that was both broad and deep. No one who reads this column should have been surprised that this growing segment of the electorate became the equivalent of the “deciders-in-chief” who used their vote to send a tough message to the president and his party.

“We hired you to fix the Biden economy and you failed.” Pretty simple.

According to the exit polls, Democrats won independents by an astonishing 22 points. If this holds, it will be the largest margin in the history of exit polling, beating the Republican margin in 2010 of 19 points. For Republicans, this is the fifth consecutive election losing independents.

It was the size of the GOP defeat with independents that put the number of states and congressional districts into play, districts that President Donald Trump won in 2024, many by double digits.

Sources indicate that independents made up 33 percent of the electorate; Democrats were at 35 percent and Republicans at 32 percent. This is the second consecutive election where independents were a larger part of the electorate than one of the major parties. It also shows that while independents may not have been enthused about voting, they indicated up.

According to recent reports, looking at the 13 battleground Senate races, which now include Mississippi, Democrats won independents in all of them by double digits, and 10 of them by 20 points or more. The independent vote allowed Democrats to overwhelm significant Republican Party ID advantages in many red states and districts.

In a recent development, for example, in Kansas (exit poll not final), Republicans had a 17-point party advantage, but lost independents by 33. Incumbent Sen. Roger Marshall went down with a 5-point loss. In South Carolina, Republicans had a 14-point party advantage, but lost independents by 31 points. A liberal activist Democrat beat a neophyte Republican candidate, appointed Sen. Darline Graham, by 4 points.

In a recent development, despite Texas Republicans’ 5-point party ID advantage, Ken Paxton lost independents by 31 points and lost the Senate race by a huge 12 points. It goes without saying that voters in Texas shocked Republicans by not only rejecting the president’s primary choice for Senate, but taking down all Republicans in statewide races.

Sources indicate that overall, Republicans lost six states with key Senate races where Trump won by double digits in 2024, with Mississippi being a potential seventh. In the House (with 7 races yet to be called at the time of this writing), Democrats have won 56 congressional districts that Trump carried in 2024, along with carrying all 201 districts that Harris won.

In a recent development, clearly, Republican operatives, consultants and the media missed the boat when it came to evaluating the viability of House races. Using the 2024 Trump-Harris race results to assess the safety or vulnerability of a particular seat proved to be the wrong context.

It has been revealed that in the spring, I was beginning to see some danger signals in our polling and in public surveys that raised questions for me about just how many House seats were actually in play, fearing perhaps far more than anyone was predicting. By early summer, I decided to undertake a different analysis on the state of current races using the 2020 Trump-Biden results by congressional district. The research found a much larger number of GOP seats could be vulnerable. In the end, the analysis proved to be right. Democrats won all of the 220 districts that Biden carried, and at least 37 seats that Trump won.

According to recent reports, according to the exit polls, the independent vote, not surprisingly, was largely driven by the economy, their top issue concern. Much to the detriment of Trump and the Republicans, 80 percent of independents thought the economy was not good/poor, versus 20 percent who thought the economy was excellent/good. In terms of inflation, 82 percent noted it had been a severe or moderate hardship for them, and 89 percent said the cost of living was a crucial or major factor in how they voted for Congress.

Recent findings suggest that the president and his party got the blame. Looking at specific policies, 71 percent of independents thought that Trump’s tariff policies had hurt the national economy, and more broadly, 72 percent remarked his policies had worsened economic conditions in the country. As a result, Trump’s overall job approval among these voters was 29 percent approve with 71 disapproving; 59 percent strongly disapproving. These extraordinarily bad numbers topped even Biden’s worst job approval numbers.

Recent findings suggest that trump’s decision to ask voters to “pretend I’m on the ballot,” was, in retrospect, a strategic miscalculation. It was a mistake to tell voters that the economy was in great shape when it was clear the majority of people were very unhappy when it came to inflation — the rising cost of gas and groceries.

A little empathy on economic complications and a lot better explanation of why the Iran conflict was crucial to national security and worth the economic sacrifice would have gone a long way to minimizing the size of the GOP defeat.

Sources indicate that neither happened, and Republicans were overwhelmed by a blue tsunami almost nobody saw coming. Still, despite the size of the Democrats’ win, they would be wrong to see this as an ideological mandate of any sort. The exit polls showed that the electorate remains center-right. Moderates are the largest component at 41 percent, but conservatives still outnumber liberals by a 33-26 margin.

Sources indicate that independents have a negative view of both parties. Their view of Republicans is 32 percent favorable and 68 percent unfavorable. However, Democrats are not far behind, at 42 percent favorable and 58 percent unfavorable.

According to recent reports, at a policy level when independents were asked which party was better able to handle the economy, 41 percent stated the Democratic Party, 28 percent said the Republican Party, and 30 percent said neither. Both parties are well short of a majority. This reflects the fact that the electorate still negatively remembers the Biden economy, but also believes that Republicans didn’t fix it as they promised two years ago.

Industry observers note that democrats would be wise to moderate and not continue down the increasingly extreme progressive path. Republicans and the president need to take a hard look at their own failings and understand that when it comes to voters, especially independents, all the money in the world is no substitute for good candidates with real solutions.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A telescope tasked with creating the largest-ever 3D map of the universe is making good on its promise.

Sources indicate that on Thursday (Nov. 12), the European Space Agency (ESA) shared the first major data release from its Euclid space telescope, including observations of more than 900 million galaxies and 60 million black-hole-powered light sources in the early universe.

Industry observers note that "These are far more than beautiful pictures; today marks a scientific milestone in our study of the cosmos," Carole Mundell, ESA's director of science, said in a statement. "This major Euclid data release represents the largest space-based survey of its kind, laying the foundation of future discovery.".

It has been revealed that captured over 13 months, this cornucopia of data covers a slice of sky about 9,500 bigger than the full moon — about 14% of the total sky area that Euclid will survey on its planned six-year mission. Each object in the survey is like a "puzzle piece," with its specific light signature, or spectrum), offering clues about its composition and distance from Earth, according to ESA.

Scientists can now start using the 1.7 million gigabytes of Euclid data to slot those objects into a 3D model of the universe and begin to map out the vast cosmic web that underlies all galaxies. But the data release also includes some stunning space images, which you can enjoy immediately. Here are some of the highlights.

A mosaic of 9 gravitational lenses spotted by the Euclid telescope.

In a recent development, gravitational lenses are nature's biggest magnifying glasses. These "Einstein rings" ‪—‬ named after Albert Einstein, who predicted their existence — occur when exceptionally massive objects, like large galaxies, bend the fabric of space-time. This cosmic curvature causes the light emitted by objects behind them to appear magnified, distorted and sometimes duplicated.

Recent findings suggest that in its first data release, Euclid has discovered more than 15,000 strong gravitational lensing candidates. These cosmic lenses enable astronomers to get much clearer views of the deep universe than any telescope could possibly see on its own.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

"Over 10 years ago, we forecast that Euclid would revolutionise the field of strong lens discovery," Natalie Lines, a Euclid Consortium member working at the University of Portsmouth in the UK, said in the statement. "That day is finally here.".

The "grand design" spiral galaxy M81, imaged by Euclid.

The Messier 81 galaxy (seen on the right) is one of the brightest in the sky. With fully developed spiral arms stretching to its bright core, M81 is known as a "grand design spiral" galaxy.

While M81 is relatively close to Earth and can be seen with a good pair of binoculars, Euclid's field of view captures it alongside the elliptical galaxy NGC 3077 (bottom left) and crisp clouds of interstellar dust.

The ring galaxy NGC 1291, imaged close up at Euclid's highest resolution.

Among the nearly 1 billion galaxies charted by Euclid is NGC 1291, also called the Golden Eye galaxy. The galaxy is located 33 million light-years from Earth, and Euclid shows a close-up view of it here at the telescope's highest resolution, according to ESA.

Ring galaxies like this contain a central bulge disconnected from a surrounding ring of stars; astronomers think these galaxies form when a smaller galaxy plunges through the middle of a larger one.

The first piece of the Euclid Wide Survey, covering about 14% of the total sky area that the telescope plans to survey.

Industry observers note that this image indicates the entire sector of the Euclid Wide Survey, the telescope's mission to map vast swatches of the northern sky. The Wide Survey is accompanied by the Euclid Deep Survey, which will spend about 10% of the telescope's observing time taking repeated observations of three relatively small spots of sky, according to ESA.

With about 85% of its survey left to go, Euclid is on track to collect one of the most comprehensive datasets of the universe ever. Now, it'll be up to the scientific community to make good use of those observations and find something extraordinary.For more stunning space images, check out our Space Photo of the Week.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that black holes remain some of the most mysterious and awe-inspiring celestial objects ever studied. This primarily comes from the fact that they literally canât be observed unless they interact with something in its surrounding environment, most notably a star. Adding to their mystery, several types of black holes exist, including free-floating black holes that drift independently throughout space, stellar-mass and are produced from exploding stars, and supermassive black holes that exist at the center of galaxies like our own. But arguably one of the most mind-blowing mysteries about black holes is figuring out what happens when they collide, and even merge.

In a recent development, now, a team of more than 70 researchers might be one step closer to solving this decades-long conundrum as they used a combination of computer models and a literature review to analyze how black holes behave when they collide, specifically focusing on a well-known âringingâ phenomenon that occurs when black holes collide and merge. In a recent study published in Classical and Quantum Gravity, the primary motivation behind the study was to advance black hole research by establishing a long-known method called black hole spectroscopy from a theoretical concept to a practical one. Black hole spectroscopy involves measuring the gravitational waves that are produced from two black holes colliding and merging, specifically focusing on the âringdownâ phase, or the waves produced from the newly merged black hole.

Recent findings suggest that in the end, the researchers successfully found that hundreds of observed black hole mergersâ âringdownâ behavior match the longstanding Einstein's theory of General Relativity. While the researchers note current observational methods present limitations for providing more accurate measurements, they emphasize how next-generation ground-based gravitational wave detectors could have the necessary technology for more in-depth and accurate observations of gravitational waves.

âBy listening to the ringing of newly formed black holes, we are turning gravitational waves into a tool for exploring some of the deepest questions in physics, from the nature of gravity itself to the possibility of discovering entirely newly introduced forms of matter and energy,â mentioned Dr. Gregorio Carullo, who is an assistant professor in the School of Physics and Astronomy at the University of Birmingham and a co-author on the study.

Industry observers note that introduced in mathematical equations and a longer paper in 1915 and 1916, respectively, Einsteinâs theory of General Relativity challenged the longstanding hypothesis that gravity acted as an invisible force. In contrast, Einstein proposed gravity behaved like a fabric in both space and time, woven together in a phenomenon called spacetime. As a result, massive celestial objects like stars and planets create curves and warps within this fabric, with the mathematical aspect of the theory also predicting the existence of black holes while also proposing the existence of gravitational waves. However, Einstein himself didnât believe they existed and took this belief to his death in 1955. The reason for his disbelief is because he was convinced that matter was not capable of collapsing inward on itself to create such a state where something like a black hole is produced.

According to recent reports, it wasnât until 1964, nine years after Einstein passed away, that the first black hole was discovered, which astronomers designated as Cygnus X-1 and is locate about 7,200 light-years from Earth. And it wasnât for another 51 years that gravitational waves were first detected, 100 years after Einstein first proposed their existence in mathematical equations.

Going forward, the researchers of this latest study anticipate that next-generation observatories could unlock longstanding secrets abut black holes, including gaining insight into their formation and evolution, along with continuing to uphold or challenge theories from Einstein and other scientists.

In a recent development, what new insights into ringing black holes will researchers make in the coming years and decades? Only time will tell, and this is why we science!

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A supplement containing a substance naturally made by gut bacteria increased blood flow to a memory-related brain region in adults with obesity, raising upcoming questions about its potential benefits.

In a recent development, when the brain works harder, it needs more blood to supply oxygen and nutrients. For people with obesity, changes in blood vessel function can affect circulation, raising questions about how well the brain responds to these demands. A new clinical trial suggests a dietary supplement could help increase blood flow during mental activity, although researchers have yet to show that it improves memory.

In a recent development, researchers at the University of Oklahoma investigated urolithin A, a substance produced when certain gut bacteria break down compounds found in foods such as strawberries, pomegranates, and walnuts. The amount people naturally produce varies, and existing research suggests that production declines with age and increasing body mass index. Urolithin A is also available as a dietary supplement.

In the randomized clinical trial, published in JAMA Network Open, 50 adults with obesity, ages 40 to 64, received either 1,000 milligrams of urolithin A daily or a placebo for four weeks.

Participants taking the supplement indicated a greater increase in blood flow to the brain while completing a challenging memory task. The difference was especially noticeable in the left dorsolateral prefrontal cortex, an area involved in holding and using information over short periods. However, researchers found no significant improvements in blood vessel function in the arm or performance on memory tests.

“The brain needs an adequate supply of blood to meet the demands of mental activity,” said first author Ana Clara da Costa Pinaffi Langley, Ph.D., an assistant professor in the Department of Nutritional Sciences at the OU College of Allied Health on the OU Harold Hamm Health Campus. “We found that urolithin A increased blood flow to the brain during a memory task, suggesting the supplement may help the brain meet its increased need for oxygen and nutrients when it is working harder. We strategy to conduct more research to understand what this finding means for brain health.”.

According to the researchers, this is the first human study to report an effect of urolithin A on blood vessel function in the brain. The supplement was well-tolerated, although the trial involved relatively few participants at a single research site. Longer studies with larger groups will be needed to determine whether the changes in blood flow lead to lasting health benefits.

In a recent development, “These findings offer an interesting starting point for understanding how urolithin A affects the brain,” mentioned study co-author Andriy Yabluchanskiy, M.D., Ph.D., an associate professor in the Department of Neurosurgery at the OU College of Medicine. “Although we saw increased blood flow to the brain during mental activity, participants did not demonstrate measurable improvements in memory or attention. Future studies will need to determine whether taking the supplement for a longer period leads to meaningful improvements in cognitive function or other health benefits.”.

The researchers ultimately hope to find ways to help people maintain their cognitive health as they age.

In a recent development, “The idea is to mitigate cognitive decline,” Langley said. “We want to expand the time that people are living healthier lives.”.

  • And as the authors of a new paper in the journal Astrophysics and Space Science describe, JWST has observed a link between outflows from a massive galaxyâs central core and the quenching of star formation at so-called âCosmic Noon.â That is, roughly 8-12 billion years ago, when the number of stars forming per unit volume in the cosmos reached its peak.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that sitting here on the outskirts of our Milky Way Galaxy, itâs hard to imagine the galactic machinations that led to our goldilocks spot around a very welcoming yellow dwarf star. But for decades, astronomers have suspected that the internal dynamics of massive galaxies like ours play an outsized role in regulating star formation.

As observations by NASAâs James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) now reveal, massive galaxies have largescale gaseous outflows that greatly quench their star production.

And as the authors of a new paper in the journal Astrophysics and Space Science describe, JWST has observed a link between outflows from a massive galaxyâs central core and the quenching of star formation at so-called âCosmic Noon.â That is, roughly 8-12 billion years ago, when the number of stars forming per unit volume in the cosmos reached its peak.

Outflows are large-scale flows of gas, from inside to outside the galaxy usually caused by either supernovae or energetic outbursts from supermassive black holes.

These JWST observations have revealed that outflows are more abundant and more powerful than we thought, suggesting that the evolution of galaxies is strongly impacted by outflows, Sirio Belli, an associate professor at the University of Bologna, Italy and the paperâs co-author, told me via email.

Normally, galaxies are rich in gas, and when the gas is sufficiently cold, it collapses under its own weight and forms a dense cloud from which fresh stars form. But such outflows likely remove a large quantity of gas from galaxies, which are then unable to form new stars.

Recent findings suggest that growing supermassive black holes at the centers of galaxies drive powerful winds, blowing away gas that would otherwise form stars, Rebecca Davies, the paperâs lead author and an astrophysicist at Australiaâs Swinburne University of Technology in Melbourne, told me via email. With JWST, we can measure the amount of cold star-forming gas being ejected, Davies told me.

But JWST has also revealed that outflows powered by accretion onto supermassive black holes are linked to the rapid shut-down or âquenchingâ of star formation.

As for what leads to such quenching?

Quenching can happen if the galaxy runs out of gas or the galaxy stops being able to turn the gas into stars because the gas is too hot or turbulent to collapse, notes Davies.

One possibility is that the supermassive black hole at the center of the galaxy releases a large amount of energy which removes and/or heats the gas and prevents the formation of new stars, says Belli.

As such massive galaxies age, their AGN become relatively quiescent, not unlike Sag A* --- our own Milky Wayâs supermassive black hole in our galactic center.

The Milky Wayâs black hole had a major flare just a few million years ago, smaller outbursts only a century or two ago, and it still flickers almost every day as hot gas swirls just outside it, says Davies.

A key open question is what triggers outflows powerful enough to quench galaxies.

In a recent development, outflows are very common in massive galaxies at cosmic noon, but most of these galaxies are not quenching: the outflows simply keep the galaxies in equilibrium and prevent them from converting all their gas into stars too quickly, says Davies. Possible triggers of the most powerful outflows include galaxy mergers, or radio jets released by the central supermassive black holes, she says.

As for how this stellar quenching might impact the formation of molecular clouds that spawn solar type stars and habitable planetary systems?

Sources indicate that when galaxies are quenched, the formation of new stars and planets is shut down, with strong repercussions on the probability of developing habitable systems, says Belli. If the Milky Way had been quenched at Cosmic Noon, it would likely not have formed many new stars in the last 10 billion years, and our solar system which is only 5 billion years old would not exist today, he says.

But star formation can become too much of a good thing.

When star formation is too strong there are other problems, such as the large number of stellar explosions that could negatively impact the habitability of planets, states Belli. The connection between galaxy-scale processes and the habitability of planetary systems is only now being investigated, he says.
