New FDA-Approved Pill Lowers High Blood Pressure and May Slow Kidney Disease

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (954 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scitechdaily

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A fresh drug targeting a hormone linked to hypertension has shown encouraging results in patients with chronic kidney disease.
  • A drug that indicated early signs of protecting damaged kidneys has now received FDA approval for treating high blood pressure that remains uncontrolled despite medication.
  • Recent findings suggest that the approval follows Phase 3 clinical trials showing substantial blood pressure reductions.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A fresh drug targeting a hormone linked to hypertension has shown encouraging results in patients with chronic kidney disease.

A drug that indicated early signs of protecting damaged kidneys has now received FDA approval for treating high blood pressure that remains uncontrolled despite medication. Called Baxfendy (baxdrostat), the treatment targets a hormone involved in both hypertension and kidney disease.

Recent findings suggest that the approval follows Phase 3 clinical trials showing substantial blood pressure reductions. Earlier research also found that baxdrostat lowered a key marker of kidney damage by 55%, suggesting potential benefits beyond hypertension. Whether the medication can slow kidney disease progression remains under investigation.

The FDA approved AstraZeneca’s Baxfendy in May 2026 for adults whose hypertension remains inadequately controlled by existing treatments. It is the first approved aldosterone synthase inhibitor, a class of drugs that reduces production of the hormone aldosterone.

In the Phase 3 BaxHTN trial involving 796 patients, the 2 mg dose reduced systolic blood pressure by an average of 15.7 mm Hg after 12 weeks, compared with 5.8 mm Hg for placebo. The additional reduction of 9.8 mm Hg was statistically significant. A lower 1 mg dose also produced meaningful improvements.

According to recent reports, dr. Bryan Williams, Chair of Medicine at University College London and the trial’s primary investigator, noted: “We have been waiting for an innovative medication like Baxfendy for hypertension for many years. Its novel way of lowering blood pressure has the potential to transform clinical practice by targeting a root cause of persistently uncontrolled hypertension. In addition, the nearly double-digit placebo-adjusted systolic blood pressure reduction achieved with Baxfendy is exciting and clinically meaningful for clinicians and patients. Epidemiological data indicate that a 10 mmHg decrease in systolic blood pressure is associated with a roughly 20% lower risk of serious cardiovascular events.”.

Aldosterone regulates sodium and water balance in the body. Excessive levels cause the kidneys to retain fluid, increasing blood pressure and potentially contributing to kidney inflammation and scarring.

Baxdrostat inhibits the enzyme responsible for producing aldosterone rather than blocking the hormone’s receptors, as some existing medications do. This approach may benefit patients whose blood pressure remains high despite multiple treatments.

In a recent development, A separate Phase 3 trial, Bax24, involving 218 patients found that baxdrostat lowered average systolic blood pressure over 24 hours by 14.0 mm Hg more than placebo. The effect persisted throughout the day and night, according to findings published in The Lancet.

According to recent reports, high blood pressure and chronic kidney disease can worsen each other. Elevated pressure damages the kidneys’ filtering structures, while declining kidney function makes hypertension harder to control.

It has been revealed that “These findings are encouraging for people living with chronic kidney disease and high blood pressure, two conditions that often go hand-in-hand and create a dangerous cycle,” said lead study author Jamie P. Dwyer, M.D., a professor of medicine at University of Utah Health. “High blood pressure can worsen kidney function and declining kidney function can further elevate blood pressure, and these outcomes can be life-altering for patients.”.

Recent findings suggest that in the Phase 2 FigHTN trial, 192 patients with chronic kidney disease and uncontrolled hypertension were randomly assigned to receive baxdrostat or placebo alongside standard treatment. After 26 weeks, systolic blood pressure fell an average of 8.1 mm Hg more in the baxdrostat groups.

It has been revealed that researchers also measured urinary albumin, a protein associated with kidney damage when present in elevated amounts. Levels were 55% lower in patients receiving baxdrostat than in those taking placebo. The findings were published in the Journal of the American Society of Nephrology.

According to recent reports, the earlier kidney disease trial found elevated blood potassium in 41% of baxdrostat recipients, compared with 5% of placebo recipients. Most cases were mild or moderate, but excessive potassium can cause dangerous heart rhythm disturbances. Serious adverse events occurred in 9% and 3% of participants, respectively.

Although subsequent Phase 3 hypertension studies reported no unexpected safety findings, potassium levels and kidney function require monitoring during treatment.

Recent findings suggest that “The reduction in urine albumin gives us hope that baxdrostat may also help delay kidney damage. This potential is now being tested in two large Phase 3 trials to determine if baxdrostat delays the progression of kidney disease,” said Dwyer.

It has been revealed that larger studies are investigating whether baxdrostat can preserve kidney function over time, including trials combining it with dapagliflozin, an established kidney-protective medication. Its FDA approval currently covers hypertension, not the prevention of kidney disease progression.

Industry observers note that “These newly introduced findings are reassuring that this new class of antihypertensive medications are likely to have both kidney- and cardio-protective benefits and to be safe and effective for broad patient populations,” noted Jordana B. Cohen, M.D., M.S.C.E., immediate past chair of the American Heart Association’s Hypertension and Kidney Cardiovascular Science Committee. “Patients with chronic kidney disease were historically often excluded from drug studies. It is particularly reassuring to know that patients with chronic kidney disease, who have very high rates of hypertension and elevated renin-angiotensin aldosterone activity, were represented in their own study, tolerated the medication well, and had both blood pressure and albuminuric benefits. This medication class could be a game changer in the management of hypertension in this patient group.”.

“Efficacy and Safety of Baxdrostat in Participants with CKD and Uncontrolled Hypertension: A Randomized, Double-Blind, Placebo-Controlled Trial” by Jamie P. Dwyer, Noha Maklad, Ola Vedin, John Monyak, Robin Myte, Glenn M. Chertow, Hiddo J.L. Heerspink and Dustin J. Little, 6 September 2025, Journal of the American Society of Nephrology. DOI: 10.1681/ASN.0000000849.

The Simons Observatory is Online and Surveying the Cosmic Microwave Background

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1673 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Universetoday

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that the Simons Observatory in the Atacama Desert has begun its mission to survey the Cosmic Microwave Background.
  • In a recent development, we live in an age of large astronomical surveys, enabled by powerful computers and data handling methods.
  • There are automated surveys for transients like supernovae and asteroids, radio-sky surveys to spot objects obscured by thick dust, and massive surveys just getting started like the Vera Rubin Observatory's Legacy Survey of Space and Time (LSST) and the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope's three core surveys.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that the Simons Observatory in the Atacama Desert has begun its mission to survey the Cosmic Microwave Background. Its goal is to detect undeniable evidence of the Significant Bang and cosmic inflation. Can this unique survey succeed where others have failed?

In a recent development, we live in an age of large astronomical surveys, enabled by powerful computers and data handling methods. While powerful telescopes still perform detailed observations of individual targets, and always will, wide surveys have a power all their own. The ESA's Gaia mission, for example, has completed its survey of billions of stars and generated a massive amount of foundational data that researchers will draw on for decades to come.

There are automated surveys for transients like supernovae and asteroids, radio-sky surveys to spot objects obscured by thick dust, and massive surveys just getting started like the Vera Rubin Observatory's Legacy Survey of Space and Time (LSST) and the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope's three core surveys.

Sources indicate that but another Simons Observatory's survey hasn't garnered the same attention that some of the other have. The Simons Observatory (SO) consists of four telescopes working together: three small 0.5 meter aperture 'scopes in its Small Aperture Telescope (SAT) and one large 6-meter one in its Large Aperture Telescope (LAT).

The unusual configuration gives the SO the best chance to observe tiny details in the Universe's first observable light, the Cosmic Microwave Background (CMB).

This image of the Cosmic Microwave Background is from the Simons Observatory, the newest and most powerful observatory to study the CMB. It's unique arrangement of three small and one large telescope increases its resolution by an order of magnitude over its predecessor, the Planck satellite. The Simons Observatory's main goal is to find the elusive evidence from the epoch of inflation, and thereby confirming the Substantial Bang model of cosmology. Image Credit: Simons Observatory.

The stuff of the Universe was too opaque for light to travel through it at first. Photons were effectively scattered by the hot, dense plasma that permeated the Universe. Eventually conditions changed. The Universe expanded, the plasma cooled, and photons could travel. This was the recombination epoch and it occurred about 380,000 years after the Major Bang.

Note that the name is historical and reflected our earlier understanding of the Universe. It wasn't actually a recombination, it was the first time that electrons and protons combined to form neutral hydrogen, and that's what made the cosmos transparent. Its name should probably be changed to the combination epoch.

But regardless of its name, the cosmic microwave background is the relic radiation from the Universe's first light, and it holds clues to the Universe, especially to the Big Bang theory of cosmology.

Other efforts have been made to map the CMB. NASA's Wilkinson Microwave Anisotropy Probe (WMAP) and the ESA's Planck satellite both made the effort from orbit. At the moment, the South Pole Telescope (SPT) and related facilities are doing the same.

The SPT made an important discovery. It detected for the first time what's called the B-mode polarization of the CMB. The B-mode is important because it was created by primordial gravitational waves generated during the epoch of inflation, the first moments of the Universe's inflation. So finding the B-mode was important evidence for the Big Bang theory.

The South Pole Telescope at the AmundsenâScott South Pole Station, Antarctica. The SPT is a 10-meter telescope that is credited with the first detection of the Cosmic Microwave Background's B-mode polarization. Image Credit: By Amble - Own work, CC BY-SA 3.0, https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/Special:Redirect/page/9057466.

But there was a problem. Gravitational lensing can also create B-mode polarization, and it has nothing to do with the Substantial Bang or inflation. It's difficult to tell which source created the B-mode polarization the SPT detected. So its initial detection was put in doubt.

This is where the Simons Observatory comes into the picture. It's been calibrating its instruments for two years and is now getting down to business.

âTo have all the observatory motors humming, gears turning and data flowing makes me joyful, but even more exciting is the prospect of what we could find in its massive new deep and detailed maps,â indicates Simons Observatory Co-Director Suzanne Staggs of Princeton University.

According to recent reports, this time-lapse highlights the Simons Observatory's Large Area Telescope scanning the sky in August 2026. Credit: David Boettger.

The observatory's four telescopes collectively have tens of thousands of microwave detectors, almost 98,000 of them. That's 16 times more than one of its predecessors, the Atacama Cosmology Telescope. They're not only mapping the CMB the same way that WMAP and the Planck satellite did. They're also searching for the tiny fluctuations in the CMB, the B-mode polarizations that can confirm the Big Bang and cosmic inflation. If detected, the SO can determine if these are true artifacts of primordial gravitational waves, or artifacts of the polluting gravitational lensing that confounded the SPT.

Recent findings suggest that it'll take years of observations before that can be achieved, but the SO's first observations are already showing the observatory's power. Its sensitivity is meant to be an order of magnitude highter than its predecessor, the Planck satellite. âThe images that weâve made with just a few months of data are already deeper and less noisy than Planckâs, which were collected over years,â states Simons Observatory Spokesperson Jo Dunkley of Princeton University. That's significant, because the Planck outperformed its predecessor, WMAP, and is considered the benchmark for CMB observations. So the SO is already establishing a fresh benchmark for observations.

The SO's unique four telescope design is already showing its value. The large, 6-meter telescope is able to observe more of the sky in higher resolution than other CMB telescopes. Every couple of days, it scans half of the available sky.

âIt is incredibly satisfying to see the early maps, knowing that our initial data places us at the forefront of the field â and that we are poised to go much further,â says Jeffrey McMahon, observatory testing lead at the University of Chicago.

Industry observers note that the SO isn't isolated and alone in its work. All of these CMB surveys and observatories will work together in the end. For example, the SPT and other facilities at its site are mapping gravitational lenses that can interfere with the detection of B-modes from primordial gravitational waves in the epoch of inflation. Those templates can be used to help remove their pollution from CMB surveys. So it's all hands on deck.

Sources indicate that this cut-away schematic demonstrates the Large Area Telescope's Receiver with one of its optical tubes highlighted. Note the pulse tube coolers and the dilution refrigerator. They keep the telescope at the cryogenic temperatures necessary for microwave observations. Image Credit: Simons Observatory/Nicholas Galitzki et al. 2018. Conference Proceedings.

The SO is an observer of polarized light, and that means that while its primary goal is searching for B-mode polarization, its maps have other things to reveal, too. âThere are a number of large surveys adding to our understanding of the universe,â Staggs claims. âOur idea is that we can combine our data with theirs to further our discoveries.â.

Recent findings suggest that this is especially true of other wide surveys like the Rubin Observatory's Legacy Survey of Space and Time. The pair will create a potent combination for detecting transients across multiple wavelengths. âThe instrument is now sensitive enough that we can see small changes in transients in only a few days, whereas ACT took months,â Devlin says. âThis enables us to observe entirely new classes of objects.â Its science observations have barely begun, and it's already giant stellar flares and asteroids in the Milky Way, and activity around a supermassive black holes outside of our galaxy.

Industry observers note that but detecting that elusive evidence from the epoch of inflation is the SO's holy grail, and if it finds it, it will be a collective finding in the mass data the observatory will produce. Like other survey telescopes, the data will be released in large sequential data releases.

âWeâll be providing everything to the community through a data management tool, which we hope to have completed for the first data release,â Devlin claims.

The initial success of its first science operations is a hopeful indication that it can finally find the evidence of cosmic inflation, the B-mode polarization from primordial gravitational waves in the CMB.

Recent findings suggest that âEssentially, right out of the box, just turning on the instrument, weâre making beautiful crisp images of the Milky Way,â Staggs notes. Those images are uncovering new observations of the galaxy's magnetic fields, and understanding them is critical to understanding star formation and how the galaxy evolves.

According to recent reports, âThis moment marks a major milestone in our effort to understand these big questions about the universe,â Devlin says. âI think thereâs going to be so many scientific discoveries coming out in the next few years, itâll be hard to keep up.â.

It has been revealed that the SO's performance will improve when another three small telescopes are added in 2027. That will also double the Small Area Telescope's number of individual detectors to 48,160 detectors. The original five-year survey has been extended, too.

"Combined with a planned extension of the survey duration to 2035, this expansion will significantly enhance SO's search for a B-mode signal in the polarisation of the cosmic microwave background, a potential signature of gravitational waves produced in the very early Universe," explain the authors of a 2026 paper in the Journal of Cosmology and Astroparticle Physics.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Slashing bone-in chicken thighs (carefully, around the bone, of course) allows a punchy maple-Dijon-ACV marinade to permeate the meat deeply in a short amount of time. And that waiting time is well spent: Scatter torn sourdough bread on a baking sheet and bake until crisp, then toss croutons aside to make way for the thighs. Once the chicken is cooked through, toss the croutons in the rendered fat and cook until everything is bronzed and glistening. A few handfuls of arugula make an elegant finish—who needs a side salad?

More sheet-pan dinners this way.

Sources indicate that whisk 5 garlic cloves, finely grated, ½ cup plus 3 Tbsp. apple cider vinegar, 5 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil, 3 Tbsp. Dijon mustard, 1 Tbsp. plus 2 tsp. pure maple syrup, 2½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or 1½ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and 1 tsp. crushed red pepper flakes (if using) in a measuring glass or small bowl to combine. Transfer 2 Tbsp. vinegar mixture to a small bowl; set aside.

Arrange 3 lb. skin-on, bone-in chicken thighs (6–8), skin side up, on a cutting board. Season lightly with salt. Turn over and season lightly on other side with salt, then carefully use a sharp paring knife to make 3 long slashes, going most of the way through meat (avoid the bone). Transfer to a large bowl and pour vinegar mixture in measuring glass over. Toss chicken to coat, making sure to get liquid into slashes. Let chicken sit at least 30 minutes and up to 1 hour.

Industry observers note that meanwhile, place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 425°. Place 8 oz. country-style or sourdough bread (about ⅓ loaf), torn into 1" pieces, on a rimmed baking sheet. Drizzle remaining 3 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil over and sprinkle with a pinch of salt and a pinch of freshly ground black pepper; toss to coat. Arrange bread in a single layer and bake until golden, 12–15 minutes. Transfer croutons to a plate; reserve baking sheet.

Arrange reserved chicken on reserved baking sheet and nestle 3 large shallots, quartered lengthwise through root ends, around; pour any excess vinegar mixture in bowl over. Bake chicken until golden, cooked through, and an instant-read thermometer inserted into thickest part, avoiding bone, registers at least 165° (it should be well over), 25–30 minutes.

According to recent reports, scatter croutons over empty areas of baking sheet and toss to soak up juices. Roast until chicken and croutons are deeply browned, 10–12 minutes. Let cool 5 minutes, then top with 2 oz. arugula and drizzle with reserved vinegar mixture in small bowl.

Reconstructing Cosmic History and Earth's Evolution From Cosmic Explosions

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (887 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Universetoday

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways

  • Recent findings suggest that these include intermediate elements ranging from carbon and oxygen to iron, nickel, and radioactive isotopes thereof, as well as heavy elements like zinc, silver, tin, gold, mercury, lead, platinum, and uranium.
  • The project was recently awarded a â¬3 million grant ($3.29 million USD) through the European Research Council's (ERC) Advanced Grants program.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, when we think of the Solar System, we often view it as a self-contained entity, isolated from its cosmic neighborhood. However, scientists have long known that the planets of the Solar System are subject to activity in nearby star systems, including supernovae and other energetic astrophysical events. For example, it is established that intermediate elements and the heaviest elements on the periodic table are created when stars reach the end of their life cycle and explode, sending their outer layers (with these elements) into space.

Recent findings suggest that these include intermediate elements ranging from carbon and oxygen to iron, nickel, and radioactive isotopes thereof, as well as heavy elements like zinc, silver, tin, gold, mercury, lead, platinum, and uranium. At the Helmholtz-Zentrum Dresden-Rossendorf (HZDR), Prof. Anton Wallner and his team have launched the SUPREME project to uncover traces of these elements. Their goal is to use them to reconstruct the history of cosmic events in our neighborhood and shed light on how the heaviest elements are created in nature.

The project was recently awarded a â¬3 million grant ($3.29 million USD) through the European Research Council's (ERC) Advanced Grants program. Prof. Wallner and his team were one of 319 leading research groups across Europe selected for funding totaling â¬838 million ($918.86 million USD) to pursue projects that could lead to major scientific breakthroughs. The SUPREME project aims to address two fundamental questions in modern astrophysics, focusing on the past 500 million years.

Sources indicate that first, there's the question of how nearby supernovae have affected Earth and biological evolution since the Cambrian Period (ca. 538.8 to 485 million years ago), the geological era that coincided with the rapid explosion of complex marine life (aka. the Cambrian Explosion). When the Cambrian began, the continents were largely located in the southern hemisphere and were mostly barren. But as the period progressed and gave way to subsequent geological eras, life began to emerge from the oceans, giving rise to plants, mammals, dinosaurs, and eventually primates.

According to recent reports, supernovae, when they happen in our cosmic neighborhood, distribute heavy elements like gold, platinum, lead, and zinc to Earth. Credit: NASA.

According to recent reports, second, there's the question of how the heaviest elements in the Universe are created and distributed; in this case, to the Earth and Moon. #7604. Tech Report: Mysterious Radio Signals From 5,000 Light-Years Away Lead Scientists to a Surprising Discovery

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (819 w)

Tech Report: Mysterious Radio Signals From 5,000 Light-Years Away Lead Scientists to a Surprising Discovery

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (819 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scitechdaily

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A dead star and its Sun-like companion have given astronomers an unexpected way to investigate mysterious radio pulses and detect stellar storms thousands of light-years away.
  • Mysterious radio signals have been appearing across the Milky Way, switching on and off over minutes or hours.
  • In a recent development, now, a newly discovered star system more than 5,000 light-years away is offering an key clue.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A dead star and its Sun-like companion have given astronomers an unexpected way to investigate mysterious radio pulses and detect stellar storms thousands of light-years away.

Mysterious radio signals have been appearing across the Milky Way, switching on and off over minutes or hours. Astronomers have found only about a dozen of these unusual sources, and one question has been especially difficult to answer: What is actually producing the pulses?

In a recent development, now, a newly discovered star system more than 5,000 light-years away is offering an key clue. Known as GPM J071507−114153, it contains a white dwarf, the dense core left behind after a star dies, orbiting a companion remarkably similar to our Sun. The white dwarf spins once every eight minutes.

The discovery is unusual because astronomers have never before detected these radio pulses from a white dwarf paired with a Sun-like star. Previously identified systems producing similar signals have typically involved much smaller, cooler stars known as red dwarfs.

Industry observers note that these mysterious sources belong to a class called long-period transients (LPTs). Since researchers at the International Center for Radio Astronomy Research (ICRAR) first discovered one in 2021, around a dozen have been identified. Several contain a white dwarf and another star, although astronomers have struggled to determine which one produces the radio signals.

Scientists at the Curtin University node at the International Centre for Radio Astronomy Research (ICRAR) have linked mysterious radio pulses to an unusual pairing of stars — a dead star that spins every eight minutes and a star similar to our own Sun. Credit: Natasha Hurley-Walker.

In the newly discovered system, scientists finally had enough information to narrow down the source.

“This is the first time the pulses are clear enough to see the white dwarf moving in its orbit around its companion, so we know that the pulsations are coming from a region close to the white dwarf, or possibly even from the white dwarf itself,” stated Dr Sam McSweeney, the study’s lead author and a commissioning scientist with the Square Kilometre Array Observatory.

McSweeney made the discovery while working as a researcher at the Curtin University node of ICRAR. To confirm and better understand the white dwarf’s movement, the team processed more than 100 hours of radio observations using computing resources at the Pawsey Supercomputing Research Center.

The radio pulses also revealed something unexpected about the white dwarf’s companion. Researchers detected evidence of stellar flares on the Sun-like star, similar to the activity associated with auroras here on Earth.

“As a bonus, we also saw the white dwarf moving behind a region with a strong magnetic field, most likely a ‘stellar prominence’, which is a large loop of plasma erupting from a star’s surface.”.

The observation suggests astronomers can use radio signals to investigate magnetic activity on distant stars, even when those stars are thousands of light-years away.

“It’s amazing that by using radio wavelengths we can detect the storms on a star over 5000 light-years away.”.

Both observations were described by Associate Professor Natasha Hurley-Walker, a co-author of the paper.

Sources indicate that finding such a rare system required several powerful telescopes working together. The researchers first identified its radio signals during a large survey of the Milky Way, then used additional observations to pinpoint its location.

It has been revealed that “We detected this system in a large survey using the MWA (Murchison Widefield Array) to scan the entire Milky Way visible from Australia. We then used the MeerKAT radio telescope in South Africa to determine its precise position,” mentioned Associate Professor Hurley-Walker.

Once the radio source had been located, optical observations from the W.M. Keck Observatory on Maunakea, Hawaiʻi Island, confirmed its association with a G-type star, the same broad class as our Sun.

Recent findings suggest that the MWA, led by Curtin University, is located at Inyarrimanha Ilgari Bundara, the CSIRO Murchison Radio-Astronomy Observatory on Wajarri Yamaji Country in Western Australia. MeerKAT, meanwhile, was built and is operated by the South African Radio Astronomy Observatory in South Africa’s North Cape province.

Both facilities are precursors to the larger SKA telescopes now being developed, SKA-Low in Australia and SKA-Mid in South Africa. These future observatories are expected to provide more detailed observations of unusual radio sources and help astronomers identify additional systems that have so far escaped detection.

“If we are already making such discoveries with precursor telescopes, just imagine how many more star systems we will be able to find, and what a beautifully detailed view of their signals we will have, once the SKAO telescopes are completely built,” noted Dr McSweeney.

Reference: “A long-period transient with a Sun-like companion” by Samuel J. McSweeney, Natasha Hurley-Walker, Arash Bahramian, Csanád Horváth, Nanda Rea, Antonio C. Rodriguez and Ingrid Pelisoli, 12 November 2026, Nature Astronomy. DOI: 10.1038/s41550-026-03016-z.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Why late November 2026 is prime Uranus observing season.

The outer planets are ever so slowly starting to sneak back into the evening sky this month. First, Saturn crossed this mark last month on October 4th, then Neptune followed suit on September 26th. Now, the planet Uranus makes the transition, crossing opposition next week.

Opposition occurs on November 25th. On âU.S. Thanksgiving-eve.â We say âoppositionâ for an outer planet, as a point at which it seems to rise âoppositeâ to the setting Sun as seen from our Earthly vantage point. Orbiting the Sun at a leisurely pace once every 84 years, Uranus has a synodic period of 370 days, meaning oppositions for the planet only slide forward about five days each year. This year sees Uranus reach opposition in the astronomical constellation of Taurus, between the Hyades and the Pleiades open star clusters.

Industry observers note that uranus at opposition for 2026. Credit: Stellarium.

Shout out to the Full November Beaver Moon nearby on the same date as opposition 2026, fresh off of occulting the Pleiades for the Arctic on November 24th.

According to recent reports, uranus reached aphelion 20 Astronomical Units (AU) from the Sun in 2009, and is now inbound toward perihelion 18.3 AU distant in 2050. In 2033, Uranus will pass the point in Taurus where it was discovered by Sir William Herschel on March 13th, 1781, between the horns of the Bull very near the constellation's border with Gemini. Uranus made spurious appearances on star charts of the era at least 20 times prior to discovery.

According to recent reports, the discovery position of Uranus. Credit: Dave Dickinson/Starry Night.

It has been revealed that uranus reached its southernmost point in the sky in 2007, and crossed the celestial equator multiple times from 2011-2012. Uranus crosses the ecliptic plane northward in 2029. Uranus reaches its northernmost in 2032, and then begins the long trek southward. The Moon wonât resume occulting the planet Uranus again until a cycle starting on September 29th, 2029.

In a recent development, the Moon occults the Pleiades on November 24th. Credit: Occult 4.2.

Observing +5.5 magnitude Uranus is as easy as sweeping the suspect field at low power, and looking for a blue-green âstarâ that obstinately refuses to snap into focus. To my eye, Uranus looks like a tiny planetary nebula or perhaps a distant fuzzy comet. In fact, thatâs exactly what Herschel thought heâd first discovered, back on that fortuitous night in 1781. He later correctly realized after following the new object for several nights that it was a distant, and therefore intrinsically large object far out in the solar system beyond Saturn, then thought to mark its outer boundary. All of this happened in his backyard garden in Bath, England. We can, however, be thankful that the name âGeorgeâ that Herschel proposed to honor his benefactor King George the III didnât stick (!).

One of Herschel's speculum metal mirrors and telescopes at the London Science Museum. Credit: Dave Dickinson.

Industry observers note that can you see Uranus with the naked eye? Topping +6th magnitude near opposition, itâs knocking on naked eye visibility from a good dark sky site. At the eyepiece, Uranus only highlights a 4â disk at around opposition, barely resolvable with a telescope and tough to tease out detail.

A fine capture of Uranus from 2017. Credit: Szabolcs Nagy.

Uranus is tipped over 98 degrees (prograde) on its side, the result of some ancient encounter with another large body early in the solar systemâs history. At the moment, weâre staring nearly directly at the rotational (north?) pole/hemisphere of the planet, which will be pointed nearly directly towards us in late 2029.

Challenge: Catching the Uranian Moons.

Recent findings suggest that though Uranus has 29 known moons, only five are within potential reach of amateur telescopes, with +13.9 magnitude Titania being the brightest. Orbiting Uranus once every 8.7 days, Titania reaches a greatest elongation of 28â from Uranus. We once saw a sharp view of the moons observing through the Steward Observatoryâs Kuiper Telescope in the Santa Catalina Mountains outside of Tucson, Arizona. They were a surprisingly easy catch through the enormous 61â telescope.

A fine capture of Uranus and its moons. Credit: Ralph Smyth.

A planetarium program such as Stellarium and Starry Night will show you the current orientation of the moons of Uranus, to help parse them out from any nearby background stars.

In a recent development, the orbits an orientations of the major Uranian moons. Credit: Starry Night.

The orbits of the moons are right now nearly perpendicular to our view in 2026, though theyâre edge-on and can transit Uranus as seen from our view once every 42 years. This last occurred on 2006-2009, and will happen again starting around 2048.

Industry observers note that hubble captures a shadow transit of Ariel in 2006. Credit: NASA/ESA/L. Sromovsky/University of Wisconsin.

Recent findings suggest that will we return to Uranus in the coming years? To date, only one mission has seen the planet close up: NASAâs Voyager 2, which flew past Uranus and its moons in 1986. Cassini-style orbiters have been proposed, though such a mission would be a lengthy affair, needing to first make the trip to the distant ice giant then slow down to enter orbit. As it stands, such a mission would be feasible for around the 2040s time frame.

JWST's view of Uranus and its rings. Credit: NASA/JWST.

In a recent development, certainly, Uranus calls out for a dedicated mission. But you can explore the planet yourself tonight as it nears opposition for 2026.

#7601. Tech Report: A New Light-Powered Quantum Processor Could Overcome a Major Computing Barrier

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (952 w)
📖 Baca
Hardware & Chips ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Scitechdaily ↗ Open Full Page

Tech Report: A New Light-Powered Quantum Processor Could Overcome a Major Computing Barrier

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (952 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scitechdaily

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A new light-based processor suggests future quantum computers could tackle very different problems without being rebuilt, while laying the groundwork for more reliable calculations.
  • Light has enormous potential for quantum computing, but one of its greatest strengths is also a major obstacle.
  • Researchers from Imperial College London’s Department of Physics and collaborating institutions have developed a new approach that could help overcome this limitation.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A new light-based processor suggests future quantum computers could tackle very different problems without being rebuilt, while laying the groundwork for more reliable calculations.

Light has enormous potential for quantum computing, but one of its greatest strengths is also a major obstacle. Photons, the tiny particles that make up light, are excellent carriers of quantum information because they rarely interact with one another. Yet those interactions are essential for many of the calculations that quantum computers need to perform, making it difficult to build versatile machines using light alone.

Researchers from Imperial College London’s Department of Physics and collaborating institutions have developed a new approach that could help overcome this limitation. Their programmable quantum processor, called Clavina, combines different types of quantum operations in a single system, allowing it to tackle multiple computational tasks without requiring an entirely new hardware design.

The research, published in Nature Photonics, offers a promising direction for building more flexible light-based quantum computers, including systems that could eventually detect and correct their own errors.

Recent findings suggest that most photonic quantum processors are designed with a particular task in mind. Adapting them to solve another problem can require substantial changes to their hardware, limiting how easily the technology can evolve.

Clavina takes inspiration from ordinary computers, which use specialized components to handle graphics, artificial intelligence, and other demanding tasks. Instead of relying on one fixed arrangement, the latest processor uses a central control unit to direct information through a programmable optical network and specialized modules.

The optical network handles linear operations, which manipulate light without requiring photons to interact. The additional modules provide nonlinear operations, expanding the kinds of calculations the system can perform. Because these components can be combined in different ways, researchers can change the processor’s functions without rebuilding it from scratch.

Dr. Shang Yu, the study’s lead author and a Marie Skłodowska-Curie Fellow at Imperial, remarked, “We set out to build a photonic quantum processor that provides a step change in functionality over our previous designs. Our upcoming architecture ‘Clavina’ is scalable, modular and extensible, allowing different functional modules to be used depending on the computational task we wish to perform.”.

To test what this flexibility could achieve, the researchers put Clavina to work on two very different challenges.

Sources indicate that the first involved simulating the Bose-Hubbard model, a well-known problem in condensed matter physics that describes how quantum particles interact. These calculations involve many-body interactions, where the behavior of multiple particles must be considered together. Such simulations are challenging even for other quantum computing technologies, including superconducting quantum computers.

Sources indicate that dr. Jinzhao Sun of Queen Mary University of London explained, “The versatility of our hardware enables us to integrate nonlinear operations and linear operations. We use these operations to perform simulations involving many-body interactions, which are also restricted on superconducting quantum computers.”.

The second demonstration addressed another major challenge facing quantum computing: keeping delicate quantum information safe from errors.

In a recent development, quantum systems are vulnerable to noise and disturbances that can interfere with calculations. One possible solution involves creating specially structured quantum states that encode information in ways that make errors easier to detect and correct.

Among the most promising are Gottesman-Kitaev-Preskill (GKP) states. Producing these states has been difficult for light-based systems because earlier approaches worked probabilistically, meaning researchers could not reliably generate the required states whenever they needed them.

Using Clavina, the team demonstrated a much more consistent method of generating GKP states. Although this does not mean they have built a fully error-correcting quantum computer, it addresses an notable obstacle to making error correction practical.

Dr. Raj Patel, a UKRI Future Leaders Fellow who leads Imperial’s photonic quantum computing program, noted, “Our architecture allows the generation of exotic quantum states such as Schrödinger cat states and Gottesman-Kitaev-Preskill states, which are valuable resources for fault-tolerant quantum computing. The nonlinear operations in our architecture provide a universal gate set at the physical level which is required for the future implementation of bosonic error-correcting codes.”.

In a recent development, A universal gate set provides the fundamental operations that can be combined to carry out different quantum computations. Having these capabilities available in one programmable processor could support future error-correction techniques that use specially encoded states of light.

It has been revealed that the architecture also offers possibilities beyond the two demonstrations. By allowing researchers to change or introduce functional modules, Clavina could be adapted to different scientific problems as quantum computing systems become larger and more complex.

In a recent development, co-author Ying Dong of China Jiliang University said, “Previously, researchers would have to build photonic hardware tailored to a specific task. The ability to switch in different functional modules in our architecture enables a single set of hardware to perform multiple functions without overhauling the design. Clavina can solve graph problems, simulate quantum systems or generate large entangled states and resource states for error correction.”.

Sources indicate that rather than developing a separate photonic processor for every upcoming challenge, researchers could eventually build on the same adaptable foundation. Clavina’s demonstrations suggest that the ability to change what a quantum computer does may become just as valuable as increasing its computational power.

Euclid's Hunt for Strong Gravitational Lenses is Off to a Strong Start

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1362 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Universetoday

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that if dark matter and dark energy were a part of our everyday lives, we would live in a perpetual state of dumbfoundedness.
  • Recent findings suggest that luckily, dark energy and dark matter aren't everyday concerns.
  • One of the spacecraft astrophysicists built to study dark matter and energy is the European Space Agencyâs Euclid space telescope.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that if dark matter and dark energy were a part of our everyday lives, we would live in a perpetual state of dumbfoundedness. Imagine living in a world where 95% of the matter and energy were invisible and undetectable. It would be impossible to make sense of our surroundings.

Recent findings suggest that luckily, dark energy and dark matter aren't everyday concerns. They're interesting problems for people who are intellectally curious about Nature. But for physicisits, the questions surrounding dark matter and dark energy are much more acute. Some of them dedicate their entire lives to understanding dark matter and dark energy. They design and build special telescopes, instruments, and spacecraft to make progress toward an answer.

One of the spacecraft astrophysicists built to study dark matter and energy is the European Space Agencyâs Euclid space telescope.

In a recent development, this artist's illustration shows the Euclid Space Telescope doing its thing in its halo orbit at L2. The telescope is on a six-year mission to create a 3D map of the sky, revealing how dark energy and dark matter shape the Universe. Image Credit: By ESA, CC BY-SA IGO 3.0, CC BY-SA 3.0 igo, https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/Special:Redirect/page/128347141.

Dark matter and dark energy are foundational in our Universe. Dark matter doesn't interact with any light, but it's clearly there. It's some form of mass, but we don't know what. Dark matter is a placeholder term.

Dark energy is another placeholder term. It describes the force driving the expansion of the Universe. Like dark matter, we can measure its effect, but we don't know what it really is. And the puzzling thing is that dark matter and dark energy make up most of the Universe.

Industry observers note that âIt turns out, the stuff humans are made of is relatively rare in the universe,â remarked Dr. Douglas Scott, professor at the University of BC's department of physics and astronomy (PHAS) and member of the Euclid collaboration. âAnd what dominates â dark matter and dark energy â is invisible so we're not used to dealing with it. But it makes the universe what it is, it drives how the universe expands and what the past and future of the universe will be. Where did these things come from? What properties do they have? Euclidâs data gives us the potential to answer those questions.â.

In a recent development, this image reminds us that Euclid does more than study dark matter and dark energy. It's a powerful camera, after all, and can also capture stunning images of regular, baryonic matter, the kind that stars, people, and planets are made of. This image is from Euclid's Early Release Observations, and shows the Messier 78 star formation region about 1300 light years away in Orion. This is the first time Messier 78 has been imaged with such width and depth, hallmarks of Euclid's observations. Image Credit: ESA/Euclid/Euclid Consortium/NASA, image processing by J.-C. Cuillandre (CEA Paris-Saclay), G. Anselmi.

Euclid released in July 2023 and orbits the Sun-Earth Lagrange point 2 (L2), roughly 1.5 million kilometers away from Earth, a popular spot for space telescopes. From that perch, it uses its wide-angle, 600-megapixel camera to capture visible light, and a photometer and a near-infrared spectrometer to measure the redshift of about 10 billion sources out to redshift 2. That's roughly equivalent to about 10 billion years ago, or about 3.7 billion years after the Massive Bang.

Among these sources, Euclid is especially interested in strong gravitational lenses. These are massive objects like galaxies, galaxy clusters, and dark matter halos. These objects can magnify background objects that are otherwise beyond observing. But they're critical for mapping dark matter itself, because their lensing effect is based on the total mass of these objects, not just their visible mass. So strong gravitational lenses are a way to measure the presence of dark matter. But they're not easy to find.

Industry observers note that euclid delivered its first data release on November 12th, called DR-1 Foundation, and it holds a whopping 1.7 million gigabytes of data. The data revealed almost 5% of the night sky in 13 months of observations. That data holds 900 million galaxies, and 60 million quasars, which are the extremely luminous cores of far-away galaxies. Euclid also found 15,000 new strong gravitational lens candidates, a massive increase in the potential number.

"Strong lenses have been difficult to find â the odds were about one in 10,000,â said Hrishabh Srivastava, doctoral student in the UBC department of physics and astronomy (PHAS). âBefore Euclid, we had less than a thousand confirmed strong lenses. Now we have 15,000 fresh candidates.â.

There's more than one type of gravitational lens. This is a collage of some of the different types of strong gravitational lenses Euclid has found so far. The top row highlights, from left to right: a classic galaxyâgalaxy lens, an Einstein ring in a face-on spiral lens, and an inclined dusty disc lens galaxy. The middle row shows an edge-on dusty lens galaxy, a lensed galaxy with visible star-forming regions, and a compound lens.The bottom row shows a galaxy group lens, a lensed quasar, and a galaxy group lens. Image Credit: ESA/Euclid/Euclid Consortium/NASA, image processing by N. Lines and T. Li. Licence: CC BY-SA 3.0 IGO or ESA Standard Licence.

Overall, Euclid is expected to find more than 100,000 strong lenses over the course of its nominal six year mission. That would increase the number of known strong lenses by two orders of magnitude, a transformational advance for dark matter science.

âI like to call these gravitational lenses ânature's own magnifying glassesâ to probe the dark matter distribution of our universe,â said Srivastava.

Strong gravitational lensing is an notable tool, but so is weak gravitational lensing. They can be used together to build a fuller picture of dark matter and dark energy. The weak gravitational lensing signature is most apparent around massive galaxy clusters. Since weak gravitational lensing extends beyond a cluster's virial radius, it can help constrain a cluster's overall mass.

Finding huge numbers of gravitational lenses is clearly key in the quest to understand the Universe, but Euclid has other tasks, too. It will slowly build a 3D map of the Universe that covers greater than one-third of the sky. This map will comprise the actual tool used to measure dark matter and dark energy. The map will show how matter is distributed, and then that map can be tested against models of the Universe, especially Lambda-Cold Dark Matter, which is the standard Substantial Bang model of cosmology.

Industry observers note that lambda-CDM predicts how matter, including dark matter, is spread throughout the Universe, and how its structure is shaped by dark energy, which drives the Universe's expansion. So Euclid's 3D map can test both facets of Lambda-CDM: dark matter and dark energy. Dark energy is directly tested, and dark matter is tested more indirectly.

Euclid's test of Lambda-CDM won't be in one substantial grand finale, where physicists around the world wait with bated breath to find out the answer. The test is ongoing. Each latest data release will generate rounds of new research, as physicists and cosmologists dig into it. It'll be fuel for the different lines of detailed research that different teams of scientists pursue. It's like a process of elimination. Eventually, hopefully, the possible answers and explanations for dark matter and dark energy will be constrained and refined until only one is left standing.

Then, in all likelihood, Nobel prizes will be awarded.

But that won't be the end of cosmology. Latest questions will arise, intellectual curiosity will be piqued in new ways, and the quest to understand the Universe will continue.

But Euclid and its 3D map will be in history of science textbooks for a long time.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that mississippi Democrat Scott Colom, here at a news conference in Jackson on Nov. 4, has defeated Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith. (Rogelio V. Solis/Getty Images).

In a recent development, democrat Scott Colom has unseated Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith to become Mississippi’s first Black senator since Reconstruction.

The result is a stunning flip for Democrats in a deep-red state where they last won a Senate election in 1982, and it brings the Senate Democratic Caucus to at least 55 seats in the next Congress.

Colom was leading Hyde-Smith 49.2 percent to 48.7 percent — or by just over 4,600 votes out of more than 960,000 cast — when The Associated Press called the race Wednesday, a little over a week after Election Day. Ty Pinkins, the 2024 Democratic Senate nominee who ran as an independent this year, had 2 percent.

In recent days, as absentee and provisional ballots were counted, Colom had all but declared victory, repeatedly saying that Hyde-Smith had no path to victory.

“I'll work every day in the U.S. Senate to build a future that generations of Mississippians can be just as proud to call home,” he posted Monday on social media.

In a recent development, with his victory, Colom joins several other Democrats who flipped seats in deep-red states, including Texas’ James Talarico, Kansas’ Adam Hamilton and South Carolina’s Annie Andrews. Democrats have so far flipped eight Senate seats to win control of the chamber, overcoming a difficult Senate map and giving them their largest majority in the chamber since 2011.

That majority could expand further if Democrats flip the Senate seat in Alaska, where former Rep. Mary Peltola narrowly leads Republican incumbent Dan Sullivan.

It has been revealed that republicans have dominated Senate elections in Mississippi in recent decades. The last Democrat to be elected senator in the Magnolia State was John C. Stennis, who won his sixth full and final term in 1982. Colom will be the third Black man to serve as a Mississippi senator after Republicans Hiram Revels and Blanche Bruce during Reconstruction.

While Revels and Bruce, who left office in 1881, were elected by the state Legislature, Colom will be the first Black senator elected directly by voters.

Colom has served as a district attorney for four counties in northeast Mississippi since 2016. President Joe Biden nominated him for a federal district judgeship in 2022, but Hyde-Smith effectively blocked his nomination by not returning a so-called blue slip, a Senate Judiciary Committee tradition that lets senators derail district judge nominees in their home states.

Senate Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer noted last week that he’d had Colom in his sights for several years as a potential Senate candidate, including for a race against the state’s senior senator, Republican Roger Wicker.

“I had Scott Colom and his father come to my house, and I served them a nice little brunch or something. I stated, ‘You got to run,’” the Newly introduced York Democrat recalled to MS NOW. “They were smarter than me. This was four years ago. They said, ‘We don’t want to run this time, but we know that Hyde-[Smith], the incumbent, is so weak, we could beat her.’”.

Industry observers note that still, the Mississippi race didn’t capture as much national attention as other Senate contests until the closing weeks of the campaign. A trio of Black senators, Angela Alsobrooks of Maryland, Lisa Blunt Rochester of Delaware and Cory Booker of Upcoming Jersey, all campaigned with Colom throughout the summer and fall. Key national figures, including former President Bill Clinton, former Vice President Kamala Harris and former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg, also stumped for him in October.

Recent findings suggest that colom’s campaign engaged voters with quirky ads and unconventional forms of outreach, including meeting with people lining up to attend a Trump rally. One ad that went viral played on Hyde Smith saying earlier this year that people had “so many proteins to choose from” when asked about rising beef prices.

It has been revealed that “Pick another protein?” says a man in the ad. “I’d rather pick another senator instead.”.

Industry observers note that major Democratic outside groups made a late play in the state, with WinSenate, which is affiliated with Senate Democrats’ top super PAC, investing $2.2 million. The Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee spent $500,000 on a coordinated ad buy late last month.

The pro-Republican Senate Leadership Fund dropped $1.7 million on the race, and Trump headlined a rally for Hyde-Smith on Oct. 26.

Breaking: Scientists Discover That Producing Light More Slowly Could Improve Future Quantum Networks

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (605 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scitechdaily

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Getting the right light for future quantum networks may depend on what scientists prevent from being emitted, an approach that nearly tripled the share of desired photons.
  • Sources indicate that future quantum networks may one day allow quantum computers and other devices to exchange information through individual particles of light, known as photons.
  • It has been revealed that scientists have traditionally addressed this problem using tiny optical structures called resonators.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Getting the right light for future quantum networks may depend on what scientists prevent from being emitted, an approach that nearly tripled the share of desired photons.

Sources indicate that future quantum networks may one day allow quantum computers and other devices to exchange information through individual particles of light, known as photons. Making that possible requires reliable sources of photons with carefully controlled properties. One challenge is their frequency, which determines the kind of light they produce. A source can emit photons at several frequencies, leaving only a fraction suitable for the intended connection.

It has been revealed that scientists have traditionally addressed this problem using tiny optical structures called resonators. These structures influence a photon source so that it emits more light at a particular frequency. Although effective, resonators work within a narrow frequency range and must be precisely tuned to each source, making it difficult to use multiple sources together.

Recent findings suggest that researchers at the Technical University of Munich (TUM) and the Munich Center for Quantum Science and Technology (MCQST) have now demonstrated a different approach. Rather than encouraging a source to produce more light at the desired frequency, they change its surroundings to suppress the frequencies they do not want.

Recent findings suggest that the team uses structures called photonic crystal waveguides, which contain carefully arranged patterns on a nanometer scale. These patterns control the pathways through which light can be emitted, blocking unwanted frequencies while allowing the desired ones to remain.

According to recent reports, in initial experiments using erbium, an element already used in fiber-optic technologies, the researchers increased the proportion of photons emitted at the desired frequency from about 23% to around 72%. Previously, achieving comparable results required much more complex resonator systems.

The waveguides also offer greater flexibility. Their larger size allows multiple photon sources, known as emitters, to operate simultaneously within a single device, something that is much more limited with tiny resonators. Because the waveguides work across a broader range of frequencies, researchers can also select the desired frequency without having to precisely tune the structure to each individual emitter.

Another difference is that the new approach produces photons slightly more slowly, which can actually make them easier to manage.

In a recent development, “If photons are generated too quickly, it’s difficult for us to control their properties,” explains Andreas Reiserer, professor of quantum networks at TUM. “Our approach is therefore significantly better suited for many emitters than the resonators used to date.”.

Industry observers note that the findings could help researchers develop the interfaces needed to connect quantum devices over long distances. Such interfaces would have to convert information stored in a quantum system into individual photons that can travel through optical fibers.

Florian Burger, a doctoral student and the publication’s first author, sees the work as an early step toward that goal.

“Quantum networks are expected to connect many quantum systems with one another one day. This requires interfaces that can reliably transfer information from a quantum system to individual photons and then transmit them, for example, via optical fibers. Our work lays the foundation for this.”.

It has been revealed that reference: “Inhibited radiative decay enhances single-photon emitters” by Florian Burger, Stephan Rinner, Andreas Gritsch, Kilian Sandholzer and Andreas Reiserer, 16 July 2026, Nature Communications. DOI: 10.1038/s41467-026-75489-5.

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (959 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Universetoday

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Around four years ago, humanity intentionally hit an asteroid.
  • The lack of accurate measurement isnât for lack of trying.
  • It has been revealed that to help clear up any ambiguity about the math underlying this planetary defense mission, Hera is equipped with three main imaging tools.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Around four years ago, humanity intentionally hit an asteroid. The Double Asteroid Redirection Test (DART) was by pretty much all measures a resounding success when it struck the asteroid moonlet Dimorphos going more than 22,000 kilometers per hour. However, we still donât know just how much of a success it actually was - DART was a one-way mission with no real way to track the results of the impact close up. Enter Hera, the European Space Agency (ESA) mission that recently arrived in the binary asteroid system. Now, in a press release, ESA has provided some of the best pictures of the binary system since that fateful day four years ago.

The lack of accurate measurement isnât for lack of trying. Ground-based observatories have been watching 151m wide Dimorphos and its parent asteroid, 780m wide Didymos very closely over the last four years. They could tell that Dimorphos slowed its orbit around its larger companion by about 33 minutes. But some scientists were surprised by the magnitude of the change in orbit, based on the theoretical math done before the mission.

It has been revealed that to help clear up any ambiguity about the math underlying this planetary defense mission, Hera is equipped with three main imaging tools. Its standard âeyesâ are the Asteroid Framing cameras, which handle both black-and-white photography and navigation. The press release showcases an image from this system showing Didymos from roughly 28.5km away, with features down to roughly 2.7m per pixel.

Fraser talks about Hera's final insertion into the binary asteroid system.

In the image, you can clearly see the âspinning topâ shape of the larger asteroid in the pair. Didymos spins at a relatively rapid speed for its size, completing a rotation every 2.2 hours. That energy is strong enough to pull boulders and gravel towards the middle of the asteroid, causing a build-up of material that makes it look fatter in the middle than at its poles.

However, seeing an asteroid in black in white isnât as scientifically useful as seeing it in âcolorâ. That is what Heraâs second imaging system, the HyperScout H instrument, is designed to do. It monitors the asteroid over 25 different color bands. With that information, HyperScout H can absorb and reflect light with different unique patterns - essentially it can spectroscopy. Comparing the results to lab experiments on meteorite samples on Earth will help determine what Didymos and its smaller companion are actually made up of.

In a recent development, but why stop at simple hyperspectral imaging when you can also have heat vision? The Thermal Infrared Imager (TIRI), supplied to ESA by Japanâs Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA) gives Hera âSuperman-likeâ heat vision according to the press release. TIRI maps the temperature of the surface of the asteroids, and since solid rock dissipates heat much more slowly than porous or fragmented rock, it will also give a good indication of how solid Didymos really is.

Fraser talks about some of the results of the DART test.

Crucially, Dimorphos itself, the actual subject of the original DART test, is surprisingly absent from many of the pictures in this first round of releases. In the visible light images, Dimorphos is tucked almost entirely into the shadow of Didymos, appearing as a tiny sunlit spec beneath Didymos in one of the images. But with TIRIâs âSupermanâ view, the entire 151m wide asteroid is clearly in focus, glowing a shade of cool purple in the infrared. Cameras arenât the only thing Hera is carrying either. It will eventually launch two CubeSats, Juventus and Milan, to study the asteroid binary very closely. They will use ground-penetrating radar and even touch down on the surface of Dimorphos in an effort to understand what itstruly made of.

According to recent reports, but ultimately the overarching purpose of the mission is to get a better idea of how effectively we can move an asteroid out of the way if we need to. DART appeared to be a success on the surface. Understanding what really happened to Dimorphos is what Hera, with all its cameras and companion spacecraft, was literally designed for. And weâre just at the earliest phases of that process. The next step is a major release of even sharper images planned for a live event at the Berlin Museum of Natural History on November 25th. Asteroid watchers, and space enthusiasts more generally, should mark their calendars for our first high-resolution view of one of the biggest impacts weâve had on another body in the solar system to date.

#7594. Earth's Atmosphere Took Three Deep Breaths of Oxygen Before the Oceans Caught Up

Earth's Atmosphere Took Three Deep Breaths of Oxygen Before the Oceans Caught Up

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1452 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Universetoday

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, earth formed about 4.5 billion years ago, along with the rest of the planets.
  • The atmosphere, the oceans, and life itself are all parts of the system.
  • Recent findings suggest that cyanobacteria used sunlight to split water molecules apart.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, earth formed about 4.5 billion years ago, along with the rest of the planets. Life appeared somewhere between about 4.28 and 3.8 billion years ago; it's difficult to determine clearly. An oxygen atmosphere is a more recent development for Earth, in geological timescales, and understanding how that happened is a significant part of understanding the present-day Earth.

Earth is one massive system. The atmosphere, the oceans, and life itself are all parts of the system. In some respects, they can be studied in isolation. But when trying to understand Earth and its long history, they need to be understood together. The system changed significantly when life changed. Somewhere around 2.4 billion years ago, cyanobacteria appeared, and they brought a new trick with them: photosynthesis.

Recent findings suggest that cyanobacteria used sunlight to split water molecules apart. That did two things: it generated their chemical energy, and it released free oxygen into water, which eventually found its way into the atmosphere. That was a monumental stage of Earth's development that eventually led to an ozone layer, letting life flourish on the surface. The oxygenation of the atmosphere also led to complex life like us.

It has been revealed that but this all happened a long time ago. At first, the oxygen didn't accumulate in the atmosphere, and figuring out how it all played out isn't simple. Scientists know that the oxygenation history of the ocean and the atmosphere are coupled, but there are many questions. Some researchers argue that the atmosphere's oxygenation took place in different stages, one of which was the Great Oxygenation Event (GOE), while others have argued that the process was smoother. The debate continues.

Industry observers note that newly introduced research in The Innovation shows how Earth's atmosphere was oxygenated in three distinct steps, and that the deep ocean lagged behind in each case. In the last of the steps, deep ocean oxygenation lagged behind by 600 million years.

The research is titled "Stagewise oxygenation of the Earthâs atmosphere and oceans," and the authors are Haiyang Wang and Chao Li, geochemists at the Chengdu University of Technology.

"Earthâs surface oxygenation was a protracted, multi-step process," the authors write. "It is widely accepted that atmospheric O2 rose through three major steps, each closely linked to key evolutionary innovations.".

Industry observers note that the oceans and the atmosphere are linked, and during the quest to understand Earth's oxygenated atmosphere, researchers used the geological rock record to understand ocean chemistry. The well-known banded iron formations are a part of this. They record the ocean's oxygen levels. The atmosphere doesn't hold an ancient record, so the ocean's geological record was used as a proxy for the atmosphere's evolution and oxygenation, too.

So scientists largely think that three stages of rising oxygen created the modern atmosphere: the GOE about 2.4 billion years ago, the Neoproterozoic Oxygenation Event about 800 to 540 million years ago, and the Paleozoic Oxygenation Event about 400 million years ago.

It has been revealed that the researchers reiterate the understanding that ocean and atmospheric oxygenation are coupled. Research demonstrates that on billion year timescales, episodes of rising atmospheric oxygen precede the same episodic rise in ocean oxygenation, "whereas on shorter, million-year timescales, their redox states could diverge, exhibiting negative coupling," they write.

"Here, we synthesize geochemical, sedimentological, and palaeobiological evidence to reconstruct this coupled and dynamic atmosphere-ocean oxygenation history and to reassess its timing, mechanisms, and ecological consequences," the authors explain.

This work hinges on fresh geochemical proxies that give researchers a clearer picture of what happened so long ago.

"Recent advances in geochemical proxies, most notably sulfate triple-oxygen isotopes (Îâ²17O), provide new constraints on atmospheric oxygenation, complementing and in some cases revising interpretations from traditional ocean redox proxies," the authors explain.

The researchers say that this sulfate (SO4)offers a cleaner way to understand the oxygenation of the atmosphere. That's because of the isotopic composition of atmospheric oxygen, which is recorded when sulfate forms. It has a deficit of the isotope oxygen-17. So the sulfate can be used to track the rise of atmospheric O2, putting dates on each rise in atmospheric oxygen.

In a recent development, they found that the GOE is unchanged, sitting between 2.4â2.1 billion years ago. But this work changes the dates of the second and third oxygen rises.

The second, the Neoproterozoic Oxygenation Event was 1.3â1.0 billion years ago instead of 800 to 540 million years ago. The Paleozoic Oxygenation Event was 0.42â0.36 billion years instead of 0.44â0.41 billion.

Recent findings suggest that the researchers found something else, too. The previous dates for the Neoproterozoic and Paleozoic events still record something. But instead of dating atmospheric oxygen, they date the delayed oxygenation of the deep ocean. They lagged behind the oxygenation of the atmosphere by about 200 and 30 million years, respectively.

This graphic illustrates the results from upcoming research into the oxygenation of Earth's atmosphere that shows how Earth's O2 rose unevenly: shallow seas first, then the atmosphere, and much later the deep ocean. During a 2-billion-year transition, atmosphere and ocean O2 sometimes diverged despite long-term rise. Ocean oxygenation was highly variable, with extreme spatial heterogeneity over time. Image Credit: Stagewise oxygenation of the Earth's atmosphere and oceans. Wang and Li 2026, The Innovation.

In a recent development, on shorter timescales, the link between ocean and atmospheric oxygen is still the defining feature in this work. But it highlights that a change in one could've pushed the other in the opposite direction. The researchers think that what seems like a signal of rising oxygen levels is actually a drop. When a pulse of oxygen enters the ocean, it oxidized organic carbon and sulfide in the oceans. The organic carbon becomes CO2, and the sulfide becomes sulfate. The more organic carbon and sulfide there was in the ocean, the more it depleted atmospheric oxygen.

Industry observers note that over longer, billion year timescales, the atmophere is oxygenated as photosynthesis continues. But on shorter timescales, it can't keep up.

According to recent reports, "Earthâs surface oxygenation history reflects a dynamic and nonlinear interplay among atmospheric O2 evolution, land and ocean redox buffering, and ecological innovation," the authors write. "Overall, the trajectory from localized Archean oxygen oases to the globally well-oxygenated surface environments of today underscores how atmosphere-ocean oxygenation both governsâand is reciprocally shaped byâthe evolution of life.".

This figure shows the evolution of Earth's atmosphere-ocean redox states through time and space. (A) Before 2.4 Ga: atmosphere and oceans were largely anoxic, with oxygen restricted to localized, shallow-water oxygen oases. (B) From 2.4 to 1.0 Ga: atmospheric O2 remained low; oxygenated waters were confined to the ocean surface, and oxygen oases developed primarily along continental shelves. (C) Between 1.0 and 0.41 Ga: atmospheric O2 increased but fluctuated, while oxygenated waters progressively penetrated to greater depths, with shelf environments continuing to host oxygen oases. (D) Since â¼0.41 Ga: atmospheric O2 approached near-modern levels; deep oceans became pervasively oxygenated, whereas mid-depth waters developed oxygen minimum zones (OMZs) that waxed and waned (solid curves) in response to high organic matter export and oxygen consumption. DOC, dissolved organic carbon. Image Credit: Wang and Li 2026, The Innovation.

Industry observers note that it all happened in stages, as the different elements fed back on one another. This work indicates that during Earth's long path to an oxygenated atmosphere, the ocean and atmosphere didn't change in lockstep on shorter timescales. "Throughout the 2-billion-year oxygenation transition, atmospheric and oceanic oxygen levels were episodically decoupled on shorter timescales, superimposed on a long-term trajectory toward global oxidation," they write.

The pair of researchers acknowledge some of the weakness in the evidence that paints this picture. The record of oxygen isotopes in sulfate is coarse, not exquisitely detailed. Beyond one billion years ago, the levels aren't well-constrained. So it's still more open to interpretation. There may be other steps in the path to oxygenation that aren't clear yet.

Sources indicate that understanding how life and the planet co-evolved together is a monumental task. Scientists know it happened, but all of the details are difficult to detect. But if it happened here, it almost certainly happened on any other habitable worlds.

"These deep-time perspectives illuminate the co-evolution of life and Earthâs surface environments and provide a conceptual framework for evaluating planetary habitability," the authors write.

#7593. Scientists Uncover Why a Common Nutrient Can Be Dangerous for Blood Vessels

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (804 w)
