#7516. Tech Report: A vanished bird from Haiti may help solve an ancient Pacific mystery

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1341 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Earth ↗ Open Full Page

Tech Report: A vanished bird from Haiti may help solve an ancient Pacific mystery

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1341 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • DNA reveals how snipes and woodcocks reached distant islands, stopped migrating, changed physically, and became vulnerable to extinction.
  • The sandpiper family includes some of the most extreme long-distance migrants among birds.
  • It has been revealed that two branches of that family, the snipes and the woodcocks, have behaved quite differently.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

DNA reveals how snipes and woodcocks reached distant islands, stopped migrating, changed physically, and became vulnerable to extinction.

The sandpiper family includes some of the most extreme long-distance migrants among birds.

It has been revealed that two branches of that family, the snipes and the woodcocks, have behaved quite differently. These birds reached islands again and again, and migration was then abandoned.

Nearly every living species was examined in a new DNA study.

In a recent development, the results suggest that island settlement was accompanied by changes in body size and flying ability. Island species later proved vulnerable when people arrived with rats and cats.

It has been revealed that the work was led by Min Zhao, then a postdoctoral researcher at the Florida Museum of Natural History. Colleagues at Virginia Tech and the Field Museum in Chicago also took part.

Recent findings suggest that according to Zhao, the whole project grew out of one extinct bird from Hispaniola. That Caribbean island is shared by Haiti and the Dominican Republic.

It has been revealed that the dates reported in the study were estimated from family trees built with DNA. The uncertainty attached to them can run to millions of years.

Florida Museum researchers dug the bird’s bones out of a cave in Haiti in 1984.

In 2015, those bones were described by two scientists as a fresh species of woodcock. Woodcocks are long-billed birds that probe soft soil for food.

According to recent reports, one of the two scientists was David Steadman, who is now an emeritus curator at the museum. He is also listed as a co-author of the upcoming study.

Recent findings suggest that zhao’s team extracted DNA from two of the fossil specimens. The researchers then read the mitochondrial genome, a small set of genes passed from mother to offspring.

Both specimens were placed with the snipes, which form the sister group of the woodcocks. Their closest living relative turned out to be the giant snipe of lowland South America.

The analysis suggested a South American origin for the Haitian bird’s ancestors. The two lineages are thought to have split between 5 and 12 million years ago.

Sources indicate that why, then, did the bones resemble those of a woodcock? The authors think the bird’s build may have been altered by island living, which could explain the mix-up.

The outer wing bone of the Haitian bird was unusually short when compared with its upper wing bone. The authors wrote that it could fly but probably not well.

The team sequenced 45 samples in total. Two were the Haitian fossils and 19 were toe pads taken from old museum specimens. The remaining 24 were fresh tissue samples.

Recent findings suggest that all but one of the 29 living species of snipes and woodcocks were covered by these samples. Specimens were supplied by ten museums and research collections.

A family tree was built from the data, and both groups were traced back to Eurasia.

The ancestors of today’s American birds crossed from the Eastern Hemisphere to the Western Hemisphere four separate times.

One of those crossings took place roughly 20 million years ago. It was then that the ancestor of the American woodcock reached North America.

The researchers could not tell whether the bird arrived across the Atlantic or by way of Alaska.

The Austral snipes are found on the outlying islands of Latest Zealand. Scientists have long placed these small brown birds in a group of their own.

According to recent reports, some snipes from Eurasia spend each winter in Australia and on nearby islands. The DNA showed that those visitors are not close relatives of the Austral snipes.

Instead, the Austral snipes share a branch with several large South American snipes and the extinct Haitian bird.

Two DNA datasets placed the split between the Austral snipes and their relatives at about 14 million and nearly 18 million years ago, respectively.

Recent findings suggest that the southern continents had broken apart long before either estimate. The snipes’ ancestor most likely crossed the Pacific.

How the crossing happened remains an open question. The authors suggested that birds straying far outside their normal range may have played a role. Such straying was perhaps caused by extreme weather.

The authors also raised a route through Antarctica. Patches of treeless tundra are thought to have lasted there until at least 12.8 million years ago.

Several living snipe species still breed on tundra in the Arctic.

Sources indicate that the analysis indicated that the ancestors of both snipes and woodcocks were migrants. Their island descendants are not.

Ten of the 29 living species are found only on islands, and none of those ten migrates.

The habit was lost several times. Woodcocks gave it up when they settled the Malay Archipelago in Southeast Asia. Snipes did the same when they settled South America and Madagascar.

Body size changed as well, although not in a single direction.

Sources indicate that the Amami woodcock of southern Japan is about 45% heavier than the Eurasian woodcock, its closest mainland relative. Madagascar’s snipe is about 91% heavier than the common snipe of Eurasia.

In a recent development, the opposite change is seen in the Austral snipes. Their average weight is 3.4 ounces (96 grams), which is about the weight of a deck of cards.

South American snipes on the same branch average 8.6 ounces (243.5 grams). That is more than twice as much.

The smaller size may be explained by scarce food, the authors suggested. Competition from kiwis and other birds that probe the soil for worms was also considered possible.

Ten species of snipes and woodcocks are known to have died out in the recent geologic past. Nine of them lived on islands.

The Austral snipes suffered the heaviest losses. Three of nine known species survive. All three are ranked as Vulnerable or Near Threatened by the IUCN Red List.

The South Island snipe died out in 1964, and introduced black rats are regarded as the likely cause.

Sources indicate that no resident snipe or woodcock is left in the Caribbean. At least three species have been lost there.

According to recent reports, the youngest dated bones of the Haitian bird are about 600 years old. Rats and feral cats brought by people are suspected of causing its extinction.

Recent findings suggest that snipes nest on the ground, where they can be reached by those predators. Island species had given up migration, and in some cases strong flight as well.

The authors wrote that these changes made such species especially vulnerable to human impacts.

Overhunting was named as one of those impacts.

Jessica Oswald, a co-author, also worked on the study at the Florida Museum.

“People will eat anything,” said Oswald. She said a crew of hungry explorers or whalers could wipe out an island’s birds in a single weekend.

Recent findings suggest that island woodcocks in Japan and Southeast Asia appear to have fared better. They live in mountain forests, which may be harder for people to reach.

New Zealand may have been reached first by the Austral snipes.

From there they could have spread to Norfolk Island, New Caledonia and Fiji. The opposite path cannot be ruled out, because no genetic data exist for those islands’ extinct snipes.

More snipe species may once have lived in the Pacific and are now extinct. In that case, today’s birds would be the last survivors of a larger group. Direct fossil evidence of that link across the Pacific is still missing.

The Haitian bird’s place on the tree rests on mitochondrial genes from two specimens. A possible close relative from Puerto Rico is also extinct and has not been tested genetically.

The authors suggest that DNA from fossils yet to be found on Pacific islands could help trace how snipes spread across the region.

The full study was published in the journal Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.

#7514. Could Earth have been collecting dark matter for billions of years?

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1000 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Earth ↗ Open Full Page

Could Earth have been collecting dark matter for billions of years?

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1000 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Heat measurements from dead stars helped physicists narrow down how dark matter might interact with ordinary matter.
  • Physicists have spent decades building dark matter detectors deep underground, and they still haven’t caught a single particle.
  • A new study suggests that Earth itself, along with the Sun, Jupiter and a handful of dead stars, might trap certain kinds of dark matter better than any lab instrument.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Heat measurements from dead stars helped physicists narrow down how dark matter might interact with ordinary matter.

Physicists have spent decades building dark matter detectors deep underground, and they still haven’t caught a single particle.

A new study suggests that Earth itself, along with the Sun, Jupiter and a handful of dead stars, might trap certain kinds of dark matter better than any lab instrument.

These bodies could have been collecting slow-moving particles for billions of years.

The researchers used neutrino data and heat measurements to rule out some combinations of particle mass and interaction strength that laboratory experiments couldn’t probe.

The work was led by Alejandro Ibarra from the Technical University of Munich, Merlin Reichard from the Korea Institute for Advanced Study and Gaurav Tomar from the Sogang University in Seoul.

About 85% of the matter in the universe is dark matter. We know it’s there because galaxies spin faster than their visible matter can explain and light bends more than it should as it passes them.

Beyond that, very little is known about it. Physicists are stuck in a frustrating loop.

You can’t identify something you can’t see, and you can’t design a way to see it without some idea of what it is. So they make a guess, build an experiment to test it, and so far the answer has always been no.

One guess is that dark matter isn’t completely dark. Its particles might respond to electricity and magnetism very faintly, carrying a tiny fraction of an electron’s charge or acting like microscopic magnets.

The paper describes five such properties. One of them, the “anapole moment,” is a doughnut-shaped kind of magnetism.

Any of the five would let a dark matter particle occasionally bump into an atom.

In a recent development, underground detectors wait for those bumps. A slow particle taps an atom so gently that the instrument doesn’t notice.

In practice, these detectors are more sensitive to faster dark matter particles.

Sources indicate that planets and stars work the other way around. A fast particle shoots straight through them. A slow one only needs to lose a little speed in a collision before gravity grabs it and won’t let go.

According to recent reports, over billions of years, trapped particles would sink toward the center and crowd together. Once packed tightly enough, they could meet and annihilate, turning into other particles.

Sources indicate that some of those would be neutrinos, which pass through rock almost as if it weren’t there. The rest would deposit their energy as heat.

“In this work, we considered four celestial bodies: Earth, the Sun, Jupiter and white dwarfs,” Tomar mentioned.

In a recent development, “There are dedicated experiments, for example IceCube at the South Pole, looking for neutrinos from the Sun and Earth. For Jupiter and white dwarfs, we considered the heating possibilities.”.

For the Sun and Earth, the team used limits from IceCube, a detector built into the Antarctic ice, and from its smaller companion detector, DeepCore.

Sources indicate that that included ten years of IceCube data on neutrinos coming from Earth’s core. There was no excess.

Neither Jupiter nor the white dwarfs generate heat through nuclear fusion.

The Cassini spacecraft measured how much heat Jupiter leaks from its interior.

Industry observers note that the white dwarfs are burnt-out stellar cores in M4, a cluster of ancient stars. Each one holds about 1.4 times the Sun’s mass in a ball with a radius of roughly 1,250 kilometers.

If a candidate type of dark matter would make these objects give off more heat than they actually do, it can be crossed off.

Earth turned out to be the best test for dark matter with a tiny electric charge. For particles heavier than about ten protons, it set the strongest limits yet.

In a recent development, there are two reasons. First, a charged particle’s pull reaches a long way, so it is easily drawn in. Second, Earth’s core is full of iron, whose atoms each carry 26 protons, which makes collisions more likely.

The white dwarfs set leading limits on two of the more exotic properties, the charge radius and the anapole moment, across a wide range of particle masses.

For very heavy particles, they also beat earlier limits on dark matter’s magnetic dipole moment.

The anapole limits matter for one popular candidate whose only possible electromagnetic property is the anapole moment.

For that candidate, the white dwarfs reach places that particle colliders and underground detectors struggle to get to.

Sources indicate that jupiter was a letdown. In general, it didn’t improve on limits that already existed. None of the four bodies beat earlier limits on the electric dipole moment either.

According to recent reports, underground labs sit beneath a kilometer or more of rock to block cosmic rays. If dark matter interacts strongly with ordinary matter, that same rock could slow it down or stop it before it reaches the detector.

The shield could be hiding the very particles the experiment is looking for.

Planets and stars don’t have this problem. The more strongly dark matter interacts, the better they catch it.

Sources indicate that there is one notable caveat. The more dark matter surrounds a star, the more of it the star can capture, and nobody has measured how much dark matter M4 contains.

The team had to rely on estimates from models.

Sources indicate that “We do not know the dark matter density there. We used estimated values, so if those values change, our limits could become weaker or stronger,” Tomar noted.

Tomar suggests two places to look next. One is even colder white dwarfs in regions with more dark matter, where any extra heat would be easier to detect.

The other is beyond the Solar System, where exoplanets could serve as dark matter traps too.

The study is published in the Journal of Cosmology and Astroparticle Physics.

Industry News: Newborn stars are hiding in the red threads of a neighboring galaxy

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (781 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Webb peers into N159, where dusty filaments shelter some of the youngest stars in a neighboring galaxy.
  • Today’s Image of the Day takes us inside a cloud where stars are being born in a neighboring galaxy.
  • In this view from the James Webb Space Telescope, pale blue gas fills broad cavities, orange pillars jut from their edges, and dark red threads wind across the middle.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Webb peers into N159, where dusty filaments shelter some of the youngest stars in a neighboring galaxy.

Today’s Image of the Day takes us inside a cloud where stars are being born in a neighboring galaxy.

In this view from the James Webb Space Telescope, pale blue gas fills broad cavities, orange pillars jut from their edges, and dark red threads wind across the middle.

Some of the youngest stars in the scene are still tucked inside those threads.

The cloud, known as N159, lies about 161,000 light-years away in the Large Magellanic Cloud, a satellite galaxy of the Milky Way.

Webb’s image spans about 230 light-years. Across that distance, some stars are still gathering the material they need to grow, while others already shine fiercely enough to change the shape of the cloud around them.

Industry observers note that start with the pale blue areas. They trace hydrogen gas exposed to intense ultraviolet light from massive stars.

That radiation can knock electrons loose from hydrogen atoms. As the electrons rejoin hydrogen nuclei, the gas gives off light of its own.

A bright patch can therefore reveal where massive stars are affecting their surroundings, even if the glow itself comes from the gas.

Industry observers note that those stars also send streams of particles into the cloud. Over time, these stellar winds can help hollow out cavities and sculpt the denser material along their edges.

Industry observers note that look closely at where the blue meets the orange. Small pillars extend into the open spaces, marking places where pockets of dense gas and dust have persisted as material around them has been cleared away.

The bright knot on the left is the Papillon Nebula, an unusually compact pocket of glowing hydrogen that the Hubble Space Telescope first resolved in 1999.

In Webb’s wider view, it takes up only a small part of the frame. Its intense glow draws the eye, but the quieter areas around it hold some of the best clues to where stars are forming now.

One of the best places to zoom in is just above the blue cavity on the right. Thin red strands cross this part of the frame.

They trace molecular hydrogen, a form of the gas in which two hydrogen atoms are bound together.

Deep inside dense strands like these, gas and dust can shield developing stars from the radiation and winds of their more powerful neighbors.

Webb’s Near-Infrared Camera records light at wavelengths beyond what our eyes can see.

Some of that light gets through dust that blocks visible starlight, revealing points of light buried in the cloud.

Image processors assign visible colors to observations made through different filters.

Here, those colors distinguish the red threads of molecular gas from the orange glow of carbon-based molecules and the pale blue of ionized hydrogen.

Astronomer Nolan Habel and colleagues compared the brightness of more than 300,000 points of light across ten infrared filters.

It has been revealed that some gave off more infrared light than expected from a star alone. That extra light can come from surrounding dust, which absorbs energy from the star and radiates it back into space.

Many of the sources the researchers identified as possible young stars lined up with dusty strands and clouds of molecular gas.

In a preprint describing the observations, the team reported that the eastern part of N159 contains more developed groups of stars, while the western part reveals signs of more recent star formation.

Some groups may be less than half a million years old. That difference suggests that star formation unfolded in stages across the cloud.

The Large Magellanic Cloud has a smaller proportion of elements heavier than helium than the Milky Way does.

The early universe was also poorer in those elements, which built up over generations of stars.

Studying a region like N159 gives astronomers a chance to see how stars form with a mix of ingredients closer in some respects to what was available long ago.

Industry observers note that the image also captures a change that is easy to miss at first glance. In one part of the cloud, stars have already opened clearings around themselves.

It has been revealed that in another, dense gas still shelters stars that are just getting started. Given time, much of that gas will disperse, leaving the stars exposed.

For now, the thin red strands mark places where some of the newest stars in this corner of a neighboring galaxy are still taking shape.

Image Credit: ESA/Webb, NASA & CSA, E. Sabbi, M. Zamani.

This Is The Summer To Tick Santorini Off The Bucket List

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It’s June, and for perhaps the first time in modern history, Santorini isn’t crowded.
  • And that’s a shame, because there’s been a lovely tourism revolution brewing there, where local hoteliers are bringing back the kind of experience and hospitality that you want to come back for over and over again.
  • As someone who goes at least once or twice a year, and will again very shortly, I can only advocate to tick it off the bucket list this summer, because you’ll never find prices, availability or an experience quite like it again for a while.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It’s June, and for perhaps the first time in modern history, Santorini isn’t crowded. Those earthquakes a good few months ago? Not even a flower pot was tipped over, yet incessant clickbait headlines managed to have a lasting impact.

And that’s a shame, because there’s been a lovely tourism revolution brewing there, where local hoteliers are bringing back the kind of experience and hospitality that you want to come back for over and over again.

As someone who goes at least once or twice a year, and will again very shortly, I can only advocate to tick it off the bucket list this summer, because you’ll never find prices, availability or an experience quite like it again for a while.

According to recent reports, in the last 20 years, Santorini got totally overrun. Cruise tourism and day trip mania somewhat ruined a once idyllic, low-key fishing island and then Instagram and TikTok lit the match.

According to recent reports, but now the TikTok crowd is in Mykonos and Santorini, as unequalled in beauty as ever, is lovely again. Hotels like The Vasilicos and Santorini Sky bring wildly different, delightfully luxurious and hospitality driven experiences to the island.

Beach clubs, yes Santorini’s beaches are underrated, have made a nice little mark on quieter coasts with great effect too. Assyrtiko, the local grape has hit the world stage as a darling of sommeliers in top restaurants and vineyards like Vassaltis offer stunning tasting experiences.

In a recent development, and the food? There’s no Nobu, or Scorpios here, so there are plenty of places to feel the benefit of European pricing, including a personal favorite at Kantouni.

The trouble with Santorini has historically been that many of the best hotels are small, they fill up rapidly, and as they do, they charge a fortune. For the best, like the ones mentioned above, it’s still worth it. But this season, all across the board, prices are lower and even if you don’t care about price, many of the best which might typically be sold out for the season have rooms.

As an additional tailwind for travelers, flights between the US and Europe are quieter this summer, which means there’s deals to be had with both points and cash from major markets to Santorini. If you don’t see cheap flights to Santorini, try a major hub and booking an onward ticket separately.

Sources indicate that naturally, precaution is a good thing in life. But fear mongering for the sake of clicks is another beast and I can’t help but be fairly appalled by the many weeks and months of coverage and follow up coverage, reiterating a narrative of fear… despite no damage to anything, anywhere.

If you do bag a great deal this summer and visit one of my very favorite places, and use this great Santorini guide to make the most of your time, you can thank the media.

  • Tim Kaine, D-Va., said Thursday he is working on legislative language ending the war that he wants attached to the next continuing resolution that is needed by Dec.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that sen. Tim Kaine, D-Va., talks with reporters in the Capitol on Sept. 30. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

A group of prominent Senate Democrats is pushing to use a must-pass spending bill to cut off funding for the Iran war, complicating the path toward a bipartisan deal for averting a partial government shutdown next month.

In a recent development, sen. Tim Kaine, D-Va., said Thursday he is working on legislative language ending the war that he wants attached to the next continuing resolution that is needed by Dec. 11, when current funding runs out.

“I know it’s going to be my main push,” he remarked. “I have to work with colleagues to try to find some language that works. And I’m not there yet, but I’ve told everybody that’s an opportunity.”.

It has been revealed that democratic Sens. Michael Bennet of Colorado, Chris Van Hollen of Maryland, Tammy Duckworth of Illinois and independent Bernie Sanders of Vermont released a statement Thursday that they would oppose any deal that does not include “language that restricts the Trump Administration from using appropriated funds to continue his war against Iran.”.

According to recent reports, “When we vote on appropriations, we intend to fund the government and stop funds for this war,” the senators mentioned. “It is what the American people demand, and what they deserve.”.

It is unlikely that Republicans, who are in control of both chambers of Congress until January, not to mention the Oval Office beyond that, would agree to such a deal.

House Appropriations Chairman Tom Cole, R-Okla., noted earlier this week that “a Republican Congress is not going to send bills to a Republican president that he's going to veto.”.

According to recent reports, while ending the war is a top priority of Democrats as they take back power in the fresh Congress, insisting on doing so this year could lead to a Christmas-time partial government shutdown. If a shutdown starts after Dec. 11, it’s possible it would still be ongoing when Democrats take control of both chambers in January.

But some Democrats appeared to still be weighing how quickly to push for a cutoff of war funding.

Senate Appropriations ranking member Patty Murray, D-Wash, said that whether or not Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth remains in his job, “we’re still going to have language stopping this war.”.

She was coy on whether that fight would take place on the anticipated continuing resolution in December or wait until next year when Democrats take back power, saying that lawmakers are “looking at all options.”.

According to recent reports, democrats are committed to ending the "reckless and costly war of choice in Iran," House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., said Thursday. He deferred to House Appropriations ranking member Rosa DeLauro, D-Conn., "to see what’s possible in advance of Dec. 11" in talks with the other top appropriators.

"I don’t want to get out ahead of Congresswoman DeLauro, but House Democrats have uniformly opposed providing any additional money to Donald Trump’s war machine. to Pete Hegseth’s war machine, over in the Middle East," Jeffries noted.

It’s not clear how long a potential continuing resolution would last, and DeLauro said earlier this week that she wants it to be as short as possible.

The Office of Management and Budget has not yet submitted “anomalies” — changes to the current spending levels to be included in the continuing resolution — to Congress.

In a recent development, the administration is considering options including a stopgap bill that would run through March, sources familiar with the talks noted. But no decision on the timing covered by the anomalies has been made.

Aris Folley, Jacob Fulton and Michael Macagnone contributed to this report.

#7508. Latest Update: What to know about kratom and its powerful derivatives

Latest Update: What to know about kratom and its powerful derivatives

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1306 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencenews

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • This is a human-written story voiced by AI.
  • For the past few years, addiction specialist Roopa Sethi has been seeing a new set of patients.
  • Industry observers note that kratom is a plant used for chronic pain relief and to help people stay off opioids.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .).

For the past few years, addiction specialist Roopa Sethi has been seeing a new set of patients. They show up at the University of Kansas Health System hospital in Kansas City with what looks like severe opiate withdrawal: nausea, vomiting and muscle aches. They’re extremely anxious and sometimes hallucinating. But they haven’t taken an opioid, like fentanyl or heroin. Instead, they’ve used something labeled as kratom, though it may not contain kratom at all.

Industry observers note that kratom is a plant used for chronic pain relief and to help people stay off opioids. But souped-up new versions with hyperpotent derivatives of the active compound are sold online and in gas stations. The derivatives act strongly on the body’s opioid receptors and are often far more powerful than the opioid drugs they are sometimes intended to replace. Kratom products — sold as pills, liquid shots, edibles and more — are often mislabeled, and state and federal regulations lag far behind.

A 2026 survey estimated that about 5 million Americans have used kratom or similar products, and the increased use has sent kratom-related exposures up 1,200 percent from only 258 exposures in 2015, according to the National Poison Data System.

Now, newer versions of the substance can produce withdrawal symptoms like nausea and vomiting, which are often so severe they bring people to the hospital. Here’s what to know.

According to recent reports, kratom comes from the dried leaves of Mitragyna speciosa, a tree native to Southeast Asia. Dutch scientist Pieter Willem Korthals first described it in 1839. But “without a doubt, it was used likely for centuries prior to that” in countries including Thailand, Indonesia and Myanmar, indicates Oliver Grundmann, a pharmacologist at the University of Florida in Gainesville. “Wherever there is a stream, these trees are growing there.” People chewed the leaves for a stimulant effect and brewed them into a tea to treat pain,” Grundmann says.

In the United States, kratom is billed pain treatment that is more “natural” than opiates like morphine, Sethi says. “When you take this product at low doses, it is used for waking up … but at higher doses it becomes opiate-like.” Others take it to treat withdrawal or cravings from opioid use.

According to recent reports, the leaf form contains more than 40 different naturally occurring chemicals called alkaloids that could have psychoactive effects. The most important is mitragynine, which makes up two-thirds of the plant’s alkaloid content.

According to recent reports, mitragynine acts on the body’s mu opioid receptors. These receptors — found in the brain, spinal cord and gut — usually respond to natural peptide signals in the body such as endorphins, signaling cells to produce pain relief and release chemicals like dopamine. The receptors get their name from the most famous drug that binds to them: opium. Mitragynine is not derived from or related to opium or morphine but it binds partially to the receptor.

“It’s kind of like a dimmer switch versus turning on the lights,” states Mallory Pullman, a clinical toxicologist at the Mississippi Poison Control Center at the University of Mississippi Medical Center in Jackson. “You don’t fully light your room.”.

Industry observers note that mitragynine also hits receptors that bind norepinephrine, serotonin and dopamine receptors, indicates Grundmann. The activity at adrenergic receptors creates a stimulant-like effect. “Now I think when we look at mitragynine, it’s primarily kind of this duality of the adrenergic and the opioid receptor activity,” he says, producing stimulating and depressive results in turn.

What nature made, chemists and users are happy to tweak.

According to recent reports, as the kratom leaf is dried, Grundmann states, tiny amounts of mitragynine metabolize into another alkaloid, 7-hydroxymitragynine, or 7-OH. After someone takes kratom, the body also converts some mitragynine to 7-OH. The small chemical tweak changes the compound from one that binds partially to the mu opioid receptors to one that binds fully — like morphine or opium, Grundmann says. 7-OH binds 10 times more strongly to mu opioid receptors than mitragynine does. The resulting product is far more potent in its effects and addictive potential.

It has been revealed that when people use the leaves alone, the amount of 7-OH is extremely limited. But by the mid-2010s, scientists found products with more than 500 percent more 7-OH than in the plant alone, and now, consumers can buy products labeled as pure 7-OH.

According to recent reports, while 7-OH can be described as “natural” because it can, in theory, occur in nature, toxicologists like Pullman are also seeing synthetic derivatives that are even stronger, including one molecule named MGM-15. MGM-15 is sold as a “research chemical” and is four times more powerful than 7-OH.

According to recent reports, what is in kratom products may not always be what’s on the label, leaving people in the dark about what they are taking. In a 2026 analysis of 44 different kratom products, including tablets, dissolvable films and edibles, Pullman and her colleagues found that 85 percent of the products had contents that did not match the label. Some advertised kratom but contained very high levels of 7-OH. Others had alkaloids that weren’t listed at all.

It’s “very concerning at a consumer level if you can’t trust what’s actually on the label,” Pullman indicates.

Recent findings suggest that sethi started hearing the word kratom about 10 years ago in her work with people seeking treatment for opioid use. “I would have patients intermittently tell me about kratom use,” she states. People were using kratom to stay off opioids, or to treat pain, and didn’t report being addicted to the plant.

Now, it’s a different story, Sethi states.

Sources indicate that patients who started using kratom or 7-OH to get off opioids “now are having really bad withdrawal and cravings and ending up in the hospital,” she notes. Some are seeking addiction treatment, not for opioids, but for kratom and 7-OH. In 2025, U.S. poison centers documented 3,434 kratom-related exposure reports, reported both by people who called the center and medical professionals. “I see less fentanyl and more kratom at this point, or more 7-OH,” Sethi says.

Industry observers note that in July of 2026, the U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration temporarily classified some kratom derivatives as Schedule I drugs, meaning they have high abuse potential and no medical use. Those derivatives include 7-OH and another related kratom derivative, mitragynine pseudoindoxyl or MGPI, as well as MGM-15 and its powerful sibling MGM-16. The DEA re-upped the temporary scheduling of MGM-15 and 16 and MGPI in October. 7-OH was temporarily placed in Schedule I at any dose higher than that found in the kratom plant. The U.S. Food and Drug Administration has also issued statements warning consumers not to use the products. None of these measures affect the legality of the kratom leaf itself.

It has been revealed that regulations vary at the state level: Twenty-six states don’t regulate kratom at all, while six states and the District of Columbia list kratom’s ingredients as a Schedule I controlled substance, like the current federal scheduling. A further 18 states regulate sale and manufacture in some way.

“I think there’s a lot more concern now, especially that there might be potential opioids out on the market,” Pullman says. Regulations are trying to thread the needle between banning the plant and banning high-potency derivatives, knowing that when one derivative gets smacked down, another will rapidly appear in its place. That cycle is a familiar one, mirroring the evolution and development of synthetic opioids.

“There’s risk with everything,” she says. “I think it’s key to distinguish the difference between a synthetic product versus the natural, and that way we can clearly attribute where the risk lies.”.

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (892 w)

General 📈 Bullish 🌐 Earth ↗ Open Full Page

A man sees his cat’s eyes in other people’s faces after brain surgery

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (892 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A rare case report describes a man who sees his cat's eyes in human faces after brain surgery, showing how memory can shape face distortions.
  • On some days, a 28-year-old man identified as Karl sees his cat’s eyes in every human face he looks at.
  • The case, described in a short report in the journal Cortex, points to how face perception is built.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A rare case report describes a man who sees his cat's eyes in human faces after brain surgery, showing how memory can shape face distortions.

On some days, a 28-year-old man identified as Karl sees his cat’s eyes in every human face he looks at. The researchers who documented his case think the features may come from visual memory.

The case, described in a short report in the journal Cortex, points to how face perception is built.

The features Karl sees are not generic cat eyes. He recognizes them as his own cat’s.

The authors read that as evidence that memory can feed individual facial features back into what a person sees.

The report covers a single case, written up from Karl’s own descriptions, and its images are reconstructions he helped refine rather than scans of anything in his brain.

Brad Duchaine of Dartmouth College led the report with Antônio Mello, a doctoral student at Dartmouth, and Jennifer Nosker, a neuropsychologist at Brigham and Women’s Hospital in Boston.

“This case of Karl seeing his cat’s features in human faces and vice versa demonstrates that individual features can be pulled from memory and influence our ongoing perception,” Duchaine said.

Karl’s distortions began two years ago, after surgeons removed a tangle of blood vessels from the back of his right temporal lobe, a region central to recognizing faces.

The condition is called prosopometamorphopsia, or PMO, in which faces look distorted. His version includes palinopsia, in which something seen earlier persists in later vision.

Recent findings suggest that his gray tabby, Luna, is often the first face he sees in the morning. On those days, her enlarged pupils, cat-like eye sockets, and the shading around them can appear on human faces for hours afterward, in person or on a screen.

The transfer runs the other way too. If a familiar person is the first face he sees, that person’s eye shape and pupil size can show up in his cat’s face. Episodes often last several hours, and occasionally they last the whole day.

What makes the case useful to researchers is the precision of the swap.

Only parts of a face move, usually the eye region, sometimes with its coloring and texture, while the rest of the viewed face looks normal.

In a recent development, the transferred features also look coherent. They blend into the face rather than appearing superimposed on it, and they shift naturally as Karl changes his angle or distance.

It has been revealed that and Karl can say whose they are. He identifies the borrowed eyes as belonging to particular people he knows, or to his cat, which led the authors to suggest the features are retrieved from long-term visual memory.

He has frequently experienced human-to-human transfers as well.

It has been revealed that the report opens with a case the same journal published in 1986. Nine months after a stroke, a woman riding a bus looked at a poodle on a passenger’s lap, then looked away, and saw the poodle’s face on every passenger.

The poodle faces persisted for about 30 minutes after she got off the bus.

The 1986 case suggested faces are processed differently from other things people see, because the dog’s face appeared only on other faces.

Karl’s experience sharpens the point: the brain seems to store and reactivate identity-specific pieces of faces, not only whole faces.

Whole-face substitutions like the poodle case are rare, the authors wrote.

Over five years, about 275 people reporting face distortions have contacted the lab through its PMO website, and most describe changes to the shape, position, color, or texture of features.

According to recent reports, the 1986 case came with a line drawing. Karl’s came with photorealistic images, generated with an AI model from his verbal descriptions and from a sketch he drew.

Recent findings suggest that the images were then refined over several months until he judged they matched his experience. Karl made some of the changes himself.

“AI provides researchers like us with the ability to generate more accurate visualizations of what people are experiencing when they’re having distorted visual perceptions,” Duchaine stated.

“If you know what the person is experiencing, you can much better research what they’re dealing with and try to figure out ways to control it.”.

The images also help patients explain the condition to family and friends, he added.

Duchaine noted his lab has heard from people who were told they had a psychiatric problem, and in some cases were put on antipsychotic drugs, when their problem was visual.

The report rests on one person’s account of his own perception, which no one else can see directly. It is a clinical description, not an experiment, and it does not test what triggers an episode.

What the report can’t say is how common this feature-level borrowing is.

The authors wrote only that several other people with PMO have told them of face palinopsia, against a far larger number who report seeing faces warp in shape or color.

The team plans to keep working with Karl, and the authors expect photorealistic reconstructions to become an increasingly valuable tool for recording what patients with perceptual disorders actually see.

The full study was published in the journal Cortex.

#7504. A single drop of coolant could change how data centers cool their chips

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1067 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚠️ Warning 🌐 Earth ↗ Open Full Page

A single drop of coolant could change how data centers cool their chips

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1067 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Low-cost water handles steady heat and one costly coolant drop boils on the spikes, a data center cooling idea tested on a chip at Waterloo.
  • Cooling an overheating computer chip sounds like a job for more cold liquid.
  • Engineers placed the drop, just over a quarter of an inch across, on a heated sapphire square submerged in water.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Low-cost water handles steady heat and one costly coolant drop boils on the spikes, a data center cooling idea tested on a chip at Waterloo.

Cooling an overheating computer chip sounds like a job for more cold liquid. In a lab test, a single drop of coolant cooled a simulated chip’s hottest spot faster than a bath of the same coolant.

Engineers placed the drop, just over a quarter of an inch across, on a heated sapphire square submerged in water.

The drop boiled, and within 15 seconds the center of the hot spot had cooled by about 31°F (17°C).

The idea is to spend expensive coolant only where and when a chip needs it, and let low-cost water do the rest.

Sushanta Mitra, a professor of mechanical and mechatronics engineering at the University of Waterloo in Canada, led the work with postdoctoral researcher Tian-Yu Zhang and doctoral student Arnav Banerjee.

The test ran on a heated square of sapphire standing in for a chip, not on a working processor.

In a recent development, “It’s a division of labor,” said Mitra. “Water is excellent at handling steady, everyday heat and the drops take care of sudden spikes.”.

Operators of data centers increasingly cool their servers by submerging the electronics in a liquid that doesn’t conduct electricity.

Industry observers note that the trouble is that chips don’t heat evenly. AI workloads have pushed data centers toward denser processors that draw more power.

A processor core can run far hotter than the rest of the chip for a few seconds at a time. Such bursts make chips slow down and age faster, and a liquid that simply surrounds the chip responds slowly.

Coolants that boil pull heat away faster, but they’re costly, and boiling is hard to start at exactly the right spot.

Purified water moves heat better than the standard fluids, and with the electronics insulated it can serve as a coolant itself. In still water, though, the currents that carry heat away from a sudden hot spot can be slow to start.

The sapphire square measured 1.2 inches (30 millimeters) on each side and was thinner than a dime. An electric current heated a coating on its surface.

The chip sat under about 1 fluid ounce (30 milliliters) of purified water, less than half an inch deep.

Industry observers note that the team squeezed a drop of Novec-7100, an electronics coolant that boils at about 142°F (61°C), onto the chip through a needle. The coolant is heavier than water and barely dissolves in it, so the drop stayed on the chip.

Sources indicate that then they switched on the power. The highest of three settings was about 86 watts, roughly a bright old-style light bulb’s heat packed into an area the size of a postage stamp.

An infrared camera under the chip recorded its temperature 30 times a second, and a high-speed camera filmed the bubbles. Each test ran three times.

For comparison, the team also ran the chip in a tank of pure coolant and in water alone.

At the highest heat setting, the drop made the difference.

Once the chip’s surface passed the coolant’s boiling point, bubbles formed inside the drop while the water around it stayed liquid. Within 15 seconds, the center of the hot spot was some 31°F (17°C) cooler.

A chip in a tank of pure coolant reached a similar peak temperature, but cooled far more slowly afterward. In water alone, the chip kept getting hotter.

“Boiling soaks up a lot of heat and the rising bubbles stir the surrounding water so it carries heat away faster,” said Mitra, who is also executive director of the Waterloo Institute for Nanotechnology.

“We get the punch of boiling, but only where and when it’s needed.”.

The chip surface around the drop also ran cooler than it did in water alone, so the drop was helping beyond the patch it covered.

According to recent reports, the boiling drop had limits. At the lowest heat setting, water alone kept the chip coolest early on. And until the drop had boiled away, its own footprint ran up to 29°F (16°C) hotter than the surface around it.

Mitra’s lab specializes in wrapping one liquid in a thin skin of another, and the team tried it on the coolant drops.

Industry observers note that the team floated a small ring from a plumbing supplier on the water, poured a thin layer of silicone oil inside it, and let coolant drip through the oil. Each drop picked up a silicone skin as it sank to the chip.

The silicone skin changed the boiling. At the middle heat setting, a plain silicone skin delayed boiling by about 1.5 seconds and let the hot spot climb about 14°F (8°C) higher first.

When boiling did start, it happened all at once, as one large bubble, and that drop cooled the chip faster than any other.

Sources indicate that mixing tiny particles of a heat-conducting ceramic, aluminum nitride, into the oil did the opposite. The particles gave bubbles places to start, so many small bubbles formed instead of one big one.

At the highest heat, those skins cut the peak hot-spot temperature by about 18°F (10°C).

Industry observers note that skins have a cost, though. Leftover oil on the chip surface slowed cooling later on, so the wrapped drops did worse than bare ones over a longer period.

Everything so far happened in still water on a heated square of sapphire, not on a processor in a working server.

Real cooling systems usually pump their liquid, and the authors wrote that boiling in flowing water may behave quite differently and needs its own tests.

High-heat runs also varied noticeably from one repeat to the next, though the overall pattern held each time.

It has been revealed that mitra’s team described two ways the idea could work. Sensors could detect a hot spot and deliver a drop to it, or wrapped drops could circulate in the water and boil wherever they land on something hot enough.

Next on the authors’ list are shell liquids that leave less residue, ways to wrap drops inside flowing coolant, and tests under realistic operating conditions.

The full study was published in the journal Journal of Colloid and Interface Science.

#7503. Tech Report: What a city’s sewage can reveal about the health of the people upstream

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1052 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Earth ↗ Open Full Page

Tech Report: What a city’s sewage can reveal about the health of the people upstream

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1052 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Eight Ohio cities' sewage carried gut bacteria whose mix lined up with local obesity, blood pressure, and stroke rates, a pilot study finds.
  • During the pandemic, health departments learned to read a city’s sewage for the virus behind COVID-19.
  • The same water carries something else from every household that flushes into it: the bacteria living in people’s guts.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Eight Ohio cities' sewage carried gut bacteria whose mix lined up with local obesity, blood pressure, and stroke rates, a pilot study finds.

During the pandemic, health departments learned to read a city’s sewage for the virus behind COVID-19.

The same water carries something else from every household that flushes into it: the bacteria living in people’s guts.

In eight Ohio cities, the mix of those gut bacteria in the sewage lined up with how the cities scored on chronic disease.

Cities with more of one group of bacteria that produce hydrogen sulfide had higher rates of obesity, high blood pressure, stroke, and several other conditions.

The study rests on 27 samples collected over seven weeks in May and June 2022, and the authors wrote that the links do not show cause.

What they show is that a sample from a treatment plant can carry a readable signal about the health of the people upstream.

Emma Lancaster, then a doctoral student in the College of Public Health at Ohio State University, led the study with Jiyoung Lee, professor and chair of environmental health sciences.

Lancaster is now an environmental health consultant in Boston.

“During the pandemic, the world learned how to use wastewater to track infectious disease. We asked, what else can it tell us?” Lancaster said.

Sewage arriving at a treatment plant is a blend of everything a community has flushed.

One earlier study the authors cite found up to 97% of the microbes in human stool in untreated sewage.

So the water is a pooled sample of a whole population’s gut bacteria, collected without asking anyone to take a test.

Earlier sewage studies elsewhere had tied a community’s bacterial profile to its rates of obesity, high blood pressure, and smoking.

The Ohio team set out to build full gut bacteria profiles for a set of cities and test them against a wide range of health and social measures.

The team collected a liter of untreated wastewater from each of nine treatment plants, on three days in May and June 2022. Two of the plants serve Columbus, the state capital.

The rest serve smaller cities in central and southeastern Ohio: Zanesville, Marysville, Newark, Lancaster, Athens, Circleville, and Marietta.

Together the plants handle sewage from more than 1.3 million people.

Recent findings suggest that the smallest serves about 15,000 and the largest nearly 548,000. So the cities range from small towns to a major metro area.

Four of the cities count as rural under the federal definition the team used, with fewer than 50,000 residents. The other four are urban.

In a recent development, each sample was processed the same day. The team sequenced a marker gene to identify the bacteria present. Then they kept only those known to live in the human gut, about 37% of what they read.

For the health side, they pulled public estimates for the census tracts inside each plant’s service area, 329 tracts in all.

The CDC’s PLACES database supplied rates of 23 health conditions and behaviors.

The agency’s Social Vulnerability Index supplied the social and economic measures, such as poverty and unemployment.

Each city’s sewage had its own bacterial profile, and the profiles differed enough that the cities could be told apart.

Several of those differences lined up with health. Cities where smoking was more common had more of one large group of bacteria, the Firmicutes.

Cities with less physical activity had more of two genera, Desulfovibrio and Tolumonas.

Desulfovibrio, a genus of bacteria that produce hydrogen sulfide, appeared again and again. Its abundance was associated with eight health measures.

They were high blood pressure, obesity, stroke, mobility disability, chronic kidney disease, coronary heart disease, chronic lung disease, and cancers other than skin cancer.

Studies of patients have found more Desulfovibrio in people with colorectal, stomach, and breast cancers than in healthy people, the authors wrote.

Researchers suspect its hydrogen sulfide may damage cells.

In a recent development, asthma ran the other way. Cities with more asthma had a less even mix of gut bacteria and less of a genus called Akkermansia, which is widely treated as a marker of a healthy gut.

Social conditions revealed up too. Cities with more unemployment had less diverse gut bacteria overall and more Firmicutes.

The four rural cities carried more Desulfovibrio, more Akkermansia, and more of a major group called Bacteroidota than the urban ones.

They also generally had higher rates of the chronic conditions in the dataset.

“In many cases, poor health outcomes are worse in rural areas and to see these distinct indicators of poorer gut microbiome health in these rural areas offers us clues to some of what is driving that,” Lancaster remarked.

Marysville, an urban city, sat at the healthy end of nearly every measure, with the lowest rates of smoking, depression, unemployment, and poverty among the eight.

“Wastewater offers a unique way to understand the health of whole communities, not just the people who show up in clinics,” Lee mentioned.

It has been revealed that eight cities give eight data points. The authors wrote that their results should be read as exploratory, not as reliable estimates for any one city.

Columbus alone accounts for most of the 1.3 million people, which could tilt comparisons.

According to recent reports, the health figures are also modeled estimates for census tracts, not counts of diagnosed patients. And the samples cover seven weeks of one year.

In a recent development, A deeper problem is in the pipes. Desulfovibrio and Acetobacterium live in sewers as well as in guts, and their numbers in wastewater can rise or fall with how long sewage stays in a pipe.

The authors wrote that future studies should record sewer conditions to separate the human signal from the plumbing.

A larger study could test whether the same patterns hold across more cities and over longer periods while accounting for diet, access to health care, and sewer conditions.

Wastewater already tracks viruses such as those behind COVID, flu, and mpox, Lee mentioned.

Tracking a community’s gut bacteria the same way, she stated, could eventually show whether a nutrition program is improving its gut health.

The full study was published in the journal Environmental Research.

#7502. Dragonfly wings inspired a new way to build materials that can take a hit

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1067 w)
📖 Baca
General 📈 Bullish 🌐 Earth ↗ Open Full Page

Dragonfly wings inspired a new way to build materials that can take a hit

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1067 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Engineers took cues from dragonfly wings to 3D-print materials that spread damage and absorb energy when compressed.
  • Industry observers note that A neat grid or honeycomb looks like the smartest way to build something light and strong, and engineers have borrowed both for decades.
  • One row buckles, then the next, in a band that runs across the whole piece.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Engineers took cues from dragonfly wings to 3D-print materials that spread damage and absorb energy when compressed.

Industry observers note that A neat grid or honeycomb looks like the smartest way to build something light and strong, and engineers have borrowed both for decades. Squeeze a printed grid hard enough, though, and it fails the way a stack of cans does.

One row buckles, then the next, in a band that runs across the whole piece.

A leaf’s veins, a dragonfly’s wing and a spider’s web are built the opposite way, from struts of wildly different sizes tangled together.

Recent findings suggest that materials printed on that blueprint spread the damage out instead of concentrating it. They also absorbed as much energy as the tidy lattices, or more.

Engineers at MIT and network scientists at Northeastern University’s Network Science Institute designed the new materials, which they call scale-rich metamaterials.

So far the team has tested them as flat, credit-card-sized polymer plates in a lab, not as helmets or packaging.

“This is a completely latest way of thinking for metamaterials,” stated study author Carlos Portela, associate professor of mechanical engineering at MIT.

Industry observers note that metamaterials get their properties from their internal architecture rather than their chemistry. Engineers usually design one small building block, a unit cell, and repeat it over and over.

So every strut inside is about the same length and thickness.

Albert-László Barabási, a physicist at Northeastern, has spent his career mapping networks from the internet to the brain. Those networks don’t look like a grid at all.

The veins in a dragonfly’s wing run from about four thousandths of an inch (0.1 millimeters) to about two inches (50 millimeters) long.

Leaf veins and spider silk span a range at least as wide, and the struts inside bone vary tenfold in thickness.

Recent findings suggest that barabási asked whether that spread of sizes could be built into a solid material on purpose. He took the question to Portela’s lab, with a mathematician at Utrecht University in the Netherlands joining the team.

According to recent reports, the team’s recipe is short. A computer picks a random point inside a square and draws a straight beam through it at a random angle, until the beam hits the edge.

The computer picks another point and draws another beam, which stops when it meets the first.

In a recent development, each latest beam is thinner than the last, by a rate the designer sets. Only two settings matter: how thick the first beam is and how fast the thickness shrinks.

The program repeats the step hundreds of times, so the last beams are short and fine while the first few stay long and thick.

The finished design has no typical strut. Lengths, thicknesses and the number of crossings per beam all run across orders of magnitude inside one sample, the same pattern network scientists find in road maps and food webs.

Changing those two settings also changes how stiff the material is in different directions. Across 2,600 computer-generated designs, the directional stiffness varied 24-fold.

That is far more range than a square grid, a honeycomb or a random foam-like Voronoi pattern can offer.

Industry observers note that the researchers 3D-printed the designs in a stiff polymer. Each sample was a few inches across, with beams from a few thousandths of an inch up to an inch or so long.

Then they squeezed the samples in a press, alongside square, honeycomb and Voronoi samples of the same density, about 42% solid, three of each.

The square grid buckled first in a single row, and the collapse spread sideways across the whole sample before the next row went. The honeycomb formed wide crushed bands.

Even the random Voronoi foam compacted from the bottom up while its top stayed untouched.

According to recent reports, the scale-rich samples didn’t do that. Their stress rose smoothly as the press pushed down, with no sudden drops, and the crushing stayed spread across the whole piece.

The team scored that spread on a scale where zero means perfectly even deformation and one means all the damage in one spot.

The fresh samples stayed at or below 0.2 even after being compressed by 25% of their original height.

The energy they soaked up before packing down matched or beat the three conventional designs.

“Because there is such a richness of length scales in these networked materials, if one part fails, there is a strong web of structures around it that keeps the entire material from failing catastrophically,” Portela mentioned.

“It’s more efficient at distributing damage and absorbing energy.”.

For a final test, the team borrowed from the thick, graded rind of a pomelo, denser toward the outside.

They generated a network whose beams crowded the edges and steered load around a disc of clear acrylic embedded in the middle.

In a recent development, under compression, the acrylic disc inside a square or honeycomb lattice highlighted bands of stress under polarized light. Inside the scale-rich network, the bands were far fewer.

Computer simulations put the stress on the disc at as little as about one-fifth of the stress in the conventional lattices.

The same two settings can also tune how fast vibrations travel through the material. The team used that to design a lens that focuses sound waves, so far only in simulation.

Everything the team crushed was a flat plate of one polymer, printed at a resolution of about four thousandths of an inch.

The authors highlighted on paper that the recipe extends to three dimensions, with plates or beams instead of lines. The stiffness trends carry over, but those 3D versions were simulated rather than squeezed.

In a recent development, the study didn’t test the materials as any product. Helmets, armor, packaging and crash parts are the uses the authors named, and each would need its own tests at full size.

The group has posted its generator code publicly. The authors wrote that a design needing only two inputs is well suited to AI-driven searches for structures with a target stiffness or energy absorption.

Future studies could run those searches, and print the 3D versions to see whether the even crushing holds in a solid block.

The full study was published in the journal Nature.

LSD changes the brain’s rhythm in a way earlier studies missed

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1125 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Brain recordings from 17 volunteers show that LSD speeds up two brain rhythms even as it weakens them.
  • Brain recordings of people on psychedelics have told the same story for years: the brain’s steady electrical rhythms get weaker, as if the drug were turning the volume down.
  • Industry observers note that A upcoming analysis of recordings from 17 people given LSD finds that the volume isn’t the whole story.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Brain recordings from 17 volunteers show that LSD speeds up two brain rhythms even as it weakens them.

Brain recordings of people on psychedelics have told the same story for years: the brain’s steady electrical rhythms get weaker, as if the drug were turning the volume down.

Industry observers note that A upcoming analysis of recordings from 17 people given LSD finds that the volume isn’t the whole story. The drug also turns up the tempo.

LSD pushes two of the brain’s main rhythms to faster beats, and it makes the brain’s electrical activity more detailed and less predictable.

According to recent reports, venkatesh Subramani, a doctoral student at the Université de Montréal, led the analysis with his supervisor Karim Jerbi. Jerbi is a psychology professor there and a researcher at Mila, the Quebec artificial intelligence institute.

Co-authors included Nicolas Farrugia and Giulia Lioi of IMT Atlantique in France and Robin Carhart-Harris of the University of California, San Francisco.

“Imagine a radio station switching its broadcast frequency from 99.5 to 100.5 FM,” Jerbi said.

“If your radio stays tuned to 99.5, the signal may seem distorted or lost. In the same way, overlooking the shift to faster brain rhythms can lead us to misinterpret LSD’s effects on the brain.”.

Groups of neurons firing together produce rhythms that a sensor outside the head can pick up. Researchers call them brain waves.

Alpha waves dominate when you rest with your eyes closed. Beta waves are faster and show up during concentration and decision-making.

It has been revealed that under psychedelics those waves look weaker, and the standard reading is that neurons are firing less in unison. Subramani’s team pointed out a catch.

According to recent reports, if a rhythm speeds up, its peak can shift outside the frequency range researchers are measuring. That shift can make the wave look weaker even if its strength hasn’t changed.

So the team pulled the two possibilities apart. They first stripped out the brain’s rhythm-free background activity.

Then they located each person’s actual alpha and beta peaks under LSD and under placebo, and measured the power at those peaks.

It has been revealed that the recordings were made at Imperial College London by Carhart-Harris’s group. Seventeen healthy volunteers came in twice, two weeks apart.

In one session, they received an intravenous injection of 75 micrograms of LSD, roughly the weight of a grain of salt. In the other they received a saline placebo, without being told which was which.

Industry observers note that about four hours after the injection, each person lay in a magnetoencephalography scanner. It records the faint magnetic fields that neurons produce, with timing down to the millisecond.

They rested with their eyes closed for seven minutes, and in a separate seven-minute block they listened to ambient music.

The Montreal team reanalyzed those recordings with newer signal-processing tools and a machine-learning model trained to tell the LSD sessions from the placebo sessions.

According to recent reports, under LSD, alpha waves ran about 2 cycles per second faster than on placebo, and beta waves about 5 cycles per second faster, across large areas of the cortex. The waves did also weaken.

Once the speed-up was accounted for, that weakening held up as real rather than an artifact of looking in the wrong place.

Recent findings suggest that the two effects didn’t fully overlap. The weakening was strongest in regions that handle hearing, language, and emotion.

The speed-up followed its own map, and the regions that weakened most tended to speed up least.

In a recent development, anesthetics do the opposite to the alpha rhythm, slowing it down as the cortex becomes less excitable. The authors read the faster alpha under LSD as a sign of a more excitable cortex.

They also noted that psilocybin and DMT haven’t been shown to shift the peaks this way, so the speed-up may be a signature specific to LSD.

A fractal is a shape that repeats itself in its own parts, the way each floret of a Romanesco broccoli is a smaller broccoli.

In a recent development, the team measured how fractal the brain signal was over time, and how varied its patterns were. Both rose under LSD.

The increases were largest in areas tied to vision, hearing, memory, and mental imagery, and smallest in the motor cortex.

Industry observers note that that split fits a familiar feature of the drug. Perception and inner experience change a great deal, while people can still move normally.

People on LSD often report seeing repeating geometric patterns with their eyes closed. The paper links the two only loosely.

In a recent development, “Our findings lend support to this intriguing hypothesis, but they do not yet confirm it,” Jerbi remarked. “We measure the fractal structure of brain signals over time, not the fractal structure of the images people perceive.”.

Given only the shift in peak frequencies, the machine-learning model identified the LSD session more than 82% of the time.

It has been revealed that models trained on the fractal and complexity measures did almost as well. The brain regions the models relied on matched the ones the conventional statistics had flagged.

“Our machine-learning algorithm can distinguish brain states under LSD from those under placebo using brain signals alone,” Subramani remarked.

“By examining the clues it relies on, we can identify LSD’s signatures in brain activity.”.

Industry observers note that music, which is routinely played during psychedelic therapy, didn’t amplify any of these effects. If anything the trend ran the other way, with slightly smaller brain changes during the music block.

That difference didn’t survive the statistical correction, and the authors called it exploratory.

Seventeen people is a small group, and everyone received a single dose while healthy, so the study indicates nothing about whether any of this helps patients.

The volunteers rated their experience at the peak of the drug’s effect, while the scanner ran about two and a half hours later.

The authors wrote that this gap may be why brain changes and reported experiences lined up only loosely.

It has been revealed that the recordings also included no direct measure of muscle activity, which can contaminate the fastest brain signals. So the authors treated their high-frequency results with extra caution.

The next question is whether the speed-up really belongs to LSD alone.

Subramani and his colleagues are now running the same analysis on recordings taken under psilocybin, the active ingredient in magic mushrooms, and under DMT.

The aim is to see whether the three drugs produce the same signatures in the brain or different ones.

The full study was published in the journal Communications Biology.

Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., left, has declared a challenge to current Senate Minority Leader Charles Schumer, D-N.Y. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call file photo).

Angus King, a Maine independent who caucuses with the Democrats, said in a statement. “Why would you fire the manager when you just won the World Series?”.

Industry News: Wind turbines may have killed nearly 19 million bats in the U.S. since 1981

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (914 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A new study draws on decades of wind farm surveys to estimate how many bats turbines killed across the lower 48 states from 1981 to 2024.
  • The bats that die under wind turbines are picked up one carcass at a time, by crews walking the ground under each tower.
  • For decades, those site-by-site counts were the main tally anyone had.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A new study draws on decades of wind farm surveys to estimate how many bats turbines killed across the lower 48 states from 1981 to 2024.

The bats that die under wind turbines are picked up one carcass at a time, by crews walking the ground under each tower.

For decades, those site-by-site counts were the main tally anyone had.

Combining those counts with a statistical model, researchers estimated that wind turbines killed about 18.7 million bats in the lower 48 states from 1981 through the end of the study period.

Since 2021, the toll has run above 1.5 million a year. That is a scale the authors wrote may rival the fungal disease that has devastated cave-hibernating bats.

Charles Labuzzetta of the U.S. Geological Survey‘s Fort Collins Science Center led the analysis with colleagues at the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and the National Laboratory of the Rockies.

The figures are model estimates with wide ranges, built from monitoring that was never designed to be added up, and the relationships they found are correlations, not proven causes.

In an interview with Earth.com, Labuzzetta said the data behind the study were richer than their patchy origins suggest.

“We found that there could still be a lot to learn from the rich monitoring data that has been collected since the late 1990s and continues to be collected,” he noted.

The team pulled together 499 monitoring reports from 277 wind facilities in the lower 48 states, filed with the Fish and Wildlife Service since the late 1990s.

It has been revealed that each report counted the carcasses found under turbines and estimated how many were missed. But the searches differed in length, area and method, and many reports are confidential.

A statistical model pooled them, corrected for what the searchers could not see, and projected fatalities back to 1981.

The median came out at 18,696,140 bats across ten species, with a plausible range of about 13.3 million to 25.7 million.

That is the estimate for the lower 48 states that the compliance reports could never produce on their own.

Four species account for nearly all of it. The authors estimate about 6.7 million hoary bats, 5.8 million eastern red bats, 3.4 million silver-haired bats and 1.5 million major brown bats.

On average, a turbine killed close to six hoary bats a year. At the other end, the rare Indiana bat accounted for about 6,000 deaths over the whole period.

The last national figures date from 2013, and they put the toll in the hundreds of thousands a year.

Those estimates leaned on a single rule of thumb, about 1.7 hoary bats per megawatt of capacity.

According to recent reports, A projection built on it assumed roughly 113,000 hoary bat deaths in 2012, and the upcoming model estimates about 268,000 for that year. The old figure was less than half the new one.

The gap matters because of what the old projection, built on expert judgment, already noted.

It has been revealed that run on the lower numbers, it warned that hoary bats could lose 50% to 90% of their population within 50 years. Eastern red bats have been dying faster still, more than 500,000 a year since 2021.

Recent findings suggest that rated capacity, the usual yardstick, turned out to be a poor predictor of deaths. The area swept by the blades was a better predictor.

On most turbines built since 2020 that is 2.5 to 5 acres (10,000 to 20,000 square meters).

Researchers estimated more deaths among several bat species at turbines whose blades swept a larger area or passed closer to the ground.

Recent findings suggest that for all ten species, estimated deaths were higher at wind farms closer to rivers. The study couldn’t determine whether being near a river was itself responsible for the higher toll.

Labuzzetta told Earth.com those patterns point to siting and design as levers, but not to a single fix.

“There is still a great deal to learn about what strategies may be optimal and could provide the greatest conservation management return on investment for individual species and across all species,” he remarked.

White-nose syndrome, a fungal disease first seen in 2006, has cut some cave-hibernating species by more than 90%.

The authors compared their total with one rough estimate of the disease’s losses and found the two comparable in size.

The two threats mostly hit different bats. The disease kills bats that hibernate in caves, while turbines mostly kill the migratory tree-roosting species.

Across North American bats as a whole, the authors wrote, the two may compound.

Whether 18.7 million deaths translate into shrinking populations is the question the study can’t answer.

In a recent development, data on how many hoary or eastern red bats exist, how long they live and how fast they breed are largely unavailable, the authors wrote. So the same number of deaths could mean a crisis or a dent.

“Our research alone cannot answer whether fatalities from wind energy are leading to similar population-level declines for migratory tree-roosting bat species,” Labuzzetta said.

Population trends from the North American Bat Monitoring Program could begin to fill that gap.

The authors also called for monitoring at wind farms to be collected and shared in a form that can be pooled.

The full study was published in the journal Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.
