#7496. Tech Report: The U.S. just lost its measles elimination status. What now?

📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1866 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Sciencenews ↗ Open Full Page

Tech Report: The U.S. just lost its measles elimination status. What now?

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1866 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencenews

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • This is a human-written story voiced by AI.
  • After two years with nearly 100 measles outbreaks, thousands sickened and nearly a dozen deaths, the United States has officially lost its measles elimination status.
  • The highly contagious disease is now endemic in the United States, the Pan American Health Organization declared November 17.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Updated November 17, 2026 at 12:50 pm.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .).

After two years with nearly 100 measles outbreaks, thousands sickened and nearly a dozen deaths, the United States has officially lost its measles elimination status.

The highly contagious disease is now endemic in the United States, the Pan American Health Organization declared November 17. Analyses of cases dated from when the first outbreak began in 2025 in West Texas through part of 2026 revealed the virus has been spreading uninterrupted for more than a year. That benchmark signals measles is no longer under control.

Recent findings suggest that the United States is not alone. Mexico and Bolivia also lost their measles elimination status, PAHO revealed; Canada had lost it in 2025. “Measles is resurging globally amid persistent gaps in vaccination coverage,” PAHO director Jarbas Barbosa said in a Nov. 17 news conference. “And this global trend is also affecting the Americas.” Countries will need to not only stop ongoing outbreaks, but also prove that no one caught measles within their borders for a full year to regain measles-free status.

That won’t happen overnight. But there is a way, experts say. Vaccinating people across the country, particularly in areas with low vaccination rates, will stifle the virus’s spread. But so far, the U.S. federal public health response has taken a back seat to efforts from state and local health departments to curb ongoing outbreaks.

It has been revealed that measles’s return “is an enormous black eye on the reputation of the United States,” said epidemiologist Jennifer Nuzzo of the Brown University School of Public Health in Providence, R.I., in a Nov. 9 webinar hosted by the university. The Americas led the global campaign to control the virus, and in 2016 the region became the first to eliminate measles transmission from all its countries.

It has been revealed that “To lose [elimination status] means we’re going backwards… meaning decades of progress lost,” Nuzzo noted. “It’s an indicator of our lack of protection. It is an indicator of our lack of preparedness for disease threats in general.”.

In a recent development, PAHO’s verdict comes amid a surge of measles not seen in the United States since 1991. Health officials have recorded more than 7,000 cases since the beginning of the West Texas outbreak. That tally includes nearly 2,300 measles cases in 2025 and 5,412 in 2026 as of November 12, according to the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Over 90 percent of cases have been in people who are unvaccinated or whose status is unknown. States report that 13 people have died, although the CDC so far recognizes only nine of those deaths.

While mild measles symptoms include high fever, cough and a rash, roughly 1 in 5 people will be hospitalized with complications such as pneumonia or brain swelling. Children younger than 5 years and adults over 20 are more likely to get sick, as are pregnant women and their infants. At least 13 babies were born infected, called congenital measles, since the beginning of 2025, researchers report November 16 in NEJM Evidence. Those babies are at risk for developing dangerous brain swelling that is almost always fatal later on in life.

The measles, mumps and rubella, or MMR, vaccine helped eliminate measles from the United States in 2000. After that, cases still sometimes popped up. Those cases were mostly in unvaccinated people traveling from parts of the world where the virus still widely circulates. At least 95 percent of people in a community need to be vaccinated to prevent outbreaks.

But widespread misinformation, including a disproven claim that the vaccine causes autism, means fewer children are receiving the MMR shot and more people are questioning its safety. According to the CDC, roughly 92 percent of kindergarteners across the United States had gotten the vaccine in 2025, down from 95 percent in 2019. And in 2025, 83 percent of U.S. adults viewed the MMR vaccine as safe, down from 86 percent in 2024, according to a survey from the University of Pennsylvania’s Annenberg Public Policy Center. Yet decades of evidence show the vaccine is safe and highly effective.

According to recent reports, that measles made a comeback is not a surprise, claims Nathan Lo, an infectious diseases physician and epidemiologist at Stanford University School of Medicine. Until recently, outbreaks were largely isolated to communities with low vaccination rates and swiftly contained. But now, outbreaks seem to be more likely to spill over into neighboring communities, Lo says. “There’s a lot of potential connectedness between the outbreaks.”.

What’s more, some infected people aren’t getting tested, making them invisible to officials who are now struggling to trace chains of transmission. An outbreak that hit Arizona and Utah, for instance, was far larger than official numbers suggest, researchers reported July 15 in a preprint at medRxiv.org. The roughly 1,000 confirmed cases may represent just 20 to 30 percent of the outbreak’s true size.

A functional surveillance system is crucial to keeping outbreaks under control, Jonathan Temte, a family medicine physician at the University of Wisconsin School of Medicine and Public Health in Madison, said in the Brown University webinar. Without good surveillance across the entire country, “we can miss pockets out there if people aren’t reporting, if people are hiding cases.”.

But surveillance alone won’t stop the virus from “popcorning across the country,” Nuzzo remarked. “Measles has returned, and it’s going to take vaccination to stop it.”.

It has been revealed that over the last two years, measles outbreaks have popped up across the United States, sickening thousands of people since mid-January 2025. Most of those cases, shown by county where they were reported, are in people who are unvaccinated. Colors on the map indicate the relative number of cases reported. Green represents the lowest and red the highest number of cases. Notable outbreaks have appeared in Utah, Arizona, Texas, South Carolina, Wisconsin and Pennsylvania.

Michael Mitchell and Andrea Uhlig/Brown University School of Public Health.

Sources indicate that efforts to boost vaccine uptake could be targeted toward areas with low vaccination rates. Most places across the United States still have vaccination rates high enough to fend off measles, but not all. “Figuring out which ones are [high risk] can be a little tricky,” Lo says. “But if you do, then intervening in those places can be quite helpful to mitigate spread.”.

Homing in on school districts or individual schools could also help. State health departments typically report vaccination rates among school-age children by county. But that broad metric can hide high risk schools with low vaccination rates, epidemiologists Siyu Chen and Ana Bento reported in August in Nature Medicine. Computer simulations relying on data that included 50,000 schools across the United States showed that school-level estimates best revealed where the virus could gain a foothold. That was true even if county-level vaccination rates were close to 95 percent.

Another element that influenced where measles took off was whether communities with cases were near other areas with low vaccination rates, the team found. The outbreak in Texas, for instance, may have ended faster because communities with low vaccination rates were farther away from one another compared with outbreaks in South Carolina and Pennsylvania, says Bento, of Cornell University. Neighboring areas where many are unvaccinated may face longer-burning outbreaks. “Which is what we are now seeing,” Bento says.

Industry observers note that measles elimination status can be regained. The declaration that the virus is endemic is “not a punishment,” Bento notes. It’s a sign that something needs to change. That might include vaccine catch-up campaigns, community outreach or getting rid of nonmedical vaccine exemptions.

Sources indicate that local public health officials are “doing every last thing that you can imagine with limited resources,” health psychologist Noel T. Brewer remarked in a Nov. 12 webinar hosted by the Association of Health Care Journalists. But a cohesive blueprint at the federal level could bolster defenses before the virus arrives in new states, noted Brewer, of the University of North Carolina Gillings School of Global Public Health in Chapel Hill.

Such efforts could be targeted toward areas with low vaccination rates. Most places across the United States still have vaccination rates high enough to fend off measles. “A subset [with low vaccination rates] are high risk,” Lo indicates. “Figuring out which ones are which can be a little tricky. But if you do, then intervening in those places can be quite helpful to mitigate spread.”.

There’s also wiggle room in the childhood vaccine schedule to provide kids extra protection. Normally children don’t get their first MMR dose until their first birthday. But doctors can give infants an extra MMR dose at 6 months if there is an active outbreak in their area. Pediatricians can also offer the second dose a month after the first one, rather than waiting until around the time children start kindergarten. Adults, particularly those who received only one dose, can also get a booster. It’s unclear whether health officials will officially recommend such actions.

“The problem is that there’s no trusted source for this vaccine decision anymore,” Lo says. Previous vaccine recommendations were up to the CDC’s Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices, which was disbanded in March after lawsuits blocked appointments made by Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. “Now, there’s a lot of different medical societies and initiatives to try and fill that void,” Lo says. But it’s unclear which would be best positioned to lead.

CDC director Erica Schwartz has said the health agency will not be changing its response to ongoing outbreaks. “We’re going to be doing the same exact thing that we’ve been doing today, which is working with the states,” she told Reuters. The CDC did not respond to Science News requests for an interview, but shared in a Nov. 17 statement that the agency will “encourage MMR vaccination, expand access to vaccines, and help communities close gaps in protection.”.

According to recent reports, eliminating measles again will take dedicated resources and more funding funneled to public health departments across the country, Lo notes. “You see increasing measles outbreaks and a lot of time and resources to contain these outbreaks at a time where you’re slashing budgets,” Lo says, “that’s a really bad mismatch.”.

Recent findings suggest that public health responses to measles are expensive. Officials in Upcoming Mexico spent an estimated $5.4 million — over $53,000 per case — responding to a 2025 outbreak that was linked to West Texas. The CDC has provided an additional $100 million to states to help fight measles.

According to recent reports, other countries have beaten back measles after an unwelcome return. Extensive vaccination campaigns helped Venezuela and Brazil regain measles elimination status after briefly losing it in 2017 and 2019. The Public Health Agency of Canada also confirmed that its nearly two-year-long outbreak officially ended in October, though it’s unclear when the country might earn its status back.

Industry observers note that “It is not hopeless,” Nuzzo said. “It can be done, and I hope it will be done [in the United States].”.

#7495. Tech Report: A giant planet stopped crossing its star while astronomers watched, and it never left

Tech Report: A giant planet stopped crossing its star while astronomers watched, and it never left

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1167 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that astronomers saw a planet around a single star stop crossing it, a first.
  • Industry observers note that astronomers had been watching a giant planet pass in front of its star for years.
  • Industry observers note that the planet, TOI-2535 b, hasn’t gone anywhere.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that astronomers saw a planet around a single star stop crossing it, a first. A hidden neighbor is likely tipping its orbit.

Industry observers note that astronomers had been watching a giant planet pass in front of its star for years. Then, in March 2026, it stopped showing up.

Industry observers note that the planet, TOI-2535 b, hasn’t gone anywhere. Its orbit has tipped, most likely from the pull of a second planet in the same system, one that astronomers haven’t detected directly.

TOI-2535 b, more than 1,000 light-years away, is the first confirmed planet around a single star that astronomers have seen stop crossing. Samuel Yee, a 51 Pegasi b Postdoctoral Fellow at UCLA, led the work with UCLA astrophysicist Erik Petigura.

It has been revealed that each of those crossings is called a transit. “The planet’s orbit is tilting so promptly that its transit disappeared while we were watching,” Yee stated.

According to recent reports, when a planet passes between its star and Earth, it blocks a little of the starlight. The star dims for a few hours, and that small dip is how NASA’s Transiting Exoplanet Survey Satellite (TESS) finds newly introduced worlds.

According to recent reports, A transit only indicates up if the star, the planet and Earth line up almost perfectly. If the orbit tips by just a few degrees, the planet passes above or below the star as seen from Earth, and the star never dims.

TESS checked on the star, called TOI-2535, five times between April 2019 and March 2026.

The planet orbiting it is a hot Jupiter, a gas giant that orbits very close to its star. It goes around once every 8.24 days. Mercury takes 88 days, more than 10 times as long.

Industry observers note that to confirm the planet, the team used an instrument on the 11.5-foot (3.5-meter) WIYN telescope at Kitt Peak National Observatory in Arizona. It tracked how the star shifted back and forth, and the measurements ruled out a small star.

Industry observers note that most planets that cross their stars keep a steady schedule. TOI-2535 b’s crossings came as much as six hours early or late. No hot Jupiter that circles its star in under 10 days has a bigger timing swing on record.

Each crossing was also a little shorter than the last, and each one dimmed the star a little less.

A planet blocks less light, for less time, as its path moves from the middle of a star toward its edge.

Over seven years, the path likely moved across more than half of the star’s face. It passed the middle, grazed the edge, then missed the star entirely.

From the ground, the team tried 15 times and caught a crossing only six times, because the planet kept arriving when it wasn’t expected.

When TESS looked again in March 2026, it found no crossing anywhere in the window where the planet could have shown up.

According to recent reports, so what’s pulling on it? Planets in the same system tug on each other. If two orbits are tilted relative to one another, those tugs slowly swing the direction each orbit faces.

Industry observers note that the team’s computer models suggest the neighbor is at least as massive as Saturn, so it’s probably a second giant planet. The two likely move in a simple rhythm, such as one circling twice for every lap of the other.

By the models, the two orbits must be tilted at least 5 degrees apart to turn this fast.

Sources indicate that in most tightly packed systems, orbits stay within 1 to 2 degrees of each other. If this tilt holds up, the system will be one of only a handful so far out of line.

Recent findings suggest that “We think of the universe as resembling clockwork, where everything is regular, but that’s not true. If there are multiple planets in a system, they can affect each other’s orbits,” Yee said.

Sources indicate that “We know of a few systems that are like this. This is the most extreme example we’ve seen because the two planets are interacting so strongly.”.

Petigura used Earth’s moon to explain it.

“If the moon’s orbit around the Earth was perfectly aligned with the Earth’s orbit around the sun, we would see an eclipse every month,” Petigura said.

“But because the moon’s orbit is tilted, eclipses are less common. The tilt of the moon’s orbit is a relic of its violent formation history, which resulted from a collision with the early Earth.”.

It has been revealed that the same geometry decides when TOI-2535 b will be back. The team calculated that each orbit goes through a full cycle every 30 to 50 years.

The researchers expect the planet to start crossing its star again within that span. Its hidden neighbor could start crossing even sooner.

Early planet formation models suggested giant planets need lots of ice to form. So hot Jupiters probably formed far from their stars and moved closer later.

How? Yee and Petigura see two ways. One is violent. A near-collision knocks the planet onto a stretched-out orbit, and the star pulls it in.

Recent findings suggest that the other is slow. The planet drifts inward with other planets through the gas and dust around a young star. This way should leave the orbits flat.

TOI-2535 b has a close giant neighbor, so it couldn’t have come the violent way, the team wrote.

It has been revealed that “Because TOI-2535 b has a close neighbor, it probably migrated by slowly spiraling in instead of getting flung in,” Yee stated. “We may be seeing a formation channel that doesn’t happen very often but is very interesting.”.

Industry observers note that the tilt is still a loose end. The researchers think parts of the system may have tugged on each other later, tipping the orbits over time.

Hundreds of hot Jupiters are known around other stars. Few have a planet close enough to change their orbits. When one does, the neighbor is almost always much smaller. The only other known exception is WASP-148.

According to recent reports, the team can’t say how massive the neighbor is or where it orbits. The crossing times also scattered more than the models predicted.

Recent findings suggest that the star’s back-and-forth motion was jumpier than expected for an old, calm star, too. Both clues could mean there’s more than one unseen planet.

TESS’s first four years of data alone couldn’t have clearly shown the shrinking crossings.

Recent findings suggest that with no crossings left to time, the researchers wrote that the best way forward is to measure the star’s back-and-forth motion often. A neighbor as heavy as the models suggest should show up in that data on its own.

The full study was published in the journal The Astrophysical Journal Letters.

The 8 Best Shop Vacs for Tackling Tough Messes

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review.
  • According to recent reports, you can’t make an omelet without breaking a few eggs, and you can’t complete a project at home or in your workshop without making a mess.
  • Recent findings suggest that but because of this, I also know the importance of a reliable shop vac.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

According to recent reports, you can’t make an omelet without breaking a few eggs, and you can’t complete a project at home or in your workshop without making a mess. These are the laws of the universe. I don’t write them; I just obey them.

Recent findings suggest that but because of this, I also know the importance of a reliable shop vac. Unlike the vacuum you use to clean the floors in your home, a shop vac gobbles up large, chunky messes, including sawdust, screws, bits of wood, and other debris (not to mention spills and other wet messes). So if you’re using woodworking tools like sanders, miter saws, and table saws on a regular basis, you need to have one close by.

Recent findings suggest that when it comes to choosing the right shop vac for your home, there’s a lot to consider. Shop vacs come in both cordless and corded electric models and range in size from small, 1.6-gallon portable vacuums for cleaning out cars to large, 12-gallon shop vacs capable of keeping your entire garage sawdust-free.

All of the products written about below were tested by members of the Popular Mechanics team, including myself (Tony Carrick) and Test Editor Brad Ford.

According to recent reports, in an effort to evaluate the performance of the shop vacs on this list, we put them through tests that involved collecting both dry materials and liquid. We conducted three timed tests using only each vacuum’s hose, no attachments. The first test involved vacuuming up 12 cups of sawdust to determine how quickly each vac could collect dry material. We then used each vac to drain 2 gallons of water from a bucket. Lastly, we tested suction power by attempting to use each vac to suck up wood screws and metal bolts.

It has been revealed that along with grading each shop vac’s vacuuming capabilities, we also evaluated how easy each model was to use, based on factors like weight, size, capacity, and cord and hose length. Since every person’s shop vac needs may vary, the list below includes a broad range of sizes.

Industry observers note that in the latest patch of this guide, we tested and added two new shop vacs. The Vacmaster Professional Beast Series FLT+ is a shop vac with next-level features you won’t find on any other shop vacs. Not only does it connect to the exhaust ports of the large sawdust-producing power tools in your workshop, table saws, miter saws, and the like, but it also syncs with them via a wireless remote. With a vacuum cleaner–like dust collection bag and top-mounted HEPA filter, it’s ideally equipped for collecting sawdust.

The Craftsman CMXEVBE17595 Wet-Dry Shop Vac is our largest pick (with its 16-gallon tank) and also one of our most powerful. With a max airflow of 185 cubic feet per minute (cfm), it sucks up material faster than any other shop vac we tested. It’s also powerful enough to pull in heavier objects, including bolts and small chunks of wood.

In a recent development, the Vacmaster’s impressive power and compact design make it the perfect all-around shop vac. One of our editors owns the previous iteration of this model and has found it to be the ideal shop vac for home use. Its 5.5-hp motor is much more powerful than what you’ll find with most other 5-gallon shop vacs. It also has a small, 18.6-by-13.4-inch footprint, so it’s easy to carry and store, though its smaller capacity may not be enough for busier workshops.

With an 18-foot power cord and 7-foot hose, you won’t need an extension cord to clean up a large two-car garage or reach a car in the driveway. Plus, the newest version of the Vacmaster adds wheels that make it even easier to move around. There are also four attachments, which offer enough versatility to handle different jobs, and all of the Vacmaster’s attachments fit neatly into a storage compartment on the vacuum.

Full Vacmaster Beast Series 5-Gallon Shop Vacuum Review.

Recent findings suggest that stanley’s 6-gallon wet-dry vac is a fraction of the cost of other shop vacs, yet it still packs enough power and capacity to handle most cleanups. Though it lagged behind the top performers we tested, it still completed our sawdust test in a respectable 21 seconds, and it swallowed up 2 gallons of water in just 11 seconds. And with its smaller-diameter hose, it produced enough suction to pick up both screws and bolts.

Sources indicate that it’s not too bulky, so it won’t crowd your workshop floor, nor is it so compact that it requires emptying too frequently. It sits on swiveling casters and is relatively light, which made it easy to wheel around our tester’s garage. We also liked its accessories, which include two extensions and three nozzles for both floor and spill cleanup. The crevice tool was particularly impressive in that it reached easily into the tight spaces between the seats of one of our cars.

We did find ourselves wishing the power cord was longer than 10 feet so we could reach all corners of the workshop without having to use an extension cord. Still, with its low price and ample capacity, this Stanley vac is a great value option for any home workshop.

Ridgid's shop vac is powerful and affordable enough to fit most budgets, making it an ideal companion for those bigger and messier home improvement projects.

During testing, it collected a pile of sawdust in just over 16 seconds before proceeding to drain a bucket of water in about 6 seconds. While we liked how quickly it picked up light debris, the Ridgid left a little to be desired with lift power. Its large-diameter hose made quick work of lighter material, but it struggled to pick up larger bolts (though we should note that this was an issue with most other vacs with large 2-1/2-inch-diameter hoses).

Recent findings suggest that the Ridgid also has a sturdy feel to it. The hose resisted cracking or denting, even after mistakenly stepping on it, and the tub is made of thick plastic. There’s also a locking system on the hose, which prevents attachments from falling off when the vacuum is in use.

The vacuum’s long, 7-foot hose made it easy to clean a work area without having to repeatedly reposition the base. Attachments include two extension wands, along with a crevice tool and floor tool, all of which fit onto the shop vac for storage. An included wet filter would make this shop vac a real no-brainer purchase, but it’s not far off from that even without one.

Full Ridgid 12-Gallon 5.0 Peak HP NXT Shop Vacuum Review.

The speed and capacity the DeWalt Stealthsonic displayed during my tests makes it a great choice for cleaning up wet messes.

According to recent reports, it produced some of the most impressive vacuuming results during our tests. Backed by its 5.5-hp motor and 2.5-inch-diameter hose (about the same size as a fire hose), the Stealthsonic gobbled up our pile of sawdust in just 16 seconds and drained our bucket of water in just 5 seconds, which was among the fastest of any shop vac we tested.

It was also one of the largest of the shop vacs we tested, with a 12-gallon capacity. Thanks to its 20-foot-long cord, it covers an entire two-car garage without the need for an extension cord, and it sits on heavy-duty rubber casters that make it easy to wheel around.

Industry observers note that while its larger-diameter hose worked well for the quick collection of lighter materials, it’s not ideal for heavier objects. The Stealthsonic struggled to produce enough lift to suck up wood screws and was unable to collect larger bolts like some shop vacs with smaller-diameter hoses could. It also is a bit too bulky to get into tighter spots, such as the small gaps in and around the seats in a car. But if you’re looking for something that swiftly cleans up larger spills and messes at the job site or in a workshop, this vacuum is it.

It has been revealed that milwaukee’s M18 Fuel wet-dry vacuum, which runs off an 18-volt lithium-ion battery, is one of the most powerful shop vac options when there’s no electrical outlet in range. The vac impressed during testing, even matching some of the corded shop vacs we tested. It consumed our sawdust pile in 20 seconds flat and a bucket of water in just 11 seconds, which is saying something given that it has a long, 9-foot hose.

We also loved the design of this wet-dry vac. The accessories, which include a floor utility nozzle and crevice tool, fit nicely inside a compartment on the top of the shop vac, and the tray holds both extensions. The extra-long hose and the small profile of the crevice tool were particularly valuable when we used the M18 Fuel wet-dry vacuum to clean out a car.

The M18 6-gallon vacuum is also easy to maneuver. It sits in a sturdy tray with four casters with rubber wheels that rolled easily over our tester’s garage floor and driveway. The M18’s run time was also impressive. When loaded with a 12.0-ampere-hour (Ah) battery, we got 31 minutes of run time when set to high and a whopping 48 minutes on its lower power setting.

This was the priciest wet-dry vacuum we tested, but it’s worth the investment if you want to cut the cord without compromising power.

If the primary demand for your shop vac is to collect the mountains of sawdust left behind following a carpentry project, then look no further than the recently launched Vacmaster Professional Beast Series FLT+. Not only will this shop vac attach to your power tools’ exhaust ports, but it also synchronizes with them. It comes with a Synchro key remote, which you attach to a power tool via a neoprene strap. The key communicates wirelessly with the shop vac. When it senses the vibration of the tool turning on, the key sends a signal that turns on the vacuum, eliminating the need to walk across the room to turn it on manually. I used it with a table saw, and it worked well, reliably turning on as soon as I fired up the table saw and dutifully sucking up dust as I cut, then turning off when I shut down the saw.

The Vacmaster is designed for collecting dust particles, and it did that extremely well. It sucked up 12 cups of sawdust in under 20 seconds, which is impressive given that it comes equipped with a smaller 1-7/8-inch-diameter hose. The Vacmaster Beast FLT+ also comes with a dust bag similar to a vacuum cleaner and a HEPA filter, making it ideal for trapping fine dust particles.

Sources indicate that while most shop vacs have a filter located inside the collection tank, the Vacmaster’s is on top. This frees up space inside the tank for more debris collection while also preventing the filter from becoming inundated with dust. Other notable features you won’t find on most shop vacs include an LED display that demonstrates the vacuum's airflow percentage, so you know when it’s time to clean the filter, and a self-cleaning filter. It’s an excellent workshop shop vac for those who don’t mind springing for it.

Recent findings suggest that with its cordless design, light weight, and compact, box-shaped design, Milwaukee’s M12 Fuel shop vac is made for the road. At just 15 inches long, 13 inches wide, and 12 inches high, and with a weight of just under 10 pounds, Milwaukee’s M12 Fuel shop vac was by far the easiest to carry around of the wet-dry vacuums we tested. Its shape also made it ideal for sitting in the trunk of a car or storing on a set of garage shelves.

Per its name, the M12 Fuel shop vac uses a smaller power source—a 12-volt battery—so it doesn’t have the power of the corded and 18-volt cordless models we tested. Still, it took a respectable 35 seconds for it to complete our sawdust test and was capable of sucking down both bolts and wood screws. Its 1.6-gallon capacity and a max runtime of 26 minutes on low and 14 minutes on high limit it to small cleanup jobs, however.

While it lacks the power of larger shop vacs, it’s hard to overstate how convenient it is to use. We appreciated its compact size and cordless design when we toted it into the car for some detailing, then later up to a second-floor bonus room to clean up drywall dust after mounting a TV.

The M12 Fuel is pricey when you factor in the cost of a battery and charger, but its convenience is unmatched, especially if you’ve already bought into Milwaukee’s 12-volt power tool universe and have a 12-volt Fuel battery to load into it.

Full Milwaukee M12 Fuel 1.6-Gallon Shop Vac Review.

The Craftsman 16-gallon wet-dry shop vac was built to clean up large masses fast with a max airflow of 185 cfm, well above the 100 cfm I see on most shop vacs. It vacuumed up 12 cups of sawdust faster than any other shop vac I tested and gulped down 2 gallons of water in 5 seconds flat. Most of the shop vacs I tested with a larger 2-1/2-inch-diameter hose struggled to generate enough lift to pick up heavier debris. That wasn’t the case with the Craftsman, which effortlessly vacuumed up a pile of screws, washers, and large bolts.

The Craftsman sits on four sturdy casters that made it easy to maneuver around when I was using it to clean up my large two-car garage, which I was able to do thanks to its 20-foot-long power cord and 7-foot hose.

With its 16-gallon size, the Craftsman was also the largest shop vac I tested, which made it handy for cleaning up major messes and large open areas. It was less effective for cleaning out a car. The crevice tool and its bulkier hose made it difficult to maneuver around a car interior, and there are no crevice tools for cleaning the gaps between seats and other tight spaces.

Sources indicate that while its large size makes the Craftsman capable of cleaning up large messes, it also makes it a bit of a space hog in a garage or shed. You also won’t be carrying it inside the house to clean up messes in the home. But if you’re after a shop vac with the muscle and capacity to handle large postproject messes, this is the one.

The drum capacity of a shop vac determines how much material you can vacuum without having to empty it out. While sizes range from 1.6 to 16 gallons, smaller-capacity shop vacs, like the Milwaukee M12 Fuel 1.6-Gallon Wet-Dry Vacuum, provide more versatility to the average user through easier transport and storage. If you’re short on space, a smaller unit that you have to empty more frequently could be more convenient than a larger-capacity machine cluttering up your garage. Keep in mind that the stated gallon capacity doesn't factor in the space taken up by the filter, so don’t expect a 6-gallon model to suck up exactly 6 gallons of material.

While the majority of shop vacs use corded power, cordless models are becoming more common. These battery-powered options offer more mobility—especially useful for car, boat, or RV cleaning—but they lack the runtime for extended projects. If you prefer the mobility of cordless models (especially if you’re interested in a larger-capacity model that requires a lot of power), choose one from the same brand as your existing power tools. This enables you to extend runtime by using additional batteries you already have on hand.

Recent findings suggest that if you decide to go with a corded model, pay attention to the length of the cord. Models with a longer cord, such as the DeWalt Stealthsonic Wet-Dry Shop Vacuum, give you the freedom to cover larger workshops or reach to your driveway without having to get out an extension cord.

It has been revealed that A shop vac’s airflow—measured in cubic feet per minute (cfm)—represents the amount of air a vacuum pulls through its nozzle. Roughly speaking, a shop vac with a higher cfm sucks up material faster than one with a lower cfm, though keep in mind this doesn’t include other factors like nozzle design, motor size, and suction power. As we found during testing, shop vacs with smaller-diameter hoses, such as the Milwaukee M18 Fuel 6-Gallon Wet-Dry Vacuum, often produce greater suction power. So while a larger shop vac with a larger-diameter hose will remove lightweight material, such as sawdust, more rapidly than a shop vac with a narrower hose, that smaller vac is better able to pick up heavier objects, such as bolts and coins.

While most shop vacs include several nozzle attachments for the hose, some models offer a more useful variety of accessories. Think about the type and scope of your cleaning tasks, and look for a vacuum with applicable accessories. For example, we’ve found a brush-tip nozzle to be essential for automotive interior cleaning, allowing us to quickly clean dust and pet hair from the dashboard and display screen—areas easily scratched by a hard plastic nozzle. Or, if you want to suck up the cobwebs in the corner of your garage or sawdust deep under your workbench, look for vacs with multiple extension wands to extend the nozzle reach.

Cattails send oxygen into marsh mud, where it can change the soil chemistry

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1421 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, cattails grow in mud with almost no oxygen, but their roots bring some in.
  • Recent findings suggest that the roots of cattails can grow in oxygen-poor marsh mud.
  • Part of that oxygen then escapes into the surrounding mud.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, cattails grow in mud with almost no oxygen, but their roots bring some in. A new study found that growing roots release oxygen even at night.

Recent findings suggest that the roots of cattails can grow in oxygen-poor marsh mud. To keep these roots alive, the plant carries air down from its leaves.

Part of that oxygen then escapes into the surrounding mud.

It has generally been assumed that this leak occurs mostly in daylight. During the day, the leaves produce oxygen and their pores stay open to the air.

In a recent development, A laboratory study of narrowleaf cattails has found that daylight altered the leak only slightly. Instead, oxygen appeared wherever a new root or underground stem was growing. It remained there through the night as well.

The findings suggest that the season of root growth may matter more for marsh chemistry than the time of day.

Industry observers note that the study was conducted by Ilana Stein and Zoe Cardon of the Ecosystems Center. This center is part of the Marine Biological Laboratory (MBL) in Woods Hole, Massachusetts.

In a recent development, four plants were examined one at a time in boxes of marsh mud. No measurements were made in a marsh itself.

Recent findings suggest that flooding leaves the soil of a wetland without oxygen. Most wetland plants cope with this through spongy tissue in their leaves, stems and roots that is filled with air.

This tissue serves as a kind of snorkel for the plant. Oxygen travels through it from the air above the water to the root tips below.

Industry observers note that narrowleaf cattail is particularly well adapted to flooded ground. Air spaces were found by earlier studies to make up as much as 74% of its leaf tissue.

In the roots, the figure reached as much as 32%.

Sources indicate that some of the oxygen that arrives is used by the roots and the rest can leak away. This leaked oxygen allows microbes that depend on it to survive in mud where they otherwise could not.

In a recent development, certain microbes consume methane before the gas can enter the plant and escape through its leaves. Others break down organic matter in the mud and could reduce how much carbon the soil stores.

It has been revealed that the same leak is also valuable to people. Cattails are planted in constructed wetlands that treat wastewater and are used to clean up contaminated soil. Both of these uses rely on the oxygen released by their roots.

In a recent development, cattails and mud were collected by Stein and Cardon from a marsh along the Parker River in northeastern Massachusetts. This marsh forms part of the Plum Island Ecosystems Long Term Ecological Research program.

Each plant was placed in a narrow clear plastic box filled with live mud from the same marsh. The box measured about 15.5 inches tall and 8 inches wide (39 by 20 centimeters).

Recent findings suggest that much of one inside wall was covered with a film containing a dye that responds to oxygen. A camera photographed the film under blue light.

The colors in every image indicated how much oxygen was present in the mud behind the film.

These films were made by hand by Suzanne Thomas, who works as a senior research assistant at MBL.

Images were captured every few minutes over periods that usually lasted two to three days.

Industry observers note that the box itself remained in darkness behind black cloth. Meanwhile, the leaves grew outside under a lamp that was switched on from 5 a.m. to 7 p.m.

It has been revealed that A sensor attached to one leaf collected readings once every minute. It recorded how swiftly the leaf absorbed carbon dioxide and how widely its pores had opened.

The team could therefore compare the activity of the leaves with the oxygen in the mud.

It has been revealed that mud that held no roots also held no oxygen. This changed as soon as part of a cattail grew into it.

Industry observers note that cattails spread by means of horizontal underground stems known as rhizomes. New roots then emerge from these stems.

Recent findings suggest that whenever a new rhizome or root entered a patch of mud, the oxygen level there rose rapidly from zero. It climbed to between 25% and 35% of the amount found in water that is fully saturated with air.

Industry observers note that this oxygen did not persist for long. Around a rhizome, it disappeared after about three days on average. Around a main root, it lasted about four days.

Industry observers note that according to the authors, a seal may be partly responsible. Older sections of a cattail root develop a barrier that is thought to keep oxygen inside. This would allow more of it to reach the growing tip.

Stein and Cardon wrote that this barrier and the steady demand for oxygen in the mud may explain the decline.

In many cases, oxygen returned to the mud a second time. Fine side roots broke through the sealed surface of a main root and oxygen spread through the mud around them.

These later pools of oxygen persisted for about three weeks on average. In one plant, they lasted longer than five weeks.

An earlier study had found that cattail side roots do not develop the barrier that seals a main root.

As a result, a single root released oxygen into the mud on two occasions. The first release lasted a few days near the tip and the second continued for weeks along the sides.

Earlier studies of rice and a salt marsh cordgrass had reported strong control of the leak by day and night. In the cattails, light did have some effect and this was mostly seen around the side roots.

Across three plants, the gap between the highest and lowest oxygen levels of each day averaged about 3% of saturation. No daily pattern could be detected in the fourth plant.

New growth therefore changed oxygen levels far more than the cycle of day and night.

The oxygen in the mud also did not follow the activity of the leaves. It increased during the first two to three hours of light. For the rest of the day, it declined even though the leaves were becoming more active.

After the lights were turned off, the oxygen fell for about two hours. It then rose slowly until the following morning.

In a recent development, mud consumes oxygen swiftly on its own. Oxygen-rich water was injected into mud that held no roots. The oxygen was gone within about an hour and a half.

The roots must therefore have continued to release oxygen in the dark.

The authors wrote that it remains unclear how cattails achieve this without exhausting the oxygen in their own air spaces.

One explanation they proposed is that the leaf pores did not close completely at night. Air could then have continued to enter the plant.

Methane, soil carbon, and microbes were not examined in the study.

It has been revealed that the study also followed just four plants of a single species. None of them was kept in its box for more than two months.

If growth is what controls the oxygen, then the next question is when cattails grow underground.

Stein is a postdoctoral researcher in Cardon’s lab. She noted the results turned the team’s attention to the timing of root growth across the year.

Earlier field data and models suggest that cattail rhizomes gain the most mass in mid to late summer. This follows the expansion of the leaves.

The authors wrote that oxygen from latest rhizomes and their roots may be especially intense during that period.

Methane is released by wetlands naturally and oxygen around roots can reduce it.

“Natural greenhouse gas emissions have been happening forever,” mentioned Cardon, a senior scientist at MBL.

She noted the team hopes to identify natural processes that could act as levers on those emissions.

The cattails were not followed through a complete growing season or observed in a marsh. The authors wrote that understanding when rhizomes and roots grow through the year should become a priority.

In their view, such knowledge is needed to understand the chemistry of marshes where cattails dominate.

The full study was published in the journal Newly introduced Phytologist.

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1471 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Earth ↗ Open Full Page

Breaking: Fatal cases of Ebola often share a striking pattern

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1471 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Ebola may trap immune messages inside infected cells, keeping the body's defenses active longer and potentially worsening illness.
  • A deadly virus such as Ebola might be expected to kill by shutting down the body’s defenses.
  • Ebola virus does make proteins that block a key signal the body uses to fight infection.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Ebola may trap immune messages inside infected cells, keeping the body's defenses active longer and potentially worsening illness.

A deadly virus such as Ebola might be expected to kill by shutting down the body’s defenses.

Ebola virus does make proteins that block a key signal the body uses to fight infection. The pattern in patients, however, is the opposite.

People who die from Ebola often show the highest activity in the genes that fight viruses.

Scientists have struggled to explain this for years.

Sources indicate that A latest study points to the tiny droplets of protein and RNA that Ebola virus builds inside infected cells. These droplets are known as viral condensates, and the cell’s own immune messages become trapped inside them.

Once trapped, the messages are not broken down when they should be.

The defense therefore remains switched on. That prolonged response may be part of what makes patients so ill.

The findings come during a major outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo.

As of November 17, the CDC reported 11,613 confirmed cases and 5,678 confirmed deaths in the Democratic Republic of the Congo.

The outbreak involves Bundibugyo virus, a close relative of the virus studied here.

Seven genes is all Ebola virus carries.

Two of them make proteins called NP and VP35. Both attach to viral RNA and to each other, gathering into droplets that have no outer membrane.

During an infection they can take up between one-fifth and one-third of a cell.

Jingru Fang led the work in the Saphire Lab at the La Jolla Institute for Immunology. Fang now works at Princeton University’s Omenn-Darling Bioengineering Institute.

“When birds land in a upcoming place, they make nests where they can raise their babies,” said Fang.

“You can imagine viral condensates as nests for a virus.”.

According to recent reports, to study the droplets, NP and VP35 were introduced into human kidney cells. The actual virus was left out, and the droplets still formed.

Recent findings suggest that the messenger RNA in those cells was then stained. Messenger RNA carries the instructions a cell uses to make a protein.

Messenger RNA was more concentrated inside the droplets than in the surrounding cell fluid.

It has been revealed that in human cells, the buildup came to roughly 40%. Kidney cells from Egyptian fruit bats revealed an even greater buildup.

When NP was changed so that it could no longer attach to single-stranded RNA, that buildup fell by about half.

According to recent reports, A similar change to VP35 had little effect in human cells. NP appears to play the bigger role in collecting RNA.

That figure covers every message at once, and claims nothing about which ones are collected.

The team therefore used a method capable of reading thousands of RNA types at once, across 136 genes linked to Ebola infection and the immune response.

Sources indicate that about 90,000 cells were examined, with droplets found in roughly 30% of them. Of the 66 genes measured reliably, all but two were more concentrated inside.

In a recent development, the amount of RNA made little difference. Rare messages collected inside while far more common ones stayed out, indicating that something other than abundance determined where they ended up.

Shape proved to be the better explanation.

It has been revealed that RNA is not always a straight strand. Parts of it join together wherever the letters match, folding the molecule into loops and stems.

Messages with fewer folds in their protein-making sections entered more readily.

Recent findings suggest that to test this, the genetic instructions in some messages were rewritten. The new versions made the same protein but folded differently, and those with fewer folds entered more readily.

Sources indicate that ten viruses that carry negative-strand RNA were also examined, including Ebola, measles, rabies and Marburg. In all of them the protein-making regions had fewer folds than the human messages left outside.

The most striking finding concerned interferon. Type I interferon, released when a cell detects a virus, switches on hundreds of defense genes in nearby cells.

After the cells were treated with interferon, the droplets started collecting different messages.

Messages from more than 20 defense genes appeared in droplets.

The rule governing entry also changed. The protein-making section was no longer the best indicator.

Instead the tail of each message mattered more, the stretch that follows the instructions for making a protein.

Immune defense messages often have long, tightly folded tails.

The more folded the tail, the more of that message was found inside. Interferon also increases proteins that attach to RNA, and some of these may help pull immune messages into the droplets.

Recent findings suggest that people who die from Ebola often show stronger activity in their defense genes than those who survive. Even people who recover can show signs of inflammation-related gene activity years later.

Erica Ollmann Saphire, who led the study with Fang, is the president and chief executive of the La Jolla Institute for Immunology.

“These are strong immune responses, but they’re not working well,” remarked Ollmann Saphire.

Recent findings suggest that cells normally break down messenger RNA once it has served its purpose. Enzymes such as XRN1 help carry out that cleanup.

Staining showed less XRN1 inside the droplets than in the surrounding cell fluid.

This raised a further question: whether messages trapped inside survive longer because the enzymes cannot reach them.

Messages held in the droplets broke down more slowly than the same messages in cells carrying a modified NP that could not bind RNA. Messages that stayed outside broke down at similar rates in both groups.

“The antiviral response is like a weapon, and cells use degradation as a way to deactivate that weapon,” Fang explained.

It has been revealed that protein production also changed. A protein the cell requires in order to start building other proteins was largely missing from the droplets.

Without interferon, more messenger RNA collected inside but less protein came out of it.

With interferon, both rose: one defense message increased more than sixfold, and levels of two defense proteins rose alongside it.

A final experiment used a weakened Ebola virus, one lacking a gene needed for replication.

A defense message called IFIT3 was found inside the droplets of those infected cells as well.

Bats can carry filoviruses without getting sick. These viruses belong to the same family as Ebola.

Recent findings suggest that bat genes cannot be read with tools designed for human RNA. Computer models were therefore used to predict how 45 of the collected messages would fold, in bats, ferrets and macaques.

Ferrets and macaques can become seriously ill from Ebola, which makes them useful comparisons.

It has been revealed that within the defense genes, the bat versions had tails that were less tightly folded than the human ones. Ferret and macaque tails were much more like those in humans.

Genes outside the defense group indicated no meaningful difference between species.

Fever often comes with an interferon response, so the predictions were repeated at 102 degrees Fahrenheit (39 degrees Celsius).

Industry observers note that messages carrying bat tails then behaved as the folding had predicted. The least folded bat tail kept its message out of the droplets better than the matching human tail.

Bat immune messages may therefore be less likely to become trapped. If they remain outside, cells can break them down at the usual time.

According to recent reports, most experiments used kidney cells grown in a laboratory. The process was not tested in human patients or living animals, and for much of the work NP and VP35 stood in for the complete virus.

The cells were measured at just one point, 24 hours after the proteins were introduced, across 136 genes out of roughly 20,000.

The human kidney cells responded poorly to interferon. Higher concentrations were therefore used for longer periods than other tissues might need.

In a recent development, the RNA folding patterns were computer predictions. They cannot fully show how every RNA molecule behaves inside a living cell.

Recent findings suggest that the bat comparison included only one species. It was chosen partly because scientists have not yet identified Ebola virus’s natural host.

“We don’t know whether this difference can explain everything, but it gives researchers a place to start looking and confirm what we’ve found in additional human or animal samples,” Fang added.

It has been revealed that breaking the droplets apart may be worth pursuing as a treatment, the authors wrote. It could slow the virus and prevent immune messages from remaining active too long.

The principal challenge is achieving that inside living cells without destroying the cells.

The full study was published in the journal Cell.

#7490. Cracks in public health grew in 2026

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 16m • 📚 Deep Dive (3185 w)

Cracks in public health grew in 2026

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 16 min read (3185 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencenews

⏱️ ~16 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that this is a human-written story voiced by AI.
  • It’s tough to tally the injuries or deaths that don’t happen thanks to seat belts, lead testing, smoking bans and vaccines.
  • But when disaster strikes — say, an outbreak or a pandemic — people take notice.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that this is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .).

Public health is invisible — until it’s not.

It’s tough to tally the injuries or deaths that don’t happen thanks to seat belts, lead testing, smoking bans and vaccines. “It is the invisibility paradox,” notes Georges Benjamin, CEO of the American Public Health Association in Washington, D.C. “We are invisible because when our best work is done, nothing happens.”.

But when disaster strikes — say, an outbreak or a pandemic — people take notice. This year’s outbreaks of measles, Ebola, hantavirus and cyclosporiasis brought recent federal reductions into focus — and exposed cracks in a system that aims to keep people healthy. For years, that system functioned “reasonably well” despite chronic underfunding, Benjamin says. “But since the Trump administration has come on board, they have really made the system at all levels much more dysfunctional.”.

In 2025, the second Trump administration instituted sweeping federal funding cuts and layoffs, dismantled the global health–focused U.S. Agency for International Development and withdrew the United States from the World Health Organization. Officials reversed some of those changes in the wake of lawsuits and public backlash. But the damage persists.

In a recent development, two stalwarts of U.S. public health — the Food and Drug Administration and the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention — have lost between 20 and 30 percent of their staff, due largely to layoffs and early retirements. They have had to scale back, pause or cancel crucial disease-tracking programs at home and abroad. Some CDC divisions don’t have enough staff to function. And both agencies have cut funding to the local governments and nonprofits that shoulder much of the nation’s public health work.

Combined with deep cuts to international aid, that has stymied efforts to contain infectious disease outbreaks around the world, with Ebola in particular going undetected for months, public health experts say.

Domestically, 2026 saw a record-breaking measles outbreak, with some 5,412 confirmed cases as of November 12. That’s more than double last year’s count, and it is the highest number of annual cases since 1991. In mid November, the Pan American Health Organization determined that measles is again endemic to the United States and has stripped the country of its elimination status.

Against a backdrop of shifting federal vaccine guidance, fewer children are receiving the MMR shot that prevents measles. Roughly 92 percent of kindergartners across the United States had gotten the vaccine in the 2025–2026 school year, down from 95 percent in the 2019–2020 school year, according to the CDC. At least 95 percent of people in a community need to be vaccinated to prevent the measles virus from sparking an outbreak.

“The fact that we are spending so much time and energy [on measles] when we have a reliable vaccine is very disconcerting,” notes Lori Handy, a pediatric infectious diseases physician and associate director of the Vaccine Education Center at Children’s Hospital of Philadelphia.

The CDC has not responded to Science News requests for an interview.

It has been revealed that such issues do not bode well for the future. Public health is tested during times of crisis, and the world will eventually face another pandemic, says Michael Osterholm, director of the Center for Infectious Disease Research and Policy at the University of Minnesota in Minneapolis. “We’ve not responded [to the 2026 outbreaks] in a way that would give me confidence that the public health system … is prepared for what’s coming down the pike.”.

Recent findings suggest that on the heels of multiple 2025 outbreaks, measles continued to wallop parts of the United States this year. Communities in South Carolina, Utah and Wisconsin have been among the hardest hit, with sporadic outbreaks also popping up in other states. Until August, however, none of this year’s outbreaks had turned deadly. That all changed in Pennsylvania.

About a quarter of this year’s cases stem from an outbreak in central Pennsylvania, where the virus has spread widely in communities with low vaccination rates. Since April, seven people in the state have died, including two infants too young to be vaccinated. The CDC has so far attributed just six deaths to measles, despite the insistence of Pennsylvania state public health officials. Three children died of measles in November in New York and Wisconsin.

As of November 12, U.S. health officials recorded 5,412 measles cases for 2026. The last time this many cases were recorded was 1991, nearly a decade before the disease was eliminated from the country.

According to recent reports, measles spreads like wildfire, and one sick person can infect more than a dozen others in an unvaccinated community. While milder symptoms include fever and a hallmark full-body rash, infection can lead to pneumonia, brain swelling and even death. Statistically, the virus kills one to three out of every 1,000 infected people.

The United States eliminated measles in 2000, thanks to the MMR vaccine. “Elimination” means the virus was not spreading widely, and any outbreaks were controlled within a year. But dropping vaccination rates have reestablished the conditions to sustain multiple outbreaks — and may have done so as early as 2022, researchers reported in August in Nature Medicine.

In the wake of losing measles elimination status in November, beating back the the virus again “will take a true change in the public’s trust of health care,” Handy states. That means figuring out how to get people vaccinated — and to encourage them to work with public health officials on testing and contact tracing after exposure.

During the 2009–2010 school year, 20 states had MMR vaccination rates equal to or above 95 percent among kindergartners. Just 10 states hit that threshold for 2025–2026, and 18 states had vaccination rates below 90 percent.

Sources indicate that it has been more than three decades since measles caused widespread outbreaks in the United States, and many have never experienced the devastation it can cause. When one community hears about an outbreak halfway across the country, “it still feels very foreign,” Handy says. When the threat feels far away, people are not likely to line up to get a vaccine. Yet measles is so contagious that one unvaccinated traveler can bring the virus back home and spark an outbreak in their own community.

Even with the recent spike in cases, there is hope vaccination rates can catch up, says Cornell University epidemiologist Ana Bento. She points to California and Latest York, which experienced outbreaks in 2015 and 2018; they ended non-medical exemptions for school vaccinations shortly thereafter. Both states now have vaccination rates above 95 percent in kindergartners. “This is not a tipping point where there’s no coming back,” Bento says.

If measles exposed the consequences of long-simmering vaccine hesitancy, then this summer’s cyclosporiasis outbreak was a quick lesson in food safety screening.

Industry observers note that in June, Michigan detected its first cases of the foodborne illness. By August 31, contaminated lettuce had caused the largest outbreak of explosive diarrhea ever in the United States, with 12,883 cases reported across 21 states. By the time the CDC declared the outbreak over on September 11, some 570 people had been hospitalized and two had died. Another 8,113 cyclosporiasis infections have not been traced back to any source. “[This] was one of those events where you felt like the cracks highlighted,” Handy says.

According to recent reports, but it isn’t easy to track the origins of foodborne illness. Typically, local and state public health officials report cases to the CDC — and investigate the outbreak, with the agency lending support as needed. If patient interviews reveal the culprit to be produce, dairy or packaged food, the CDC contacts the FDA, which identifies the producer and the distribution area — and coordinates recalls. The FDA also conducts on-the-ground investigations at the farms and processing facilities that supplied the food.

Recent findings suggest that it can take weeks to identify which contaminated foods are behind a foodborne illness outbreak. Each outbreak is different and timing can depend on the pathogen, laboratory evidence and availability of records, an FDA spokesperson told Science News. After Michigan health officials notified CDC that something was amiss on June 25, it was another 21 days before federal officials announced a possible culprit: shredded lettuce ultimately traced to a Taylor Farms processing facility in Mexico.

Of more than 20,000 cyclosporiasis cases reported this year, nearly 13,000 occurred across 21 states, with the preponderance of them in the Midwest.

The FDA aims to complete investigations as soon as possible. But delays in agency reporting early in the investigation led to unnecessary confusion about which foods to avoid in which states, said Sarah Sorscher, director of regulatory affairs at the Washington, D.C.–based Center for Science in the Public Interest, at a July 16 news briefing. “It’s a perfect storm for viral news. A lot of people have been posting on social media about avoiding fruits and vegetables, which is not good public health messaging.”.

In a recent development, sorscher applauded the dedication of public servants working to contain the outbreak. But she noted they were working with inadequate support. “These programs are completely overwhelmed by the scale and scope of the work of solving and communicating these novel emerging outbreaks with a dwindling set of resources.”.

Due in part to funding squeezes, in 2025 the CDC stopped mandatory surveillance of six foodborne pathogens, including the single-celled parasite that causes cyclosporiasis, Cyclospora. Speaking at the July 16 news briefing, epidemiologist Barbara Kowalcyk of George Washington University’s Institute for Food Safety and Nutrition Security in Washington, D.C., noted that half of CDC’s food safety budget goes to states to support surveillance and other programs. Yet that budget has remained flat for nearly a decade.

It has been revealed that FDA investigations have also been impacted, with foreign food inspections at historical lows. In the case of cyclosporiasis, delays gathering testing supplies and getting clearance from the Mexican government meant it took nearly a month for FDA investigators to arrive in Mexico once the source of the outbreak was identified, according to the New York Times. Once there, inspectors found the parasite in a wastewater tank at a Taylor Farms processing plant — and in a drainage ditch at a farm that supplied the lettuce. Since Cyclospora infects only humans, the probable contaminant was sewage from a source that has yet to be identified.

Recent findings suggest that without knowing the source of the contamination, it’s hard to know how to stop the parasite from reaching produce in the future, notes Francisco Diez-Gonzalez, a food microbiologist at the University of Georgia in Athens. “It leaves us with the feeling that we most likely are going to have something similar next year.”.

Starting in 2027, FDA plans to increase surveillance of produce historically associated with Cyclospora and boost laboratory capacity in Mexico to speed up investigations.

Outbreaks of other foodborne pathogens — including Salmonella, Listeria and E. coli — have popped up this year, but not at a rate that’s out of the ordinary, says Diez-Gonzalez, who served on the U.S. National Advisory Committee on Microbiological Criteria for Foods before the Trump administration disbanded it in 2025. That suggests the sky isn’t falling, though he and others are concerned about our future ability to swiftly contain outbreaks.

Industry observers note that “We may see [fewer] cases, but it’s not that they are disappearing,” Diez-Gonzalez says. “We will not be able to detect them because we don’t have the resources.”.

Industry observers note that when the WHO announced in May that an Ebola outbreak had erupted in the Democratic Republic of Congo, the virus had been simmering for months. People in the mining town of Mongbwalu, where the outbreak was first detected, began falling ill in January or earlier, according to reporting from Science. Armed conflict in the region has made the outbreak response difficult, says the WHO, and some aid workers and health facilities have been attacked.

Confirmed Ebola cases as of November 15, 2026. To date, 5,593 people have died, and 3,109 have recovered.

In a recent development, as cases and death counts soared in May, health officials scrambled to test a backlog of patient samples for Bundibugyo virus, the species behind what has become the fastest-growing Ebola outbreak ever recorded. As of November 15, there were 11,432 confirmed cases and 5,593 deaths. Roughly 3,109 people have recovered. Cases have also been detected in France, Uganda, Kenya and Nigeria.

Before the outbreak, the United States significantly scaled back international aid that once flowed from USAID and the CDC. Such cuts may have hampered Ebola monitoring before the outbreak was declared — and affected infection control measures such as contact tracing, says infectious disease physician Krutika Kuppalli of UT Southwestern Medical Center in Dallas.

Kuppalli led an Ebola treatment unit in Sierra Leone during the 2014–2016 outbreak, the largest ever recorded. At the time, the CDC sent 1,450 physicians, epidemiologists and other experts to help out in affected areas. So far around 500 CDC employees stationed in the United States and abroad have responded to the current outbreak.

According to recent reports, by September, the U.S. State Department pledged $887 million toward the purchase of personal protective equipment and the building of new Ebola treatment units. That’s roughly a third of the total amount sent during the 2014–2016 outbreak. Still, earlier investments in public health could have saved lives and helped minimize transmission, Kuppalli indicates.

Information-sharing has also been a huge problem, Kuppalli says. Prior to the second Trump administration, U.S. health officials were in constant contact with WHO teams that shared information about cases and contact-tracing efforts. After the United States withdrew from the WHO in January 2025, CDC officials had to coordinate with other groups such as UNICEF, the United Nations Children’s Fund.

Nevertheless, there has been some progress toward developing treatments and vaccines. Researchers in Congo are testing whether antivirals and engineered antibodies can stave off severe disease and death in people infected with Bundibugyo virus, and whether those treatments can protect people after exposure. In October, a large clinical trial began testing a vaccine that is already approved against the species that caused the 2014–2016 outbreak. Kuppalli and colleagues argued in September in the Lancet Infectious Diseases that the vaccine’s potential for cross-protection merited its use in high-risk situations.

Two Bundibugyo-specific vaccines are poised to join the new trial after early evidence in animals and people demonstrated the shots are safe — and suggested they may be protective.

Conditions have improved in some parts of Congo, according to the WHO. But there are still hundreds of latest cases per week, and other countries should be prepared to respond swiftly if the virus crosses borders. “The longer this outbreak continues, the more opportunities the virus has to reach new communities,” Kuppalli states.

The M.V. Hondius was in for a rough voyage the moment it set off from Ushuaia, Argentina, on April 1. A passenger on the small ship had contracted Andes hantavirus, a rodent-borne disease that can cause severe respiratory illness and death. By the time the outbreak was contained, 13 people were infected and three people had died. Public health experts say a lagging U.S. response let other countries take the lead — and suggests the country is not prepared for future epidemics.

It’s unclear how the first patient, who died on April 11, was infected. Another patient died on the ship, and a third — who was allowed to board a plane — died in South Africa.

More than 300 high-risk contacts, including people who spent more than 15 minutes with an infected individual, were quarantined and monitored across 33 countries and territories. None of them got sick. Nor did another 336 low-risk contacts who had brief encounters with someone who fell ill, and who monitored themselves for symptoms.

The United States’ severed relationship with the WHO “in many ways hampered the [country’s] hantavirus outbreak response,” claims Benjamin, of the American Public Health Association. Before 2025, U.S. experts frequently received information about emerging health threats from the organization. But confusion over who government officials could talk to likely resulted in knowledge gaps and communication delays, Benjamin says. “CDC was not engaged as early on as they needed to be on that outbreak.”.

Instead, other countries including Spain, South Africa, Argentina and Chile played leading roles. After scientists in South Africa determined that Andes hantavirus was behind the outbreak on May 2, passengers disembarked in mid-May in Tenerife, Spain, where health officials screened for symptoms and helped people travel home.

“Outbreak response depends on the knowledge and the relationships that already exist.”.

The CDC didn’t set up a response team until after May 2, according to the Newly introduced York Times. And controversy erupted over uneven U.S. quarantine practices, with some people forced to remain for weeks in quarantine units in Omaha, Neb., while others remained at home. “There was nothing standard” about the protocols, Osterholm says. “Almost everybody got a different approach.”.

Industry observers note that the outbreak, which ended July 2, was promptly contained in part because Andes hantavirus isn’t very contagious. Of more than 50 known hantaviruses, Andes hantavirus is the only one known to spread from person to person. Although some rare superspreaders transmit the virus to others through casual contact, transmission typically happens through close contact, such as spending long periods of time together or kissing. It would have been harder to stop a pathogen that spreads easily through the air, Osterholm indicates. “By the time that they recognized what was going on, transmission would have already occurred.”.

Recent findings suggest that the international collaboration had some successes, says virologist Gustavo Palacios of the Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai in Fresh York City. Experts in South Africa “kept digging when everything was negative,” he says, until they finally identified Andes hantavirus as the cause.

In a recent development, hantavirus infections are also relatively rare in the Americas, for now. Studies suggest climate change will increase the likelihood that hantaviruses — and other zoonotic illnesses like Ebola — will make the jump from animals to humans. Dense cities can make it easier for diseases to spread. And such threats don’t disappear when funding for studying them dries up.

Sources indicate that “The strongest lesson [from the M.V. Hondius] is that outbreak response depends on the knowledge and the relationships that already exist before the event,” Palacios says. Of the billions of viruses on Earth, just a few hundred pose threats to people. With enough resources, researchers can work together to learn as much as possible about those pathogens and be better prepared when a fresh one emerges — just as previous work on coronaviruses made the rollout of COVID-19 vaccines possible within a year of the pandemic’s start.

“We will not always know in advance which [pathogens] will become important,” Palacios says. But by not tracking rare threats that could one day become larger problems, “we are shooting ourselves in the foot.”.
